title: Supply Chain Executive Appointments in November 2026
content:
Supply Chain Executive Appointments in November 2026
Prioritise Us
on Google
Francois Lacombe has taken on the role of President of Danone USA
Leadership appointments across the supply chain industry this month includes moves within Danone, ADM, FedEX and Accenture
Francois Lacombe, Danone
Francois has spent his almost 30-year career at Danone working in various countries around the world, including Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and Amsterdam. Now, he is returning to the US as President of Danone USA. He will be bringing his rich career experience of operating with trusted brands and innovative strategies in order to lead the US branch of the company.
I’m ready to hit the ground running alongside our U.S. teams, to listen and learn from our consumers and customers, and to keep growing a business that can make a real difference to people’s health.
Francois Lacombe, President of Danone USA
Ian A. Arroyo, Accenture
Ian A. Arroyo, Managing Director at Accenture
For more than 20 years, Ian has worked within global logistics, technology and corporate growth leading strategy. In his roles, he has helped enterprise leaders as they scale and unlock measurable operating outcomes through complex strategies. In his new role at Accenture, Ian is leading Logistics, Transportation & Fulfillment (LTF) transformation, partnering with C-suite and senior supply chain leaders to scale next-generation supply chain networks.
I’m happy to share that I’m starting a new position as Managing Director, Logistics, Transportation, and Fulfillment at Accenture!
Ian A. Arroyo, Managing Director at Accenture
Jamere Jackson, FedEx
Jamere Jackson will be joining FedEx on November 30.
Jamere Jackson will be starting his new role at FedEx, joining the company as EVP and CFO, effective November 30. Throughout his career, he has used strong financial management and precise capital allocation in order to develop business growth. Upon joining the global logistics company, Jamere will be working to support FedEx's profitable growth strategy and deliver long-term value.
I am pleased to welcome Jamere to FedEx and the executive leadership team. Jamere brings a deep understanding of how disciplined financial strategy translates into strong operational performance.
Raj Subramaniam, President and Chief Executive Officer of FedEx Corporation
Ralf Finzel, ADM
Ralf Finzel is joining ADM in a new career move
Ralf Finzel has joined ADM, a global agricultural supply chain manager and processer, empowering across beverages, biofuels, home care and pet treats. Ralf is joining from his four-year career at IFF, and brings more than 23 years of experience working within the supply chain at Honeywell. In his new role, he is leading the nutrition team and working to strengthen ADM's end-to-end supply chain capabilities.
I am honored to be part of the Nutrition leadership team and look forward to working with colleagues across the global business to strengthen our end-to-end supply chain capabilities, support growth, and create value for our customers and stakeholders.
Ralf Finzel, President, Nutrition E2E Supply Chain at ADM

title: Rio Tinto expands lithium production in Argentina - electrive.com
content:
Mining giant Rio Tinto has commissioned two additional lithium projects in Argentina. The 'Fénix-1B' expansion and the 'Sal-de-Vida' plant in Catamarca province are now ramping up. At full capacity, they are expected to achieve a combined annual production capacity of 25,000 tons of lithium carbonate equivalent.
Image: Rio Tinto
Rio Tinto has announced the official opening of expansion project ‘Fénix 1B’ and the ‘Sal de Vida’ lithium operation in the province of Catamarca. According to the British-Australian mining giant, it has invested a total of around US$1.4 billion (approx. €1.25 billion euros) in the two projects. Production at both sites reportedly began ahead of schedule in the second quarter of 2026, as stated in an accompanying release. The projects are intended to strengthen “Rio Tinto’s standing and Argentina’s position as a leading supplier of lithium for global markets.”
Background: ‘Fénix’ is considered Argentina’s first commercial lithium operation and began production in 1997. The ‘Fénix 1B’ expansion is said to have increased the annual capacity of the existing facility by 10,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE), bringing the total on-site capacity to around 40,000 tonnes. ‘Sal de Vida’, on the other hand, is a completely new lithium carbonate operation located approx. 20 km northeast of ‘Fénix’, with a targeted annual capacity of 15,000 tonnes. Both sites are located in Catamarca, a province in northwest Argentina. Rio Tinto also operates or plans additional lithium projects in the Argentine provinces of Jujuy and Salta, including the flagship lithium project ‘Rincón’, which is expected to have a long-term capacity of 60,000 tonnes per year. Commercial operations there are set to begin in 2028.
Commenting on the launch of the two operations in Catamarca, Simon Trott, CEO of Rio Tinto, said: “Today is a proud moment for Rio Tinto and an important milestone for Argentina’s lithium industry, as we grow our position as a leading global supplier. […] These two projects build on nearly three decades of lithium production in Catamarca and the expertise of our Argentine workforce. They demonstrate our industry-leading project delivery capability, as we execute with discipline towards our global target of 200,000 tonnes lithium carbonate equivalent annual production capacity by 2028.”
Rio Tinto has also long had an interest in developing a lithium project in Europe – namely, in Serbia.
However, the company pulled away from the so-called Jadar project at the end of last year
and stated that it would prioritise other ‘short-term opportunities’. The pause on the project in Serbia, which was still in the permitting phase, was one of several measures taken by Simon Trott, who was appointed CEO of Rio Tinto in August 2025, to rationalise operations and reduce costs. One of his first decisions was also to reorganise Rio Tinto into three business units: iron ore, aluminium combined with lithium, and copper.
In general, Rio Tinto has made significant investments recently, including earlier this year
in the Canadian company Nemaska Lithium
. Rio Tinto also incurred substantial costs in 2024 for the
acquisition of lithium producer Arcadium
in a US$6.7 billion deal. This was also because the mining company announced plans to massively invest in its first proprietary lithium mining site in Argentina to expand its battery materials offering.
In recent years, Rio Tinto has pursued the goal of establishing lithium not only as a fourth pillar alongside iron ore, aluminium, and copper mining but also of becoming one of the world’s largest lithium producers. The geographical focus is on Argentina. However, it remains unclear to what extent Rio Tinto will continue to invest so heavily in its lithium business during times of increasing rationalisation.

title: EDENenergy builds storage systems from used e-scooter batteries - electrive.com
content:
Freiburg-based startup EDENenergy is developing stationary commercial energy storage systems from used e-scooter and e-bike batteries. The first storage system with 70 kWh capacity has already been delivered. In the future, different battery types could also be integrated.
The first tested used batteries still showed more than 90 percent of their original capacity.
Image: EDENenergy
EDENenergy, a start-up spun off from the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, aims to give used batteries from micromobility a second life. To achieve this, the Freiburg-based company is developing modular energy storage systems for commercial and industrial customers. In mid-October, the first storage system, with a capacity of 70 kWh, was delivered to a customer.
The system integrates 112 used e-scooter batteries connected in series. Before deployment, the batteries are tested for their technical condition. According to the company, the initial results exceeded expectations: among around 350 batteries examined, the remaining capacity was partially well above 90 per cent. Originally, EDENenergy had calculated with a State of Health of 80 per cent.
The technical foundation is power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE. This technology enables the combination of batteries with different form factors and varying battery management systems into a single stationary storage system, without the need to disassemble individual batteries. However, EDENenergy currently relies primarily on larger suppliers, such as e-scooter and e-bike fleet operators, to obtain sufficient batteries of the same type.
EDENenergy plans storage systems with up to 300 kWh
One advantage of the modular concept is the replaceability of the batteries. EDENenergy monitors the individual modules remotely and can replace them during operation if necessary. This approach is intended to maintain the storage capacity at a constant level over the long term. The company expects to still provide the original 70 kWh even after ten years. Batteries that are no longer usable are subsequently sent for recycling.
Initially, the offering targets small and medium-sized enterprises with their own photovoltaic systems that wish to increase self-consumption or reduce peak loads. EDENenergy also sees potential applications for municipal utilities and electricity trading. In the long term, the start-up aims to expand its storage systems to capacities of up to 300 kWh.
A challenge remains the diversity of available batteries. For each new battery type, connectors, battery management, and communication protocols must be adapted. In the long run, EDENenergy therefore considers uniform communication standards and clear legal frameworks essential for the stationary reuse of mobile batteries.
Other companies are also working on repurposing used batteries from micromobility. For example, in 2025, e-scooter rental provider Lime and US battery recycler Redwood Materials
agreed to cooperate on battery recycling in Germany, the Netherlands, and the USA
. While this initiative aims to recover valuable raw materials for new batteries, EDENenergy initially focuses on reusing functional batteries in stationary storage systems before they are sent for recycling.
For further development, the company is seeking additional pilot customers from the regional commercial sector. Through the Baden-Württemberg funding programme “Mittelstand trifft Start-ups”, corresponding projects can reportedly receive 50 per cent funding. EDENenergy also receives support from the Sustainability Performance Centre and the BW Pre-Seed programme. The first investor is JobRad founder Ulrich Prediger.

title: Japan's lead recyclers face scrap shortage as competition drives prices higher – Batteries International
content: Competition for used batteries is intensifying across Japan, pushing up scrap prices and putting pressure on recyclers. Meanwhile, the country’s lead battery manufacturers are facing higher costs and an uncertain long-term market. Japan’s secondary lead industry is facing growing competition for used automotive batteries, with shortages of recyclable material pushing scrap prices higher despite uncertainty over the longer-term outlook for lead battery demand. According to the Japanese metals newspaper Japan Metal Daily , prices for spent automotive lead batteries reached ¥115–¥120 ($0.75–0.80) per kilogram in early September, compared with ¥100–110 during the first half of 2026. On October 2, Nikkan Sangyo Shimbun , a daily Japanese newspaper,  reported that spent automotive lead-acid battery prices had reached approximately ¥115/kg, close to their highest level of the year. The paper attributed this to reduced battery replacement and vehicle-scrapping volumes, together with stronger competition among collectors. On October 10 a Kyoto scrap buyer was reported by ScraPrice, an international online platform that tracks and compares scrap metal prices, as paying ¥123/kg for automotive lead-acid batteries. Japan Metal Daily attributed the overall increase to competition among collectors and recyclers for limited supplies of scrap. Even the winter replacement season, traditionally an important source of spent automotive batteries, failed to generate the volumes dealers had expected. The shortage reflects changes taking place across Japan’s lead industry. Domestic recyclers are competing with new entrants, including Chinese secondary lead companies, while primary smelters are increasingly turning to recycled material as supplies of lead concentrates become more difficult to secure. Industry presentations suggest that two or three Chinese-backed secondary lead operations are already active in Japan. Although the number of established Japanese recyclers has remained relatively stable, the additional competition is increasing pressure on scrap collection networks. Japan’s dependence on imported raw materials complicates this further. In 2024, the country imported almost 120,000 tonnes of lead ores and concentrates, worth approximately $314 million, principally from Australia, Mexico, Bolivia, the US and Peru. Meanwhile, battery manufacturers are confronting their own cost pressures. In June, GS Yuasa announced price increases of at least 20% across its replacement automotive, motorcycle and cycle-service lead battery ranges, effective from August. The company cited higher raw material, energy, logistics and labour costs, together with continuing uncertainty over international procurement The broader market remains substantial. GS Yuasa, Energywith and Furukawa Battery are Japan’s three principal domestic lead battery manufacturers, although industry observers expect production to consolidate over time. Electrification and Japan’s ageing population present longer-term challenges, but the replacement battery market remains resilient. GS Yuasa forecasts Japanese lead battery sales of ¥117 billion for fiscal 2026, up from ¥108 billion the previous year, although the increase reflects revenue rather than necessarily higher battery volumes. The company is also developing auxiliary lead batteries for hybrid and electric vehicles, where dependable low-voltage power remains essential. For recyclers, the immediate concern is less about disappearing demand than obtaining sufficient scrap to meet it. Japan’s experience illustrates how a mature battery market can face tightening raw material supplies even as its long-term growth prospects diminish. Japanese automotive trade reporting identifies increases of at least 10% from Furukawa Battery and Energywith (which took over the battery operations of Showa Denko Materials in December 2021), and approximately 10% from Panasonic Automotive Systems in 2026. title: China’s Addimaster plans 30,000-tonne battery additive plant as exports rise – Batteries International
content: Guangzhou Addimaster Chemicals is expanding production capacity for lead battery additives as Chinese battery exports increase and domestic manufacturers report differences in demand between automotive and e-bike markets. Chinese battery additive manufacturer Guangzhou Addimaster Chemicals announced on October 19 that it is building a factory in Shaoguan with planned first-phase production capacity of 30,000 tonnes of battery additives, including tetrabasic lead sulphate (4BS), lignin, graphene and other carbon materials. The company disclosed the expansion in material published by Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) ahead of its Global Lead-Acid Battery Supply Chain Industry Conference in Ho Chi Minh City. Addimaster, founded in 2011, already reports annual production capacity of 15,000 tonnes of battery additives. The Shaoguan development could therefore increase its stated capacity to 45,000 tonnes a year if the new plant’s first phase is additional to existing operations and reaches its planned output. The company has not disclosed the investment required, a commissioning date or the proportion of the proposed capacity allocated to individual additives. The expansion comes as Chinese lead battery manufacturers report an increase in exports despite pressure on production costs and margins. According to SMM figures published on October 21, China exported 20.66 million lead-acid batteries in September, an increase of 20.92% compared with the same month in 2025. The figures suggest that overseas demand is supporting Chinese manufacturers at a time when domestic consumption is showing differences between automotive and electric bicycle applications. SMM reported that manufacturers were seeking to maintain export orders despite Chinese lead prices remaining high relative to international benchmarks, putting pressure on profitability. Higher domestic lead costs can affect the competitiveness of exported batteries, particularly where overseas customers negotiate prices against manufacturers operating in markets with lower raw material costs. Export volumes alone do not establish whether manufacturers are increasing profits. The value of sales, battery mix, raw material expenditure and transport costs also affect the returns earned on overseas orders. Within China, battery factory operating rates continued to increase during October. SMM reported on October 23 that the average operating rate among lead-acid battery manufacturers surveyed across five provinces reached 74.16% during October 16–22, an increase of 0.79 percentage points from the preceding week. The increase was attributed to automotive battery manufacturers raising production ahead of the fourth-quarter replacement season. However, the electric bicycle battery market was approaching the end of its seasonal demand period, with some manufacturers reporting a decline in orders. SMM said production had not yet undergone major adjustments but warned that manufacturers could reduce November output plans if e-bike orders continued to weaken. The figures point to differences within China’s lead battery market, where automotive replacement demand, electric bicycle sales, industrial applications and exports follow separate demand cycles. For additive suppliers such as Addimaster, the investment in production capacity reflects the role of materials technology in battery manufacturing as producers seek improvements in performance and production efficiency. The company supplies negative electrode expanders, 4BS seed materials and sodium lignosulphonate for batteries used in starting, start-stop, traction, energy storage and backup power applications. Its proposed Shaoguan factory will also produce graphene and other carbon materials, reflecting interest in additives that can improve charge acceptance and cycle life, particularly in batteries operating at partial states of charge. Carbon additives are used in negative active materials to improve conductivity and address problems associated with sulphation. Their performance depends on the type of carbon, its surface characteristics, concentration and interaction with other components of the electrode formulation. The 4BS process addresses a different part of battery manufacture. Tetrabasic lead sulphate is used in positive plate production, where control of crystal formation and curing conditions can influence plate structure, battery life and manufacturing consistency. Addimaster has developed its business around these technologies and operates a 2,000m² research and development centre in Guangzhou employing 50 technical personnel, including five PhD holders and 20 staff with master’s degrees. The centre carries out materials analysis and testing using equipment including X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy. The planned expansion would increase Addimaster’s capacity to supply manufacturers developing lead batteries for applications requiring higher cycle life, charge acceptance and performance under demanding operating conditions. However, the timing of the investment also raises questions about how much additional additive capacity China’s battery industry will require. Although exports increased in September and automotive battery manufacturers are raising production, weakening e-bike orders could affect domestic battery output during the final months of the year. Additive demand will also depend on the extent to which battery manufacturers adopt graphene, carbon formulations and 4BS-based production processes, rather than relying on existing materials and manufacturing methods. Addimaster has not disclosed customer commitments for the Shaoguan plant or indicated how much of its planned production will be sold within China and how much will be exported. The company’s expansion nevertheless comes at a time when Chinese lead battery manufacturers are seeking to defend export markets while managing raw material costs and changes in domestic demand. Whether the proposed 30,000 tonnes of additional capacity can be absorbed will depend on battery production volumes, the adoption of new additives and Addimaster’s ability to secure customers at home and overseas. title: Global lead surplus set to almost double in 2027 as Chinese demand falters – Batteries International
content: The latest forecasts from the International Lead and Zinc Study Group show a growing oversupply of lead, rising inventories and continued pressure on the metal’s prices. Meanwhile, India is emerging as a major driver of growth in both production and consumption. The global refined lead surplus is forecast to rise from 90,000 tonnes in 2026 to 163,000 tonnes in 2027, as production continues to outpace demand, according to figures presented by the ILZSG at the International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo on Monday. Speaking at the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo on October 26, João Jorge, director of statistics and marketing at the ILZSG, said the market had been well supplied for the past three years, with inventories continuing to accumulate and prices weakening. Global refined lead production is forecast to increase by 1% this year and 1.5% in 2027, compared with expected demand growth of just 0.9% and 1% respectively. The growing imbalance is already reflected in London Metal Exchange inventories, which have reached approximately 340,000 tonnes following a substantial delivery into an LME warehouse in Singapore in July. Lead prices have fallen by 6.8% over the past 12 months, underperforming most other base metals. The average LME price in October has remained below $1,850 a tonne. China and India One of the most significant findings in the ILZSG presentation was the changing geography of lead demand. China, which dominated global growth between 1995 and 2015, is no longer the principal source of rising consumption. Its lead usage is forecast to increase by just 0.2% in 2026 before declining by 0.6% in 2027. The slowdown reflects weaker automotive production, falling net exports of lead batteries and the continuing shift from conventional combustion engine vehicles towards new energy vehicles. However, several sectors are helping to maintain Chinese lead consumption. Investment in artificial intelligence data centres is supporting demand for uninterruptible power supply batteries, while motorcycles and replacement batteries remain important markets. Electric bicycles represent another substantial source of demand. China has an estimated fleet of more than 300 million e-bikes, approximately 80% of which use lead batteries. According to Shanghai Metals Market forecasts cited by Jorge, lead demand from this sector could increase by an average of 5% annually between 2026 and 2030, potentially adding almost 700,000 tonnes of annual demand by the end of the decade compared with 2025. India is emerging as one of the most important markets for the global lead industry, both as a producer and consumer. Indian lead usage in 2025 was nearly 50% higher than a decade earlier, supported by economic growth, vehicle ownership and a substantial replacement battery market. The country overtook the US in refined lead production in 2021 and is now the world’s largest producer outside China. Much of this expansion has come from secondary smelting, with hundreds of licensed (and presumably informal) recyclers operating across the country. Further growth is expected in 2026, supported by additional capacity at Gravita’s facilities in Gujarat and Rajasthan. On the demand side, India’s expanding fleet of two- and three-wheelers, commercial vehicles and passenger cars is providing a continuing market for lead batteries. Passenger car sales increased by almost 20% in the first half of 2026, while the country’s renewable energy ambitions offer further opportunities for lead batteries in stationary storage. Jorge also highlighted forecasts suggesting that lead demand from India’s electric vehicle sector could grow by an average of as much as 32% annually to 2030, although competition from lithium-ion batteries is increasing. Scrap shortages Recycling now accounts for 68% of global refined lead production, underlining the secondary industry’s importance to the market. There are considerable regional differences. Secondary lead represents 93% of refined production in the Americas and 81% in Europe, compared with just 59% in Asia. Despite substantial investment in secondary smelting capacity, the proportion of refined lead produced from recycled materials has declined from approximately 50% in 2021 to an estimated 44% in 2026. Jorge identified the availability of used lead-acid batteries as the principal constraint. Secondary smelting capacity has expanded faster than scrap supply, intensifying competition for raw materials, increasing costs and squeezing margins. Some Chinese smelters are consequently operating well below their installed capacity. The figures suggest that additional recycling investment alone will not necessarily translate into higher secondary lead output without corresponding improvements in battery collection and scrap availability. Mine production to recover Global lead mine production, which peaked above five million tonnes in 2013, has been on a declining trend for more than a decade. The ILZSG expects another contraction in 2026, followed by a recovery of 2.9% in 2027, driven largely by new Chinese mining capacity. Production increases are also anticipated in Europe, India and Peru, with Australia expected to benefit from the planned commissioning of a new lead-silver operation in the second half of 2027. In questions following his presentation that additional mine capacity would not immediately create an oversupply of lead concentrates. New mines take time to reach full production, while China remains a net importer of concentrates. Non-Asia Outside Asia, the ILZSG expects lead consumption to increase in both Europe and the US during 2026 and 2027. European usage is forecast to rise by 1.3% this year and 0.7% next year, supported by automotive production and replacement battery demand. Although battery electric vehicle sales in Europe increased by 35% in the first half of 2026, vehicles with combustion engines, including hybrids, still represented nearly 80% of Western European passenger car sales. In the US, lead demand is forecast to increase by 2.5% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. Declining net imports of SLI batteries suggest that domestic manufacturers are meeting a greater proportion of US demand. Tariffs could also encourage higher utilisation of domestic smelting capacity. The ILZSG’s overall outlook is therefore one of modest global demand growth, increasingly concentrated outside China, against a background of expanding refined metal production. For the secondary lead industry, the findings point to two distinct challenges: a global market facing persistent oversupply and a recycling sector in which access to spent batteries, rather than processing capacity, is becoming an increasingly important determinant of competitiveness. title: Iranian manufacturer begins commercial production of graphene-enhanced lead battery – Batteries International
content: Iranian battery manufacturer, Platin Iran,  has begun commercial production of a graphene-enhanced lead battery, claiming the technology can increase capacity by more than 60% and significantly extend service life. The development follows four years of research involving Platin Iran, the Graphene and Advanced Materials Laboratory at Amirkabir University of Technology in Tehran and the Institute for Color Science and Technology. The company says its technology uses three-dimensional graphene incorporated into both the positive and negative active materials of conventional lead batteries, improving performance without changing the underlying chemistry. Mehdi Orouji, research and development manager at Platin Iran, said the project began in 2021 and had progressed through laboratory testing and pilot production to industrial manufacturing and commercialisation. “After four years of research and development, the project reached the stages of industrial production and commercialization,” he told Iranian news agency Tasnim. According to Orouji, testing has demonstrated capacity improvements exceeding 60% and service-life gains of at least 10% compared with conventional batteries. The company also claims its batteries could last twice as long as some commercial alternatives, potentially reducing operating costs by as much as 50% over their lifetime. However, the performance figures have been reported under different testing conditions and have not been independently verified at commercial scale. The technology is intended to address some of the longstanding weaknesses of lead batteries, including positive grid corrosion, hydrogen evolution and sulphation, which can accelerate degradation and shorten operational life. Orouji said hydrogen gas release had been reduced by at least 10%, while graphene’s conductive and capacitive properties contributed to improved battery performance. The company is targeting industrial and stationary applications, including telecommunications, power generation, electricity networks, data centres and solar energy storage. Although Platin Iran describes the technology as having reached commercial production, sales remain at an early stage. Two batteries were sold during the previous Iranian year, with one supplied to Iran’s Nanotechnology Development Headquarters and the other to the Tabriz Gas Transmission Company. The company has also pursued international patent protection for its graphene-based technology. A US patent application covering porous carbon-based materials for lead batteries was published on October 29. Earlier this year, Platin Iran said its graphene-enhanced batteries could offer approximately twice the cycle life of conventional products at a purchase price around 30% higher. The development comes as manufacturers continue to investigate advanced carbon additives as a means of improving the performance and competitiveness of established lead battery technology. For Platin Iran, the next challenge will be demonstrating whether the reported laboratory improvements can be reproduced consistently in commercial production and sustained under real operating conditions. title: China’s lead battery export boom faces test – Batteries International
content: Chinese customs figures reported by Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) on October 21 showed that exports reached 20.66 million lead-acid batteries in September, an increase of 20.9% year-on-year and 5.6% compared with August. The recovery in international demand has yet to reverse the decline earlier in the year. Cumulative exports remained 2.3% below their level in the same period of 2025. The question now is whether Chinese manufacturers can sustain growth while preserving profitability. “Chinese lead-acid battery exports surged by almost 21% in September, but a widening gap between domestic and international lead prices threatens to undermine manufacturers’ profitability,” say analysts. “The question is whether Chinese producers can maintain their overseas market share without sacrificing margins — and whether competitors in India and elsewhere stand to benefit.” Overseas sales are recovering, but the domestic cost of the lead needed to manufacture their batteries is rising relative to international prices, threatening the competitiveness of one of the world’s largest battery exporting industries. Lead is the largest raw material component by weight in a conventional lead-acid battery and a huge proportion of its manufacturing cost. Higher prices hit manufacturers’ margins, particularly in competitive export markets where prices are often agreed before production and delivery. Manufacturers sourcing metal within China may find themselves paying more than overseas competitors purchasing lead at prices linked to the London Metal Exchange. A Chinese exporter facing higher metal costs has three choices: increase selling prices, accept lower margins or reduce manufacturing and distribution costs. Raising prices risks losing business to competitors, while accepting lower margins may be sustainable only for manufacturers with sufficient scale, financial resources or integrated recycling operations. China’s secondary lead industry complicates things further. Recent SMM reports indicate that scrap availability has constrained some secondary lead producers, even as smelter operating rates have recovered following China’s October holiday period. The effect is to expose Chinese battery exporters to a cost structure that may become increasingly disconnected from that of their overseas competitors. For Indian manufacturers, this could present an opportunity.  India has a substantial lead-acid battery manufacturing industry, with established producers serving automotive replacement, industrial, telecommunications and standby power markets. Its recycling industry is also expanding, with companies investing in additional refining capacity and international scrap collection networks. If Chinese manufacturers are unable to pass higher domestic lead costs to overseas customers, Indian producers may find themselves better placed to compete in price-sensitive export markets across Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. However, the advantage is far from automatic. Indian battery manufacturers are also exposed to fluctuations in international lead prices, currency movements and recycling costs. Their competitiveness will depend on whether they can secure reliable metal supplies at prices that remain favourable relative to those paid by Chinese competitors. The longer-term figures underline the scale of the challenge. According to SMM’s February 2026 industry outlook, Chinese lead-acid battery exports fell 12.79% in 2025 to 219 million units. At times during the preceding two years, the domestic lead price premium over international prices exceeded RMB3,000 per tonne, contributing to lost overseas orders. The report also identified India as China’s largest lead-acid battery export destination in 2025, although shipments to the country fell 33.39% year-on-year. Exports to the US declined by 48.59%. These figures suggest that Chinese manufacturers were already encountering difficulties in maintaining their international competitiveness before September’s recovery. There is another possible consequence. Chinese battery producers have increasingly been establishing manufacturing operations outside China, particularly in Southeast Asia. Locating production closer to overseas customers can reduce exposure to tariffs and shipping costs while potentially allowing manufacturers to source lead under different pricing arrangements. Such investments could help Chinese-owned businesses maintain their international market positions, even if direct exports from China become less competitive. SMM’s October 21 assessment described the September recovery as being driven more by the need to maintain market share and fulfil seasonal orders than by improving profitability. It warned that persistently high Chinese lead prices could discourage smaller exporters from accepting new business. September’s figures therefore present a paradox. China’s lead-acid battery industry is exporting more batteries, but higher sales volumes don’t necessarily mean stronger financial performance. Whether the recovery continues into 2027 may depend less on the strength of overseas demand than on the ability of Chinese manufacturers to bring their raw material costs closer to those of their international competitors. For the moment, China’s battery exporters appear to be winning back sales. The unanswered question is how much profit they are making from them. title: E-bikes, ‘potential saviour of the lead battery industry’ – Batteries International
content: Electric bikes and three-wheelers could offer a lifeline to the lead battery industry as vehicle electrification threatens demand for traditional starter batteries, according to Huw Roberts, director of CHR Metals. Speaking at the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo on October 26, in a presentation on key developments in production and prospects for the next 10 years, Roberts revealed that electric two- and three-wheelers in China alone account for approximately 18% of global lead demand. This is a market he believes has been largely overlooked in discussions about vehicle electrification. “The market for batteries in China is unlike anywhere else in the world, and that’s because of this thing called an e-bike,” he said. “Quite remarkably, the lead use in e-bikes and e-trikes in China represents around 18% of global demand for lead, and this is a number which has, in some way, been airbrushed from history.” Roberts estimates there are around 300 million electric two-wheelers and another 80 million to 90 million electric three-wheelers operating in China, with approximately 85% to 90% still powered by lead batteries rather than lithium. He questioned why such an enormous market receives comparatively little attention in international reporting on electrification. “A year or two ago, I was looking at a report, and I was staggered to see that they really were barely mentioning e-bikes. So I got hold of them, and I said, ‘Look, there’s this huge market that you seem to be ignoring.’“ He said the International Energy Agency’s 2026 report excludes e-bikes with a maximum permitted speed  of 25km/h, despite their widespread use in China. “It’s a strange thing how this huge use of lead is missing from a lot of the official data,” he said. The implications for the lead battery industry are significant. Most Chinese e-bike batteries last approximately two years, creating an enormous replacement market and a continuous supply of spent batteries for recycling. And Roberts believes the opportunity could extend far beyond China.”I have argued for a number of years that this has been the potential saviour, really, of the lead battery industry as conventional cars are replaced,” he said. However, he warned that other markets have been slower to embrace lead batteries for electric mobility. “We’ve seen a little bit in Indonesia, but the big market is India, and at the moment, the bulk of the two-wheel e-bikes in India are lithium-powered.” He attributed this largely to government policy, which he said had “dramatically favoured lithium batteries over lead batteries”. Similar developments are taking place in Africa, where electric motorcycles are increasingly being introduced for deliveries and local taxi services. “Unfortunately, there again, it seems like lithium is the dominant battery. I don’t think lead’s really even getting a look in at the moment.” But Roberts believes lead has an important advantage that competing chemistries have yet to match: an established recycling infrastructure. “When you take your battery back to the battery shop to get a new one, you’re getting a very significant discount now,” he said, contrasting this with lithium batteries, which retailers are often reluctant to accept because they have little residual value. Nevertheless, he warned that lead’s position in China is not guaranteed. “The risk is probably not immediately from lithium-ion, but possibly from sodium-ion batteries, which are coming.” With the traditional automotive SLI market facing long-term decline, China’s vast electric two- and three-wheeler fleet demonstrates that lead batteries could still play a significant role in the transition to electric mobility. But whether the industry can capitalise on that opportunity beyond China, before competing chemistries establish themselves, remains an open question. title: Secondary lead industry launches training academy at 10ISLC – Batteries International
content: An initiative to preserve technical knowledge, develop new talent and improve understanding of lead recycling across the industry was launched in Colombo, Sri Lanka last week alongside the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference. Opening the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference, organiser Mark Stevenson said the new training academy had evolved from discussions dating back four or five years about how the industry could address gaps in technical knowledge and professional development. The academy, Stevenson said, was intended to provide a broader foundation of knowledge for everyone involved in lead production, recycling and associated activities, including regulators, non-governmental organisations and newcomers to the sector. Four factors had driven its creation: the need to preserve expertise accumulated by experienced industry professionals, growing demand for information from governments and NGOs, support from industry associations and the need to attract younger people. Stevenson recalled discussions with Dr Mike McDonagh about the failure of experienced professionals to pass on their knowledge to succeeding generations. “We both said, ‘Let’s do something different,'” he told delegates. He also highlighted the importance of providing a common foundation of understanding for people approaching the industry from different backgrounds. “Let’s bring people together and start teaching them, so their foundation is just as strong as ours, and it includes everybody.” The initiative has received support from Battery Council International, the International Lead Association and the Indian Lead Zinc Development Association. The Colombo meeting also marks a departure from the conference’s traditional format. The International Secondary Lead Conference has normally been held alongside the Asian Battery Conference, but was separated this year to accommodate the academy and mark its tenth edition. The first conference was held in Macau 17 years ago. Stevenson said the event would return to its association with the Asian Battery Conference next year. ILA managing director Andy Bush, speaking at the opening, said understanding developments in secondary lead markets, regulation, worker health and production technologies was essential to the industry’s future. Stevenson also envisaged the conference becoming a training ground for younger professionals, giving them opportunities to chair sessions and present papers before moving on to larger international battery conferences. He stressed that the academy’s remit extended beyond established manufacturers and recyclers to include those working to improve lead recycling practices in countries such as Nigeria, Ghana and India. The objective, he said, was to encourage knowledge sharing across the entire lead industry rather than treating its different sectors as separate communities. title: GAZ Energy partners with Minespider to introduce digital battery passports for European BESS – Batteries International
content: European battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturer GAZ Energy has partnered with Minespider to introduce digital battery passports across its industrial battery systems ahead of new European Union requirements taking effect in February 2027. The agreement, announced on October 29, will allow GAZ Energy to link product, compliance and lifecycle information to individual battery systems, providing customers and project developers with access to data throughout their operational lives. GAZ Energy currently has more than 2 GWh of BESS projects at various stages of implementation across Germany, Finland, Czechia, Poland, Slovakia and Romania. Under the partnership, Minespider will establish a digital infrastructure connecting each battery system to a persistent identifier, accessible through a physical data carrier such as a QR code. The system will bring together manufacturer information, product documentation, regulatory compliance records, circularity data and relevant operational information. Application programming interfaces (APIs) will allow information to be updated throughout a battery’s lifecycle, while public and permission-controlled data layers will determine which information is available to different stakeholders. The initiative is designed to prepare GAZ Energy for the EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, which requires industrial batteries with a capacity greater than 2 kWh to have a digital battery passport from February 18, 2027. The requirement applies to batteries placed on the EU market or put into service from that date and is intended to improve transparency and access to information throughout the battery value chain. Nathan Williams, founder and CEO of Minespider, said the value of digital battery passports extended beyond meeting regulatory obligations. “A Digital Battery Passport becomes much more valuable when the data behind it remains connected to the battery after it enters the market,” he said. “GAZ Energy is connecting regulatory and product information through persistent identifiers and APIs. That gives GAZ Energy a foundation for the 2027 requirement and for battery data that stays useful across the life of the system.” David Vodička, a member of GAZ Energy’s board of directors, said maintaining access to information over the long operating lives of energy storage systems was becoming increasingly important. “Our customers invest in battery systems with a long operational lifetime, and the information associated with those systems needs to remain accessible and useful throughout the project,” he said. “As our BESS portfolio grows across Europe, we see Digital Battery Passports as an important part of building a consistent and transparent data environment around our systems.” The companies are also developing the identifier and QR-code structure that will connect individual battery systems to their digital passports. GAZ Energy said the partnership would support both regulatory compliance and the development of a consistent data management system as its European energy storage portfolio expands. title: Chinese lead battery demand diverges as e-bike market weakens – Batteries International
content: China’s lead-acid battery market is showing contrasting demand trends, with automotive battery manufacturers maintaining relatively stable production while the electric bicycle sector faces weakening orders as its traditional peak season draws to a close. According to Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), reporting on October 23, demand for automotive lead-acid batteries remained steady, with some manufacturers recording modest increases in production. The picture was less positive for electric bicycle batteries. Seasonal consumption had weakened, while several manufacturers had completed deliveries of earlier orders and were increasingly adopting a production-to-sales approach. SMM said some e-bike battery producers were seeing weaker new orders, although production levels had not yet undergone any major adjustments. The market’s performance was also being affected by regulatory difficulties in China’s electric bicycle sector. The suspension of compulsory 3C product certification for certain electric bicycle models has prevented some consumers from registering their vehicles, making sales more difficult for dealers. SMM said the certification issues could continue to affect the wider electric bicycle market in the coming weeks. The divergence between the two battery segments was also reflected in manufacturing activity. SMM reported that the comprehensive weekly operating rate of lead-acid battery manufacturers across five Chinese provinces reached 74.16% during October 16–22, an increase of 0.79 percentage points from the previous week. The improvement was largely attributed to automotive battery manufacturers gradually increasing production ahead of the traditionally stronger fourth-quarter period. By contrast, the traditional peak season for electric bicycle lead-acid batteries was approaching its end. Some manufacturers reported that new orders were already beginning to weaken, raising the possibility of production adjustments in November if the trend continued. According to data cited by Caixin Global on October 15, domestic electric two-wheeler sales fell 4.8% year on year to 48.4 million units during the first nine months of 2026. However, the market had shown signs of recovery during the third quarter, when sales increased 9% year on year to more than 20 million units. The improvement followed a difficult first half, during which sales were affected by the high comparison base created by China’s 2025 trade-in programme and the introduction of stricter electric bicycle safety requirements. The suspension of 3C certification for certain models in October introduced another source of uncertainty, disrupting vehicle registrations and dealer sales. These developments are important for the lead-acid battery industry because electric two-wheelers represent a significant end-use market for conventional lead-acid batteries in China. While the growth of lithium-ion batteries has increased competition in the segment, lead-acid batteries remain widely used in China’s electric bicycle market, particularly in lower-cost models. The immediate outlook is therefore likely to depend on how quickly manufacturers and dealers can resolve certification issues, as well as whether consumer demand recovers following the seasonal slowdown. For lead-acid battery producers, the contrast with the automotive replacement market is becoming increasingly apparent. Automotive battery demand is providing a degree of stability as manufacturers prepare for the fourth-quarter peak season, while e-bike battery producers face a more uncertain order environment. SMM said that if the weakness in new e-bike orders continues, some manufacturers may reduce production plans in November. title: India must tighten dealer rules to tackle informal lead recycling – Batteries International
content: India’s battery dealers must be made accountable for the collection and disposal of spent batteries if the country is to tackle its persistent informal lead recycling problem, according to L Pugazhenthy, executive director of the India Lead Zinc Development Association (ILZDA). Speaking at the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo on October 26, Pugazhenthy (known informally as “Mr Pug”) called for tighter regulation of battery dealers, mandatory reporting of spent battery collections and regular audits of authorised recycling facilities. He warned that India’s Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, which introduced extended producer responsibility (EPR) requirements across battery chemistries, do not adequately address the role of dealers in directing spent batteries into legitimate recycling channels. Pugazhenthy identified battery dealers as a major route through which spent batteries are diverted into the informal recycling sector, arguing that their responsibilities are not sufficiently defined under the current regulations. He estimates that approximately 65% of India’s recycled lead production comes from authorised recyclers, while around 30% is attributable to the informal sector. India is one of the world’s largest secondary lead producers, with Pugazhenthy estimating annual secondary output at around 1.6 million tonnes. He also cited authorised recycling capacity of approximately 3.5 million tonnes, based on figures from the Central Pollution Control Board. Despite the country’s substantial investment in formal recycling infrastructure, he said the continued presence of informal operators remained one of the industry’s most pressing concerns. “The most important concern as far as lead battery, as far as lead is concerned, [is] to eliminate or to minimise the role of informal sector,” he said. “We cannot go on talking about that disorganised sector for a long time because of safety concerns and human exposure.” His proposed solution places battery dealers at the centre of a more accountable collection system. “All the battery dealers have to be made accountable. Let them get registered. Let them submit periodical returns,” he said. Under such a system, dealers would be required to disclose the quantities of spent batteries collected, the volumes transferred for recycling and the identities of the recyclers receiving them. Pugazhenthy argued that this information should be submitted regularly to regulators, allowing authorities to track the movement of used batteries and identify where material is being diverted away from authorised facilities. He also called for stronger oversight of licensed recycling operations, warning that obtaining regulatory approval should not be treated as a one-off exercise. Registered recyclers, he said, must be subject to periodic audits to establish whether environmental and occupational safety standards are being maintained. “They all need to be audited periodically as they are really following all the best practices, or only one-time exercise, and after that they get the approval. Everything goes away. That cannot go on.” Pugazhenthy also questioned whether India’s recycling industry should continue to accommodate facilities operating at widely differing scales. He suggested that an individual firm’s minimum annual recycling capacity of 10,000 to 12,000 tonnes could provide a more appropriate operating benchmark, although he presented this as a proposal rather than an existing regulatory requirement. The recommendations come as India’s lead consumption continues to expand, supported by automotive batteries, backup power systems, telecommunications and renewable energy installations. Pugazhenthy forecasts that total Indian lead consumption could reach approximately two million tonnes annually by 2030. But he insisted that growth must be accompanied by stronger environmental safeguards and greater accountability throughout the battery supply chain. For India’s formal recycling industry, the challenge is not simply to increase processing capacity, but to ensure that spent batteries reach the facilities equipped and authorised to handle them safely. title: Loadsmart Adds AI Agents for Enterprise Shippers
content:
Loadsmart Adds AI Agents for Enterprise Shippers
Prioritise Us
on Google
Marine services provider SSA Marine implemented Opendock at its Port Arthur, Texas and Gulfport, Mississippi locations in 2021, before expanding its use to three further locations. Credit: SSA Marine
Loadsmart CEO Felipe Capella launches new logistics AI agents to automate dock and yard management for global enterprise shippers.
Enterprise shippers are under constant pressure to streamline complex freight lifecycles and reduce manual data entry across their supply chain networks. Addressing this operational bottleneck, logistics platform Loadsmart has expanded its digital ecosystem by adding five new AI agents to its enterprise suite. The new agents cover: detention handling, purchase order follow-up, warehouse customer service, dock door management and yard task orchestration.
The newly added AI agents expand the number of AI agents supported by Loadsmart to eleven. The platform launched AI agents in September to handle scheduling, tracking and status updates, document collection, tender failures, load audits and claims. The expanded platform now automates repetitive tasks spanning from initial purchase orders all the way through to final dock door scheduling.
The evolution of freight technology is rapidly mirroring the expanding use of AI in the autonomous vehicle sector. While most enterprise shippers currently operate at automation levels one or two - in other words, relying on software to simply flag issues for human intervention - the integration of agentic AI is pushing the envelope of industry applications. By 2030, industry leaders expect supply chains to reach levels three and four, where AI agents execute autonomous decisions within strictly defined shipper rules.
The most valuable commodity in global logistics is time, not data or fuel. Our autonomous technology is designed to buy back that operational time, empowering entire freight teams to step away from manual systems and focus on strategic execution
Felipe Capella, Chief Executive Officer of Loadsmart
Felipe Capella, CEO of Loadsmart
Automating the Freight Lifecycle
To manage this digital transition, Loadsmart’s newly expanded AI agents work directly on top of the Transportation Management Systems (TMS), Warehouse Management Systems (WMS), and Yard Management Systems (YMS) that shippers already utilise. Functioning through everyday communication channels like email, phone, and chat, these autonomous agents successfully complete 70 to 90 percent of logistics tasks on their own.
For the remaining exceptions, human freight experts intervene to guarantee 100% task resolution, ensuring supply chain continuity without disruptions. During a recent live demonstration at the Sightline 2027 event in Chicago, the platform successfully processed a single load from order to settlement, with an AI agent autonomously making a phone call to reschedule a delayed dock appointment.
Ralph Moyle uses Loadsmart's Opendock tool to coordinate up to 500 appointments per week. Credit: Ralph Moyle
Extending AI into the Dock, Yard, and Warehouse
The five newest AI agents are specifically designed to eliminate the manual emails and phone calls that historically plague warehouse and yard operations. The targeted logistics workflows include:
Detention Handling:
Autonomously warns the warehouse dock before a truck exceeds its free time, accurately reports detention fees owed, and automatically approves carrier requests that match gate records.
Purchase Order Follow-up:
Scans the system for purchase orders lacking a dock appointment and proactively contacts the supplier or carrier to book, ship, or reschedule the freight.
Warehouse Customer Service:
Directly manages incoming warehouse emails and phone calls regarding truck arrivals, receipt confirmations, and updated Estimated Times of Arrival (ETAs).
Dock Door Management:
Optimises the physical flow of inbound and outbound trucks, autonomously handling late arrivals, carrier no-shows, and unexpected dock door closures.
Yard Task Orchestration:
Intelligently generates and assigns yard moves, temperature checks, and safety inspections in the correct order triggered by specific supply chain events.
Aaron Thomas, Director of Engineering, Dock and Yard at Loadsmart, and Nate Allan, VP of Enterprise and Partnerships at Loadsmart discuss applications of AI in Dock, Gate and Yard management. Credit: Loadsmart
Key Logistics and Technology Tools
Loadsmart
: Operating as a premier connected logistics platform, Loadsmart spans the entire global freight lifecycle. By combining advanced artificial intelligence with experienced human operators, the company provides enterprise shippers with customised automation tools. Their agent-led execution model transforms how logistics professionals interact with core systems, ensuring 100% resolution across highly complex supply chain networks.
Opendock
: Functioning as a critical component of the broader logistics software ecosystem, Opendock provides specialised dock, yard, and gate scheduling solutions. By integrating directly with enterprise AI agents, the platform allows warehouses to seamlessly automate inbound and outbound freight appointments, drastically reducing truck detention times and optimising physical facility throughput for enterprise shippers.
ShipperGuide
: Serving as a robust transportation management system (TMS), ShipperGuide centralises freight procurement, routing, and carrier tracking. When paired with autonomous AI agents, the platform eliminates repetitive manual data entry. It enables supply chain operators to transition from merely clicking through software workflows to actively managing intelligent agents that execute strategic logistics rules.

title: FarEye: Reducing the Cost of Carrier Fragmentation With AI
content:
FarEye: Reducing the Cost of Carrier Fragmentation With AI
Prioritise Us
on Google
Last-mile delivery costs are rising, but FarEye is looking at ways to optimise planning. Credit: Getty
As last-mile delivery continues to face ongoing challenges, Kushal Nahata, CEO and Co-founder of FarEye explains that visibility is key to success
FarEye has published findings from its Eye on the Last Mile EMEA 2026 research, exploring the challenges within the logistics sector.
In the past year, supply chains have faced significant volatility, but the rising costs of last-mile delivery have been a major focus of the report.
As a critical and complicated aspect of the journey, the last mile needs to be as accurate as possible – and FarEye is aiming to simplify spend.
Modern supply chain challenges
Logistics companies have been put under much pressure in recent years, faced with geopolitical instability, rising costs and heightened demand. Businesses are working out where to cut spend, while also meeting rising expectations for sustainable operations – such as alternative fuels and electrification.
Last-mile is already a complex challenge,
being what the customer sees. As a result, it is critical to ensure the last-mile operates without issue. Recent years, however, have increased consumer scrutiny, alongside more congestion to tackle, more instability from weather and rising costs of fuel.
According to FarEye’s report, last-mile delivery costs across EMEA rose by 9% over the last 12 months, and 96% of firms paid more money per delivery. Much of this has been attributed to the ‘fragmentation tax’, which consists of hidden costs from disconnected carriers, data and systems.
The report found that 51% of fully outsourced firms cited unreliable carrier information as their biggest challenge, whereas 22% cited cost.
"Businesses may outsource execution, but they cannot outsource accountability for cost and customer experience," explains Kushal Nahata, CEO and Co-founder of FarEye.
Kushal Nahata CEO & Co-Founder of FarEye
"The last mile is still waiting for its container moment."
To ensure businesses operate cost-effectively, Kushal states leaders must know the location of each delivery, carrier allocation and cost at all times, with full visibility into operations. Exceptions and failed attempts need to be tracked, and there needs to be options for delivery – some customers prioritise reliability, whereas others prioritise speed.
Kushal also recommends leaders integrate AI on trusted data, with standardised milestones, exception definitions and more, all while maintaining human oversight.
At a glance
Last-mile delivery costs across EMEA rose by 9% in the last year
51% of fully outsourced firms state unreliable carrier information is the largest challenge they face
41% of total supply chain cost is in the last mile
Own-fleet operators are 2.3x as likely to see costs outrun revenue
69% of leaders are building with AI
Cost concerns
In a year which has been incredibly volatile, balancing cost and customer experience is a difficult task but a crucial skill to have. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted due to the conflict in Iran, meaning that insurance premiums have been heightened, fuel prices have increased and time taken to deliver products has gotten longer.
According to the study, 41% of total supply chain cost sits within the last mile, making it even more exposed to disruption. Balancing the cost and customer experience requires technology, people, carrier relationships, agile operations and capital.
Leaders need to have full visibility into the costs and demands of each necessity, but this is another challenge on its own. The report found that fuel and insurance both rose in the last year, meaning that nearly everyone is paying more to deliver their products, though there is a disparity within this.
Out of respondents, 76% report costs growing at least as fast as revenue. Though the typical rise was 9%, one in four respondents saw rises of 15% or more. Own-fleet operators are likely to see costs outpace revenue, meaning it becomes more cost-effective to outsource – but reliability and trust is lacking.
Businesses who outsource more find issues in failed deliveries, unreliable information, lack of customisation and poor customer experience. If the final mile is being poorly managed, the company risks its reputation.
FarEye is using AI agents to simplify logistics (Credit: FarEye)
AI integration
To help manage changing demand better, more teams are turning to AI. Within the study, 69% of teams are already building with AI, though as few as 18% are running it at scale. This is limited by expertise and trust, poor data quality and unclear ROI.
However, integrating AI successfully can help leaders grow capabilities in demand forecasting, customer support,
delivery time prediction and route optimisation
FarEye, therefore, aims to simplify last-mile logistics, using real-time insights to create meaningful action points and create improved value for customers and companies.
Its AI-driven orchestration platform unified planning, routing and real-time execution in order to make delivery faster, smarter and more sustainable. FarEye helps businesses forecast capacity up to 12 months in advance, predicting cost per delivery with accuracy and running what-if simulations at scale. This helps organisations plan their yearly budget and be able to roll out contingency plans if something goes wrong.
The platform completely reimagines the last-mile with AI, tailoring workflows to suit each need and scaling solutions with agility. As logistics becomes more unpredictable, FarEye offers some clarity to leaders, making use of AI tools in an
end-to-end network
in order to keep operations moving and customers satisfied.
The last mile is still waiting for its container moment.
Kushal Nahata, CEO and Co-founder of FarEye
Key partners
FarEye is a logistics and delivery management platform founded in 2013. The company provides end-to-end visibility and optimization solutions for supply chain operations, serving retailers, e-commerce, and logistics providers globally. Their cloud-based software enables real-time tracking, route optimization, and customer communication. FarEye has raised significant venture funding and operates across multiple international markets.
HelloFresh
HelloFresh is a German meal-kit delivery service founded in 2011, now the world's largest. The company delivers pre-portioned ingredients and recipes directly to customers' homes across multiple countries. HelloFresh went public in 2017 and has achieved profitability. They offer various meal plans including vegetarian and family options, emphasizing convenience and reducing food waste.
Papa Johns
Papa John's is an American pizza restaurant franchise founded by John Schnatter in 1984. It's the fourth-largest pizza delivery chain globally, operating thousands of locations worldwide. Known for their "Better Ingredients, Better Pizza" slogan, the company focuses on quality ingredients and online ordering. Papa John's has faced leadership controversies but remains a major fast-food player.
Tata Steel
Tata Steel is India's largest steel producer and among the world's most geographically diversified steel companies. Founded in 1907, it's part of the Tata Group conglomerate. The company operates across India, Europe, and Southeast Asia, producing automotive, construction, and engineering steel. Tata Steel emphasizes sustainability and innovation while employing over 65,000 people globally.

title: Exploring DP World’s Circular Seabed Sunglasses
content:
Exploring DP World’s Circular Seabed Sunglasses
Prioritise Us
on Google
DP World is helping fishing nets gain a new life through its circular sunglasses project. Credit: DP World
DP World is unlocking business opportunities with a new circular initiative, explains Jimena Rodriguez, Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World
Around the world, thousands of fishing nets have been abandoned, lost or discarded in the ocean.
Made of synthetic materials, the fishing gear of recent operations take hundreds of years to degrade, polluting the oceans and putting marine life at risk.
To help clear up the ocean and drive circularity,
DP World is undertaking a collaborative project
to turn ghost nets into sunglasses.
A call for sustainable solutions
Ghost nets are pieces of fishing equipment that have been left or lost in the sea, with much of it coming from large commercial fishing operations. These nets, once adrift, continue to catch marine life, impacting fish, dolphins, whales, turtles and sharks.
As they trap a range of creatures, they have a major impact on biodiversity and marine food chain stability – and coral structures can become damaged by the nets. When the materials degrade, the ghost nets fragment into microplastics, which are ingested by animals, leading to malnutrition and death. When ingested by fish, these microplastics enter the human food chain.
pollution in the seas
and the disruption to the oceanic ecosystem is having a major impact on the environment, adding to the instability of supply chains. Global warming, made worse by pollution, is impacting global supply chains – resulting in adverse weather patterns and poor crop yields. This knock-on effect has a major impact – though ocean acidification and other forms of pollution,
food supply chains are weakened
through the disrupted quality, quantity and safety of seafood.
“Sustainability is not something a business “finishes”. We move forward one practical solution at a time,” says Jimena Rodriguez, Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World on LinkedIn.
Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World
“Working alongside colleagues across DP World, I see this journey as one of constantly connecting knowledge, local context and business thinking to find better ways forward.
“That is why I love the simplicity of this initiative. It brings science, business and circularity together to create value while reducing pressure on nature.”
Key facts
Ghost nets can take up to 200 years to degrade
More than 1,000 m² of nets will be removed from the seabed
The project will collect approximately 800kg of materials
Some of the material has been collected from 50 metres deep
Each pair of sunglasses will have coordinates from where the material was found
Collaboration for recovery
Moreover, the lost nets act as a lost economic benefit for fisheries – once lost, fisheries need to purchase new fishing equipment, rather than being able to re-use the gear and gain full ROI on it.
DP World is working in collaboration with Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği (Türkiye’s Marine Life Conservation Society) in order to clean up the Sea of Marmara. Together, these organisations are removing the nets from the ocean in order to give the material a second life.
The aim is to remove more than 1,000m² of nets from the area around the Princes’ Islands. This totals approximately 800 kg of material.
“Protecting our seas requires collaboration, and the private sector has an important role to play,” Volkan Narcı, Chairman of Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği says.
Volkan Narcı, Chairman of Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği
“The partnership with DP World allows us to create a greater and more lasting impact on the health of the Sea of Marmara.”
Through reports, technology, sea charts and local knowledge, the Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği team finds the abandoned nets. They then carefully remove them from the seabed – attempting to limit the further damage – before recording the weight, size and location of each net.
In making these records, the companies can gain further information of where lost equipment has been accumulated, helping them track movements and potential damage to the ecosystem.
Much of the work takes place around the Princes’ Islands and the deeper waters around Istanbul – many have been recovered from more than 50 metres below the surface.
“A great example of how environmental responsibility, collaboration and innovation can come together to create meaningful impact,” states Alişan Koyuncu, Corporate Communications Specialist at DP World on LinkedIn.
Alişan Koyuncu, Corporate Communications Specialist at DP World
“It’s inspiring to see materials that once threatened marine life transformed into something valuable.”
Circularity and the economy
Once the material is recovered, the process of giving them a second life begins. The nets are processed into recycled plastic granules and turned into custom-designed sunglasses. This means the material gains a new life with a longer lifespan.
The coordinates and the depth of where the original net was found are stamped inside the frames. By creating a direct link to the waters, it offers these glasses an exclusivity and a reminder of the ecological benefits of the sunglasses.
“Ghost nets are a threat to marine life long after they have been lost. This project gets them out of the water and puts the material to a completely different use,” explains Nicholas Mazzei, Vice President of Sustainability, Europe at DP World.
Nicholas Mazzei, Vice President Sustainability at DP World
“Turning a net recovered from the seabed into a pair of sunglasses makes the idea of reuse very real. And stamping the location inside each pair creates a connection to where it came from.”
DP World is also working with SUSAKO, the Sustainable Art Women’s Cooperative (Sürdürülebilir Sanat Kadın Kooperatifi). This partnership works to support the economy on a more local level, running workshops where members of the public can turn the plastic into jewelry. This acts as an example of how material can be repurposed – educating the communities on
circularity and waste reduction
– and aims to support women’s participation in the economy.
Through the project, there will also be work with local fishing communities in order to raise awareness of ghost nets, helping to prevent the gear from being lost or abandoned in the first place.
DP World is focusing on its Source to Sea approach, aiming to restore water ecosystems, enhance natural carbon sinks and support biodiversity. In conducting these projects, it is driving circularity and supporting local economies while working to reduce the environmental impact of marine operations.
This is helping to restore balance to ocean quality, which helps stabilise food supply chains. Moreover, the demonstration of how these ghost nets can be used for circular purposes helps local communities think about the
circular economy and the opportunity
to create more projects with other waste products.
I see this journey as one of constantly connecting knowledge, local context and business thinking to find better ways forward.
Jimena Rodriguez, Oceans and Biodiversity Senior Manager at DP World
Approximately 800kg of ghost net will be recycled. Credit: DP World
Key partners
DP World
DP World is a leading global supply chain and logistics company headquartered in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Operating across six continents with locations in over 78 countries, it specializes in cargo logistics, port operations, and maritime services. Founded in 2005, DP World handles approximately 10% of global container traffic, employing over 103,000 people and facilitating international trade through innovative infrastructure.
Sürdürülebilir Sanat Kadın Kooperatifi (Sustainable Art Women's Cooperative) is a Turkish women-led initiative promoting economic empowerment through sustainable artistic practices. The cooperative supports female artisans by preserving traditional crafts while incorporating eco-friendly methods and materials. Members create handmade products, generating income and fostering entrepreneurship. The organization emphasizes women's independence, cultural heritage preservation, and environmental responsibility through collaborative creative work and fair trade principles.
Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği
Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği (Marine Life Conservation Association) is a Turkish environmental NGO dedicated to protecting marine ecosystems and biodiversity. The organization conducts research, rehabilitation, and conservation projects focusing on threatened species, particularly sea turtles, Mediterranean monk seals, and cetaceans. Through beach monitoring, rescue operations, and education campaigns, the association works to mitigate threats from pollution, overfishing, and habitat destruction.
