title: Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Zero Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 7:30 am PT
Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.
The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.
The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.
There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.
Zero Project Ventura: A new electric motorcycle for under $8,000
Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that
hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.
With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.
And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.
The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).
That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.
Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.
We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the
smallest of electric motorcycles
that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.
Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.
The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.
Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as
a potential gateway
to motorcycle ownership.
“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.
That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the
launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer
showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.
Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.
But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.
Zero XE electric dirt bike is finally going street-legal
Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.
The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s
more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles
, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.
Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.
The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.
Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.
The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.
For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.
That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.
The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.
Zero LS3 electric scooter makes its European debut
Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.
While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.
The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.
Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.
Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.
That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.
The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.
Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.
The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.
Zero is developing a completely new smartphone app
Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.
The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.
One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.
The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.
An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.
Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.
Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.
Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.
The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.
DC fast charging is finally coming to more Zero motorcycles
Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is
Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging
Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.
The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.
That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.
Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.
European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.
The latter is particularly interesting given the
growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America
, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.
Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.
The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.
Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.
Electrek’s Take
There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.
For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.
Now we’re seeing a different approach.
The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.
I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.
That’s an audience
I’ve been watching grow
for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.
For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.
The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.
And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.
Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.
But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.
And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

title: This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode
content:
microcar
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 7:00 am PT
The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.
teased last week
, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version
that we originally reviewed
, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.
And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.
Eli ZERO MX: Same tiny car, more power
Eli ZERO MX
retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.
But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.
The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.
That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.
The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.
Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.
Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.
There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.
The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.
The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.
For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.
A sporty Race Edition with a hidden surprise
Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.
The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.
Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.
Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.
But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.
Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.
Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.
It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.
Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.
Small electric cars finding their place
Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.
The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.
A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.
The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.
Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.
Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.
For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

title: Kia racks up another record month as its new $30K electric SUV hits dealers
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 3 2026 - 6:56 am PT
Kia is eyeing its fourth consecutive annual US sales record after another record-breaking October. With the new 2027 EV3 arriving,
is “confident” the momentum will carry into Q4 and well into 2027.
Kia extends record-breaking US sales streak in October
“With six consecutive months of record-breaking sales, Kia is accelerating toward a fourth straight annual sales record,” Kia America vice president of sales Eric Watson said on Tuesday.
Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best
October sales
month ever.
Kia said electrified and hybrid vehicles drove the growth, with sales up 112% and 114% YOY, both setting new sales records.
Several Kia models posted strong YOY sales growth, including the three-row electric EV9 (+111%), Telluride (+63%), EV6 (+58%), Seltos (+43%), Sorento (+31%), Carnival (+17%), K4 (+14%), and Sportage (+12%).
Regarding its fully electric vehicles. Sales of the EV9, Kia’s three-row electric SUV, are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.
Although EV6 sales rebounded slightly last month, they are still down 39% YTD, with 7,067 units sold through October.
2027 Kia EV9 (Source: Kia)
Kia’s new entry-level electric SUV, the EV3 (
check out our review
), is now in showrooms nationwide. After it went on sale in mid-August, Kia sold 1,496 EV3s in its first two months.

title: Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay
政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策
政策分类依据: 特斯拉获美国对外贸易区(FTZ)批准，属于政府贸易/关税管理措施的正式落实，但证据不足以细分到具体子类别
content:
Tesla Energy
Tesla Megapack
Fred Lambert
| Nov 3 2026 - 6:15 am PT
Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval,
on Monday, runs for 14 months.
It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.
What Tesla asked for
Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where
Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August
, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.
application
lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.
That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.
The tariff catch
But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.
Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.
Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:
Duties are deferred until a Megapack ships out of the zone, which helps cash flow while the factory ramps up
No US duty on Megapacks exported directly from the zone
The lower finished-product rate on parts that aren’t caught by China, steel, or other special tariffs
No duty on scrap, and fewer customs filings
Useful. Not an exemption.
Same deal everyone else got
The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”
Tesla got an
identical decision
for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.
The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when
LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan
under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.
Tesla’s China cell problem
Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that
Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs
Tesla has since brought up its own
LFP cell factory in Nevada
, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.
Tesla’s Megapacks are bringing big batteries to the grid, but you can get the same benefits at home by pairing solar with storage. title: Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 5:53 am PT
If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.
ReBake Motors
has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.
Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built
some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market
before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.
And the Abler certainly looks the part.
Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.
There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.
The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.
Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.
The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.
Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.
CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.
ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

title: Maximo milestone: friendly robot robot has completed 300,000 tasks
content:
Solar power
Jo Borrás
| Nov 3 2026 - 4:32 am PT
After completing the first half of the Bellefield complex last summer
, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)
If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast,
that’s because it is
. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now,
with 300,000 tasks under its belt
, the robot is proving to be both fast
durable.
“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.
Max’ed out
Image by Maximo Robotics.
Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.
(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.
The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one,
which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity
, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course –
but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb
The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages,
making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site

title: Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 3 2026 - 3:28 am PT
Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.
2027 Yamaha NMAX E
is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the
low-speed urban electric scooters
that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.
At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.
Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.
Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.
Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.
Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.
The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.
A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.
Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.
That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.
Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

title: Hanwha Q-Cells shifts focus to research and development in Europe - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Hanwha Q Cells has denied rumors of a market exit but confirmed plans to focus its European operations on research and development. The restructuring will lead to job cuts in sales and business development, while the company expands its R&D workforce in Germany.
Sandra Enkhardt
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Cell production at the Hanwha Q Cells facility in South Korea.
Rumors are circulating in the solar industry that Hanwha Q-Cells is preparing to withdraw from the market and shut down operations by early 2027. The speculation has been fueled by reports of the company’s products being sold at unusually low prices.
In response to an inquiry from
pv magazine
, a company spokesperson firmly denied the rumors. “Q-Cells is not ceasing its operations in Europe,” he said. However, the spokesperson confirmed that, following “ongoing reviews and close monitoring of its subsidiaries,” parent company Hanwha Q-Cells has decided to refocus its German subsidiary exclusively on its core business.
Hanwha Q-Cells GmbH’s core business in Europe is research and development (R&D). “This decision involves a restructuring,” the spokesperson said. Although he initially declined to provide further details, he confirmed that “the restructuring will, however, result in some job losses within the sales and business development departments.”
Hanwha Q Cells also recently announced its involvement in a new German research project focused on space photovoltaics. The spokesperson said the company is expanding its R&D workforce.
The market speculation extends beyond the company’s German and European operations, with rumors suggesting that Hanwha Q-Cells could withdraw from PV manufacturing altogether. The spokesperson also rejected these claims.
“In its core business areas—research and development, as well as the production of solar cells and modules—Q-Cells is guided by global market interests and economic factors,” he said. “All other regions, including the U.S. operations you asked about, remain unchanged.”
Just over a year ago, Hanwha Q-Cells announced that it would discontinue direct sales of residential PV systems in Germany and instead rely exclusively on its network of approximately 1,000 authorized partners. At the time, the company cited weak demand in Germany’s residential solar market as the reason for the decision.
The move also resulted in job cuts, although Q-Cells declined to disclose how many positions were affected.
The sales division now facing closure is based in Berlin, while Hanwha Q-Cells’ German R&D center is located in Bitterfeld-Wolfen.

title: Waaree doubles Texas solar module manufacturing capacity to 3.2 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Waaree Solar Americas has started commercial production on two new 800 MW solar module manufacturing lines at its Brookshire facility in Texas, doubling the plant’s annual production capacity.
Uma Gupta
03 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Highlights
Waaree solar manufacturing facility in Texas
Waaree Solar Americas Inc. (WSA), a wholly owned subsidiary of India’s Waaree Energies Ltd., has started commercial production on two new solar module manufacturing lines at its facility in Brookshire, Texas.
Each line has an annual production capacity of 800 MW, bringing the facility’s total installed module manufacturing capacity to 3.2 GW.
The expansion forms part of Waaree’s broader manufacturing plans in the United States. WSA is also expanding its Arizona module manufacturing facility from 1 GW to 1.6 GW, which is expected to bring the company’s total US module manufacturing capacity to 4.8 GW in fiscal 2027, which in India runs from April 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027.. Waaree’s global module order book exceeds 25 GW.
Commercial production on the new lines began on Oct. 29, 2026, following an expansion approved by Waaree Energies’ board of directors in April 2025. The additional capacity doubles the Brookshire facility’s manufacturing capacity and strengthens WSA’s ability to supply US solar developers, utilities and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors with domestically manufactured modules, according to the company.
Waaree said the expansion comes amid changes in US trade policy, including measures under Section 232, that are affecting the economics of imported solar modules. The company said its investments in domestic manufacturing are intended to strengthen its position in the US market.
Revenue from Waaree’s US manufacturing operations increased to INR 13 billion ($146 million) in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, from INR 7.32 billion a year earlier. The US domestic business accounted for 43.8% of the company’s INR 592 billion order book, up from approximately 36% at the end of the preceding quarter.
“Shifting trade policy has strengthened the case for local manufacturing, and that is exactly where we have invested,” said Sunil Rathi, director of Waaree Group. “With Brookshire now at 3.2 GW and Arizona expanding, we are serving American customers from American factories, and our US order book continues to grow every quarter.”
The expansion is part of Waaree’s strategy to manufacture solar products in both India and the United States to serve domestic and international markets.
Waaree’s consolidated revenue from operations rose 23.9% to INR 75.18 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027.
The company is also expanding its upstream manufacturing operations in India. It plans to increase its solar cell manufacturing capacity from 5.4 GW to 15.4 GW in fiscal 2027 and commission a 10 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing facility in fiscal 2028.

title: Key takeaways from All Energy Australia 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The outlook for Australia’s renewable energy transition appears positive with supportive government policies and renewable energy targets, a surge in battery installations, and a strong pipeline of grid-scale solar and storage projects helping to fuel confidence.
David Carroll
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Utility-scale
The sense of optimism within Australia’s renewable energy sector was on display at All Energy Australia 2026 conference and trade show in Melbourne on Oct. 28 and 29, where energy security, growing demand, and investment and market certainty featured prominently in discussions.
Batteries were also a major topic of conversation with the strong presence of both grid and small-scale battery suppliers on the expanded exhibition floor showcasing a growing confidence in the market.
RX Global, which organises All Energy alongside the Clean Energy Council (CEC), said more than 22,000 people attended the event this year – up about 5,000 on 2025 figures – and more than 490 national and international companies and organisations exhibited on the trade show floor.
Batteries big and small were prominent among the displays with exhibitors keen to be part of the surging small and grid-scale markets.
More than 550,000 residential battery systems have been installed by Australian homeowners in the 15 months since the launch of the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program – that subsidises approximately 30% of the cost of an eligible home energy-storage system. The growth pattern has steadied since the initial boom in installations, but the industry is confident there is still plenty of upside in the small-scale sector.
“Residential has stabilised over the past few months but there is still a lot of potential in that segment,” EP Cube Sales Manager Sudeesh V said. “Metropolitan areas like Melbourne and Sydney might be slowing but areas such as South Australia, Western Australia, Queensland, even the Northern Territory, there’s a lot of growth potential.”
The large-scale battery sector is also experiencing record growth with nine projects representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity switched on in the first six months of the year, surpassing the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh added during 2025. In addition, 13 projects totalling 1.6 GW / 6.5 GWh reached financial close in H1 2026.
“We see a very, very significant penetration of battery storage and looking ahead, we’ll see this scaling up even more,” Rystad Energy Renewables and Power Vice President Sally Bogle said, adding that battery energy storage systems are serving as “a silver bullet for the power market.”
“They have quite a multi-faceted role,” she said, highlighting their ability to mitigate the curtailment of daytime solar in our markets.
“Asset performance wise, that is really, really valuable,” she said. “It allows a solar or wind facility to really maximise their asset and optimise the grid connection.”
The outlook for Australia’s solar market is also buoyant with the federal government’s recent raising of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) eligibility cap from 100 kW to 1 MW tipped to drive growth in the commercial and industrial (C&I) segment.
The expansion extends financial incentives through the Small-scale Technology Certificate (STC) mechanism, reducing the upfront cost of qualifying mid-scale systems by approximately 20%.
“This will definitely unlock a lot of small to medium commercial projects,” said Charles Guo, Australian manager with module manufacturer Gorkin Solar.
Government policy appears to be accelerating large-scale solar development also. Australia is targeting 82% renewables share in the National Electricity Market (NEM) by 2030 while Western Australia recently committed to a renewable energy target of 75% by 2031 for its main electricity grid.
Australian Energy Market Operator data shows a record 80.9 GW of new generation and storage projects now in the pipeline but as ageing coal-fired power plants retire and electricity consumption forecast to grow by more than 40% over the next decade, getting new capacity built will be critical.
Victorian Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes said Australia said capital is available but providing investors with certainty is key.
“Investors need clear policy, predictable approvals, and confidence that the infrastructure connecting projects will be delivered,” she said.

title: Solar PV cuts Spain’s electricity costs by €17.02 billion over 18 months - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A study by Spanish solar association UNEF estimates that solar PV generation reduced Spain’s wholesale electricity costs by €17.02 billion ($19.03 billion) between January 2025 and June 2026. Without solar generation, average daily market prices would have been 86% higher, according to the analysis.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Solar PV reduced Spain’s wholesale electricity costs by an estimated €17.02 billion between January 2025 and June 2026, according to Spanish PV association UNEF.
The association estimates that average day-ahead electricity prices would have been 86% higher without solar generation.
The study compares actual day-ahead market prices with a modeled scenario excluding generation from utility-scale PV plants and self-consumption systems. Without solar, the average price would have reached €112/MWh, compared with the recorded €60.2/MWh, representing a 46% reduction.
Utility-scale PV accounted for €14.23 billion of the estimated savings, while residential and commercial self-consumption contributed €2.79 billion. The total comprised €10.86 billion in 2025 and €6.16 billion in the first half of 2026.
UNEF attributes the effect to the marginal pricing mechanism of the day-ahead market. Solar generation, with its low variable costs, displaces more expensive electricity sources, lowering the market-clearing price. Self-consumption contributes by reducing demand from the grid, benefiting consumers beyond those with rooftop installations.
The association also estimates that every euro invested in solar PV generates €8 in wholesale electricity price savings.
Greater impact during periods of high solar generation
The price effect was particularly pronounced in June 2026, when the average day-ahead market price stood at €69.6/MWh. UNEF estimates that it would have reached €162.7/MWh without solar generation, a difference of €93.1/MWh.
The analysis uses data from Iberian electricity market operator OMIE, Spanish grid operator Red Eléctrica and UNEF to model market clearing without utility-scale PV and self-consumption. It also considers how other generation technologies would respond to changes in electricity prices.
However, the findings do not translate directly into equivalent savings on consumers’ electricity bills. The analysis covers the day-ahead wholesale market but excludes other cost components, including technical constraints, balancing services and forward contracts.
UNEF also acknowledges that the response of other technologies, particularly combined-cycle gas plants and hydropower facilities, could differ under substantially altered market conditions.

title: Shenzhen Nanshan Power seeks majority stake in Trina Solar’s tracker business - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Shenzhen Nanshan Power plans to acquire a 51% to 70% stake in Trina Solar’s tracker business through a cash transaction. The proposed deal could provide Trina Solar with additional capital as it navigates financial pressure and intensifying competition in China’s solar sector.
Vincent Shaw
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Trina’s Agile tracker is designed for one in portrait or two in landscape module installation.
Shenzhen Nanshan Power, a Chinese power producer backed by state-owned capital, plans to acquire a controlling stake in Trina Solar’s tracker business.
According to an Oct. 30 announcement, Shenzhen Nanshan Power signed a preliminary equity acquisition agreement with Trina Solar and its wholly owned subsidiary, Trina Solar (Changzhou) Science & Technology.
Under the proposed transaction, Shenzhen Nanshan Power would acquire a 51% to 70% stake in the Changzhou-based company operating TrinaTracker, Trina Solar’s solar tracking unit.
The target company, established in February 2019, is currently wholly owned by Trina Solar through its Changzhou subsidiary. If completed, the acquisition would give Shenzhen Nanshan Power control of the business and allow it to consolidate the subsidiary’s financial results.
The acquisition would be financed entirely in cash and is expected to qualify as a major asset restructuring under Chinese securities regulations. It would not involve the issuance of new shares or a change in Shenzhen Nanshan Power’s controlling shareholder.
The companies have yet to agree on the final equity stake, valuation or payment schedule. The purchase price will be determined following an independent asset valuation, while performance commitments and compensation arrangements are expected to be negotiated as part of a definitive agreement.
TrinaTracker supplies solar tracking systems, including its Vanguard-1P and Vanguard-2P products, alongside intelligent control technologies. According to Trina Solar, the business had delivered more than 43 GW of tracking systems across more than 70 countries by the end of 2025, with annual global production capacity exceeding 15 GW.
Wood Mackenzie ranked TrinaTracker second in its 2026 global tracker manufacturer assessment, which evaluates companies based on service capabilities, research and development, supply chain resilience and financial strength, rather than shipment volumes alone.
In comments to Chinese media on Nov. 2, Trina Solar said it intended to introduce a strategic partner to strengthen operational synergies. The company said it would continue to focus on its solar and energy storage businesses while developing integrated energy solutions and technologies for AI data centers.
The proposed sale comes amid continued financial pressure on China’s solar manufacturing sector. Trina Solar reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of CNY 1.94 billion ($285 million) for the first nine months of 2026, on revenue of CNY 47.98 billion.
Selling a majority stake in the tracker subsidiary could provide Trina Solar with additional capital while allowing it to retain a minority interest. The arrangement could also preserve opportunities for cooperation between its module and tracking systems businesses, although the companies have not disclosed any post-transaction supply or cooperation agreements.
The proposed deal reflects a broader push among Chinese renewable energy companies to explore ownership restructuring and strategic partnerships as they seek to balance investment requirements with business specialization amid intense competition.
Both companies stressed that negotiations remain at a preliminary stage. Due diligence, financial audits, asset valuation and corporate approvals must be completed before a binding agreement can be signed.

Chinese solar cell manufacturer Yingfa Ruineng has unveiled a 7.5 GW solar cell manufacturing plant in Indonesia. The facility, presented at technology launch event hosted by Yingfa Ruineng’s subsidiary BCI, will produce n-type tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) solar cells.

title: Behind-the-meter generation could deliver five times more grid relief than data center load shifting - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
An Ember analysis finds that data center load shifting could reduce peak electricity demand by up to 1.5% in Ireland by 2030, offering limited grid flexibility. Behind-the-meter generation and storage could provide nearly five times more relief, with potential reductions of up to 2.7 GW in Texas.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
The rapid deployment of data centers is placing substantial new loads on electricity systems that, in many cases, are not expanding at the same pace. An analysis published by Ember in October 2026 examines the extent to which data centers can provide grid flexibility through two mechanisms: shifting computing workloads and using behind-the-meter generation or storage. The study covers nine markets across the United States, Europe, and Southeast Asia, with particular relevance to Ireland, the United Kingdom, and Germany.
Ireland faces one of the largest impacts on electricity demand
Data centers could account for a significant share of peak electricity demand as their capacity expands. In Ireland, one of Europe’s leading data center hubs, they already account for approximately 19% of peak demand. In January 2025, when system demand peaked at 6 GW, data centers accounted for an estimated 1.1 GW. Ember projects that this share could rise to 24% by 2030, with data center demand reaching 1.6 GW against a system peak of 6.5 GW.
The challenge is particularly acute because of the mismatch between data center construction timelines and electricity infrastructure development. A large data center can require between 200 MW and 500 MW of power capacity and be built within 18 to 24 months, while conventional grid expansions can take four to 10 years.
Load shifting offers limited flexibility potential
Load shifting involves moving certain computing workloads to different times or locations to reduce demand during periods of grid stress. However, the composition of data center workloads significantly limits this option.
Cloud services, enterprise workloads, and artificial intelligence (AI) inference require low latency and currently account for most data center capacity. Ember estimates that these workloads will represent approximately 87% of global data center capacity by 2030. By contrast, AI model training offers greater flexibility, as workloads can be interrupted or relocated with fewer operational consequences.
Under Ember’s assumptions – 35% flexibility for AI training workloads, 5% for inference, and none for traditional data centers – approximately 6.5% of global data center capacity could theoretically be shifted. Factoring in an average utilization rate of approximately 48%, the capacity effectively available to respond to periods of grid stress falls to around 3%.
The impact on peak demand would therefore be limited. In Ireland, load shifting could reduce peak demand by approximately 100 MW by 2030, equivalent to 1.5% of the projected peak. Across the other markets analyzed, estimated reductions range from 0.1% to 0.6%.
Behind-the-meter generation and storage
An alternative offering greater flexibility involves maintaining computing workloads while temporarily replacing grid electricity with on-site generation or storage. This approach, known as bring-your-own-capacity (BYOC), can combine renewable generation, batteries, and other backup technologies.
The study finds that this approach could provide nearly five times as much grid relief as load shifting. For two large data centers analyzed in Texas, with a combined projected load of 5.6 GW, load shifting could reduce grid demand by approximately 0.55 GW during periods of stress, while on-site generation could reduce it by up to 2.7 GW.
Although the Texas example is outside Europe, it is relevant to the European regulatory debate because it illustrates the scale of flexibility that behind-the-meter resources could provide when grid connections become a bottleneck.
Ireland offers a European regulatory precedent. Initial proposals by the country’s energy regulator to impose flexibility requirements on data centers were replaced, following public consultation, with requirements for facilities of 10 MW or more to provide generation or storage capacity.
Energy sources determine system benefits
On-site generation does not automatically deliver decarbonization benefits. If it relies on fossil fuel-based technologies, it could lock in infrastructure and emissions for decades. There is also a risk of duplicating investments: a data center could install its own firm capacity while the system operator procures additional capacity to meet the same potential demand.
The report recommends integrating behind-the-meter resources into grid planning and connection requirements. Renewable generation and storage could enable data centers to reduce grid demand during critical hours without passing the costs of additional infrastructure on to other electricity consumers.
Storage is particularly relevant to this approach, as it can partially decouple data center electricity consumption from real-time grid availability and supply power during periods of congestion or peak demand.
Ember’s analysis indicates that no single flexibility solution is suitable for all data centers. Traditional computing and AI inference workloads, which could account for 87% of global data center capacity by 2030, offer limited scope for load shifting. For these facilities, renewable generation and behind-the-meter storage could be the primary means of reducing grid dependence during peak periods. Data centers dedicated to AI training, by contrast, offer greater potential to shift workloads across time or locations.

title: Hybrid wind-solar-battery plants can power Kazakhstan’s demand growth - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Ember analysis finds that hybrid wind, solar and battery plants could supply electricity at an average cost of $56/MWh in Kazakhstan, compared with $70–170/MWh for new coal, while meeting up to 90% of typical demand.
Patrick Jowett
03 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Asia-Pacific
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Hybrid power plants pairing wind and solar power with a battery can supply up to 90% of Kazakhstan’s typical demand profile for a delivered cost below $60/MWh, according to the
latest report
Ember’s report says Kazakhstan needs “new power capacity quickly”, with its electricity demand rising 16% in the last five years. Coal still dominates Kazakhstan’s electricity mix, supplying 62% of electricity generation in 2025, but its coal units are on average over 50 years old, leading to frequent equipment failures. Ember says there were 891 incidents of various severity between January and July this year.
“To replace its ageing infrastructure and keep pace with fast-growing demand, Kazakhstan needs to build more capacity quickly and ensure its availability during peak periods, including winter demand spikes,” Ember’s report says. “The capacity also needs to be built close to where demand is to relieve pressure on the transmission network.”
Ember’s research analysed 15 sites, chosen for their proximity to a major demand centre and an existing power line, across all three of Kazakhstan’s power zones. It tested 125 combinations of wind, solar and battery capacity at each site, producing 1,875 simulations. Each configuration was simulated hour by hour over a 30-year project life using site a typical hourly demand profile that represented national demand patterns and was scaled to a peak of 100 MW.
Results found the best-performing configurations at each site could supply between 70% and 90% of the electricity in a typical demand profile, hour by hour, over 30 years, at a delivered cost below $60/MWh.
“This cost represents the plant’s lifetime cost per MWh actually delivered, including the cost of curtailed output,” Ember’s report says. Across all 15 sites, the average delivered electricity cost is $56/MWh. Ember says this is significantly cheaper compared to new coal, which costs $70-170/MWh, depending on the region and technology.
Kostantsa Rangelova, Senior Battery Analyst at Ember, told
pv magazine
that while there is real potential for solar-plus-battery projects in Kazakhstan, the potential is even greater when wind is added.
“Solar is really cheap and very fast to build here,” Rangelova said. “Shifting some of it to the evening with a battery unlocks its full value, making its potential contribution to electricity supply larger than with standalone solar.”
Rangelova added that the challenge for solar lies in the Kazakh winter, which often brings cloudy days that mean solar-plus-storage produces less when demand is highest.
“Solar-battery projects do not need wind to be viable, but on their own they are a summer-heavy source of power,” she continued.
“Kazakhstan’s advantage is its vast untapped wind, which is strongest in exactly those winter months. Combining wind and solar behind one grid connection, overbuilding generation capacity and accepting some curtailment by design means only a small battery is needed to reach a high capacity factor at low cost.”
Ember’s hybrid simulations feature curtailment by design in order to minimise the battery need and make it possible to meet over 70% of winter demand at most sites. The report explains that deliberately oversizing the generation means there is enough generation even on less windy and sunny days when paired with a small battery.
This offers a capacity factor comparable to that of a baseload power station, it continues, but at a lower cost than new coal.
Rangelova also told
pv magazine
the report findings can be very relevant for renewable energy procurement schemes, explaining that while hybrid plants provide flexibility for the power service, their service needs to be rewarded and priced into procurement costs.
“An auction that asks for a specific supply profile and lets bidders find the lowest-cost mix of wind, solar and battery to meet that profile would price that flexibility in and lower system costs,” she suggested.
Rangelova also recommended batteries have access to balancing, reserve and capacity revenues in order to provide the best value for the investment made in them.
“Batteries co-located with renewables under a mandate that only shift their own plant’s output remain underused and never deliver their full value to the system,” she said. “It is like owning a Swiss Army knife and only ever using the blade.”
Figures released by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy in April put the country’s cumulative renewables capacity at 3.7 GW, including
1.37 GW of solar
. At the time, the ministry said it planned to commission 245 MW of renewables this year, including five solar projects with a combined capacity of 92.6 MW.
Additional figures from Ember’s report says wind and solar could supply 23% of Kazakhstan’s electricity generation by 2035, up from 6% in 2025, bringing total renewables generation to 35%.

title: Longi launches 690 W solar panels with 25.54% efficiency for rooftops
content: Chinese solar manufacturer Longi has introduced rooftop solar modules rated up to 690 W, using a conductive backsheet that replaces conventional soldered ribbons to boost output and reduce potential connection failures.Unveiled at All Energy Australia 2026 in Melbourne on October 28–29, the Hi-MO X12 series targets residential, commercial and industrial rooftops. The modules combine the company’s hybrid passivated back contact (HPBC) 2.0 cells with a redesigned electrical interconnection structure.Longi said the design removes more than 15,000 potential solder-joint failure points per module. Australian pricing, initial shipment volumes and a commercial delivery schedule have not been disclosed.Metal foil replaces soldered ribbonsThe new architecture embeds conductive metal foil circuits within the module’s rear encapsulation structure. Solar cells connect directly to this conductive backsheet, replacing the conventional soldered ribbons used to link cells.According to Longi, the design increases the current-carrying cross-sectional area by 85 percent, delivering an additional 6 W to 8 W compared with conventional interconnection designs.The modules also incorporate what the manufacturer calls Full-Screen Technology. This combines shingled cell layouts with hidden busbars to reduce inactive areas and shading on the front of the module.Longi attributes a further 8 W to 12 W gain to that arrangement, bringing the combined power increase to between 14 W and 20 W.The company also claimed its ultra-thin stacking process reduces internal stress by 60 percent, while an integrated metal foil barrier cuts water vapor transmission by 90 percent.Two formats for rooftop installationsThe larger LR7-72WVD module, intended for commercial and industrial applications, offers power ratings from 660 W to 690 W. Longi reported a maximum module efficiency exceeding 25.54 percent.The smaller LR7-54WVD series comes in four power classes between 495 W and 510 W. Its datasheet lists efficiencies ranging from 24.25 percent to 24.99 percent under standard test conditions.This 108-cell, dual-glass module measures 1,800 mm by 1,134 mm by 30 mm and weighs 51.8 pounds (23.5 kg). It uses a black anodized aluminum frame, with 2.0 mm front glass and 1.6 mm rear glass.The datasheet specified a temperature coefficient of -0.26 percent per degree Celsius, an operating range of -40°F to 185°F (-40°C to 85°C), and a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V.Warranty covers 30 years of performanceThe LR7-54WVD series carries a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty.Longi guaranteed no more than 1 percent degradation in the first year, followed by annual degradation of 0.35 percent. That corresponds to approximately 88.9 percent of the module’s initial power output after 30 years.The datasheet lists front and rear static load ratings of 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively. It also specifies resistance to impacts from 25 mm hailstones traveling at 23 m/s.IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 are listed among the applicable certification standards, alongside certification marks from TÜV Rheinland and TÜV SÜD.At the Melbourne event, Longi also introduced its Hi-MO 9 Prime utility-scale module and displayed LongiBank 3.0 and OneMatrix energy storage solutions, together with its Longi Block modular photovoltaic system.

title: AGIBOT puts six humanoid robots in 24-hour convenience store challenge
content: Chinese robotics company AGIBOT launched a 24-hour convenience-store challenge featuring six G2 humanoid robots working alongside human customers. The livestream, titled “Robots Never Clock Out,” ran from November 2 to November 3, giving viewers an extended look at the robots performing everyday retail tasks. Their assigned duties included stocking shelves, preparing coffee and hot food, greeting customers, and clearing rubbish. According to the firm, the challenge was designed to test the robots across different store conditions, including rush-hour crowds, overnight operations, and the morning breakfast rush.Humanoids tackle retailAGIBOT deployed six G2 humanoid robots in a convenience store for a 24-hour challenge designed to demonstrate their ability to perform everyday retail tasks. The event gave viewers an extended look at the robots operating in a real-world retail environment alongside human customers and store staff.The robots are expected to handle several tasks, including stocking and organizing shelves, preparing coffee and hot food, greeting customers, and clearing rubbish. AGIBOT has divided the challenge into four operating periods: the lunch rush, evening rush, late-night duty, and breakfast preparation.Robots Never Clock Out | AGIBOT G2’s 24-Hour Convenience Store Challenge Six AGIBOT G2 take on a 24-hour shift as convenience store trainees. From rush-hour crowds to late-night solo duty and the morning breakfast sprint, can they keep up with nonstop customers and…— AGIBOT (@AGIBOTofficial) November 2, 2026The schedule was intended to expose the machines to different working conditions, from periods of heavy customer activity to overnight operations and the morning breakfast rush.The convenience-store setting brought together several technical requirements. The G2 robots navigated spaces shared with people, interacted with merchandise, reach and manipulated objects, and responded to customer requests while other activities continued around them.These tasks require more than basic movement. Stocking shelves involves locating merchandise, reaching for individual items, and placing them in the appropriate positions. Preparing coffee and hot food requires the robots to interact with equipment and objects in a controlled manner, while customer-facing duties involve responding to requests and operating around people.The different operating periods also introduce variations in the environment. During rush hours, robots must work around increased customer activity and potentially obstructed routes. Overnight operations provide a different set of conditions, while breakfast preparation introduces another sequence of tasks.AGIBOT tests autonomyThe 24-hour livestream offered a longer observation window than a short demonstration, allowing viewers to see not only successful task completion but also potential pauses, repeated attempts, and recovery from difficulties.For example, an item may be hard to grasp, a customer may block a robot’s route, or an unexpected request may interrupt an ongoing task. How the machines respond to these situations could better indicate their practical capabilities than isolated demonstrations of individual movements.The challenge followed AGIBOT’s AI Day announcements, which included new AI models, the G2 Max robot, and a proposed Worken measure of productive robot work. The company presents the convenience-store event as a practical demonstration of its technologies working together in an everyday environment. However, the announced 24-hour duration refers to the livestream and does not establish that each robot operates continuously without charging, maintenance, or human assistance.The promotional material reviewed also does not specify a complete intervention policy or a scoring system for measuring task success. Experts highlighted that these details will be important when evaluating the robots’ performance. The number of tasks completed, time required for individual activities, frequency of human intervention, and ability to recover from unsuccessful attempts would provide useful measures of their effectiveness.For now, the livestream offers an extended opportunity to observe six G2 robots performing a range of retail activities in a shared environment. It could provide a more detailed picture of how humanoid robots handle routine work beyond controlled demonstrations, although the event’s duration alone is not evidence of fully autonomous, uninterrupted operation.

title: OpenAI expands security testing with help from external experts
content: OpenAI is bringing outside security researchers into its next internal security sprint, giving them access to its models to help find weaknesses in its defenses.The company is partnering with Cathedral Systems, whose researchers will work alongside OpenAI’s teams to test its systems and help strengthen protections across its platforms.The planned exercise builds on an earlier sprint that involved 25 percent of OpenAI’s product engineers. Alongside the partnership, the company is increasing its Security Bug Bounty rewards, with exceptional findings eligible for up to $172,000, including bonuses.OpenAI has not specified when the next sprint will begin. It framed the effort as part of a broader push to use AI continuously to identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.Outside researchers join defense testingCathedral’s researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside the company’s own security teams to challenge its defenses. OpenAI said the partnership would bring different expertise and approaches to identifying weaknesses.The collaboration will also involve testing fixes, according to Gavin Kliger, Cathedral’s CEO and co-founder.“OpenAI is setting an important example by partnering with outside security firms and using its own models to continuously test and strengthen its defenses. Every company should be thinking about how to put these capabilities to work,” Kliger said.“We’re excited to collaborate with OpenAI’s teams, combining their models and security expertise with our research to find weaknesses, test fixes, and strengthen this approach to continuous defense,” he added. The announcement describes a planned collaboration rather than completed findings. It does not identify specific vulnerabilities discovered through the new partnership or detail the systems researchers will examine.Higher rewards for critical findingsOpenAI is also more than quadrupling rewards for critical findings under its Security Bug Bounty program. The maximum payment of $172,000, including bonuses, applies to exceptional findings.The company said it wants researchers to challenge its assumptions and strengthen both its systems and the methods used to defend them.During the previous internal sprint, engineers used Codex to investigate findings, reproduce vulnerabilities in isolated environments, and prepare patches for review. OpenAI dedicated a quarter of its product engineers to that effort.The next sprint is intended to build on this work by bringing new researchers and security partners together with internal teams.Expanding access to AI defense toolsOpenAI said traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient, pointing to recent industry incidents as evidence of how quickly threats can emerge. Its stated goal is to build continuous defensive loops that find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.Beyond its internal systems, the company is making its most capable models available to Daybreak customers. It has committed $1 billion in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure.OpenAI is also sharing its architecture and lessons from its previous sprint, along with a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.The company said it would keep advancing its models, applying them to its own defenses and expanding access for trusted defenders as AI becomes better at finding vulnerabilities.

title: China debuts world's first 800V DC power system for smart data centers
content: A Chinese green tech company has recently made history with the launch of the world’s first commercially deployed, fully integrated 800-volt direct current (DC) power system at a massive artificial intelligence (AI) data center.Shanghai’s Envision Energy announced the technology on Monday, November 2. It is currently powering live computer workloads at the company’s Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China.The platform combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage, as well as smart controls to deliver electricity from the grid to computing equipment. As per company representatives, it could cut energy loses, lower infrastructure costs, and support more powerful AI servers within the same space. Kevin Huang, Envision Energy’s senior VP, pointed to the technology’s potential. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” Huang explained. Powering AI serversAs AI data centers expand, they require more electricity to run. Reports show that global data center power demand could surge by 160 percent by 2030. Moreover, research suggests data centers alone could require as much as 68 gigawatts (GW) of capacity worldwide by 2027, roughly equivalent to California’s power grid. But delivering that power efficiently remains a massive challenge. Traditional data center power systems utilize multiple conversion stages to deliver electricity from the grid to servers. These stages require additional equipment, cables, and space.To address these challenge, Envision came up with a new system that can convert electricity directly from a 10-kilovolt (kV) medium-voltage input to an 800-volt DC power system. It reduces the need for extra equipment and copper cables, leaving more room for computer hardware.To maintain a stable electricity supply, the firm integrated solid-state transformers with battery energy storage. The batteries can also respond to sudden changes in power demand within seconds and provide backup power for several minutes. At the same time, Envision’s Dubhe Controller, coordinates both the transformers and the batteries through its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model. As a result, the system can respond to rapid changes in electricity demand within milliseconds.Targeting more powerEnvision’s Galaxy AI data center campus began operations in August 2026. It has a planned capacity of three gigawatts (GW). Once fully developed, the facility is expected to support up to one million AI accelerators operating simultaneously.Huang said the system uses renewable energy to power AI workloads. “This is a critical step in turning power-compute coordination from a strategic vision into an operational reality,” he concluded in a press release.In the future, the company aims to source more than 80 percent of the campus’s electricity through direct renewable energy connections. The power architecture could serve as a reference for other data centers as the industry moves toward 800-volt DC infrastructure. “Already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, the system provides a reference for the industry’s transition to 800V DC,” the firm stated. It also aims to expand the technology via its Mission Gobi initiative. It targets five GW of green AI data center capacity across desert regions worldwide by 2030.

title: US rival tests cruise missile cluster warhead with 6-hectare reach
content: North Korea has tested a dispersal warhead designed for a strategic cruise missile, claiming it can devastate a target area of up to 6 hectares. The test also assessed the missile’s ability to strike targets vertically, as Pyongyang continues to expand its range of weapons systems.The tests were conducted on Monday, November 2, and overseen by Full Gen. Kim Jong-sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea’s Central Military Commission, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).North Korea’s Warhead Institute, which operates under its Missile Administration, said the medium-sized dispersal warhead could turn an area of 5 to 6 hectares into ashes at what it described as the highest-density power.The country’s Cruise Missile System Institute also reported improvements to the missile’s terminal maneuverability, saying the changes had established its ability to conduct vertical strikes while accounting for the natural and geographical characteristics of the target area.Cruise missile gains vertical strike capabilityThe reported test involved two assessments: the destructive power of the dispersal warhead and the missile’s flight characteristics during a vertical strike. North Korea did not provide details about the missile’s range, flight profile or the technical changes behind the claimed improvement.A dispersal warhead is designed to release multiple smaller explosive devices, known as submunitions, over a wider area. Such weapons can threaten several targets within the affected zone rather than concentrating their effects on a single point.The Missile Administration’s director described the tests as a demonstration of “practical combat power.” The official also said developing different weapon systems was increasingly urgent, arguing that the country’s armed forces needed to defend national security and deter external threats.Cluster warheads expand weapons optionsThe cruise missile test followed another weapons trial on Saturday, October 31, when North Korea tested a cluster warhead designed for tactical ballistic missiles.KCNA reported that the standard Type 2 cluster warhead could devastate an area of 12 to 13 hectares at its highest density. That figure is separate from the 5-to-6-hectare area claimed for the dispersal warhead tested on Monday.North Korea’s Missile Administration said its cluster warheads fall into four categories, depending on their intended purpose. An official said the country planned to make the different types available to military units by the end of 2026, allowing them to select weapons based on operational requirements and target characteristics.The two tests indicate that Pyongyang is working on dispersal warheads for both tactical ballistic missiles and strategic cruise missiles. However, the claims about their destructive power and improved flight capabilities come from North Korean state media and have not been independently verified.North Korea has also tested other weapons systems in recent weeks, including attack drones, a precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile. The latest trials add to its efforts to broaden the capabilities of its armed forces.
