title: OpenAI builds custom Git backend in 10 weeks after 2,442% commit surge
content: OpenAI has developed a new Git backend called Pando to handle the growing volume of code changes generated by its engineers and Codex agents. The system now powers development across OpenAI’s monorepo, processing nearly one petabyte of Git data daily.The infrastructure addresses a problem that emerged as Codex accelerated software development. More engineers and autonomous agents now work on separate code changes simultaneously. Their activity creates a growing stream of branch updates, code reviews, merges, and repository downloads.OpenAI says Pando has reduced median Git push latency by nearly 80 percent. It has also improved merge reliability to 99.99 percent, compared with earlier periods when reliability sometimes dropped below 90 percent.Codex pushes Git to its limitsOpenAI’s monorepo experienced a sharp increase in development activity over the past year. Its quarterly commit growth reached 2,442 percent in Q4 2026 compared with Q1 2024.Traditional Git infrastructure struggled to accommodate the resulting workload. Engineers encountered slower pushes and downloads, alongside failed merges. Multiple automated jobs also fetched identical commits after individual code submissions.We built Pando, a new Git backend for our monorepo, to handle more pushes and fetches without changing how our engineers and agents use Git.Pando cut push latency by ~80% and now serves nearly a petabyte of Git data a day. We can grow Git capacity alongside agent usage. pic.twitter.com/4c0YXOfKqK— OpenAI Developers (@OpenAIDevs) November 3, 2026OpenAI wanted to address these bottlenecks without replacing Git or forcing developers to adopt unfamiliar tools. Its engineers therefore designed Pando around the existing Git protocol and command-line client.The approach preserves familiar development workflows while changing how servers coordinate updates and distribute repository data. It also allows improvements to the underlying Git client to benefit the wider developer community.Conventional Git infrastructure can struggle when thousands of developers update different branches simultaneously. Some distributed systems coordinate changes across multiple repository replicas. Others rely on a shared write-ahead log to establish update order.Both approaches introduce potential bottlenecks. Coordinating updates across replicas increases communication overhead. A shared log can also force unrelated branch updates to compete for the same resource.Pando takes a different approach through causal consistency. It coordinates updates independently for individual branches instead of imposing one global sequence. When a developer pushes code, Pando stores the incoming Git packfile in cloud object storage. Its metadata service then records the updated branch version and its dependencies.This arrangement allows unrelated branches to accept updates concurrently. However, readers examining multiple branches might see different update versions. Individual branch updates remain consistent. Pando also reuses previously generated packfiles during downloads. This reduces the computing work required to serve identical repository data repeatedly.Caches accelerate repository downloadsThe architecture uses regional caching to distribute Git data closer to developers and automated systems. Its Express delivery service stores packfiles in regional caches.OpenAI reports cache hit rates exceeding 99 percent. The company has also demonstrated clone and fetch operations saturating 10-gigabit-per-second network connections.Background compaction further improves performance. Workers combine smaller packfiles into larger groups, reducing download overhead and speeding up repository history searches.Built with Codex in 10 weeksOpenAI says it developed Pando with Codex in just 10 weeks. A single engineer designed its core architecture, while teams of agents handled implementation.The system entered production in April 2026. OpenAI implemented it in Rust and developed extensive testing tools to identify concurrency bugs.Pando has since handled more than 57 terabytes of Git packfiles in a single hour. The company says it achieved this using more than 99 percent locally cached data.OpenAI also plans to explore broader applications for Pando. Its architecture could support other environments where large numbers of software agents collaborate on shared repositories.

title: Scientists build virtual Earth to help search for alien life
content: Scientists have built a computer model of Earth without life to help determine whether distant planets could host living organisms or merely have conditions that resemble those of an inhabited world.Researchers at the University of Washington developed a simulation that models how chemicals move between a planet’s core, mantle, crust, surface and atmosphere over billions of years. The model could help astronomers identify atmospheric signals on rocky exoplanets that cannot be explained by geological and other non-biological processes.The distinction matters as scientists search for signs of life beyond our solar system. Astronomers have cataloged more than 6,000 exoplanets and are examining the atmospheres of promising worlds for gases that could indicate biological activity. However, finding a potentially habitable planet does not establish that life exists there.To address this challenge, the researchers simulated Earth’s geochemical evolution over five billion years, covering its formation around 4.5 billion years ago and extending roughly 500 million years into the future. The model excludes the influence of living organisms, allowing scientists to examine how a planet’s systems could evolve without biology.Simulating a lifeless EarthThe simulation builds on an earlier model developed in the laboratory of Rory Barnes, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Washington. Previous versions included the planet’s core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation but did not account for the surface and atmosphere.Lead author Samantha Gilbert-Janizek expanded the model to include those missing systems, creating a more complete picture of how chemicals move throughout a rocky planet. The simulation reproduced 19 planetary properties, including heat flow through Earth’s mantle.The model provides a baseline for understanding what a planet’s atmosphere might look like without life. Researchers can adjust its inputs to represent other rocky exoplanets and test whether their observed atmospheric conditions can be reproduced through non-biological processes.This could help scientists avoid mistaking geological activity for evidence of extraterrestrial organisms. A planet might have an atmosphere containing chemicals associated with life, but those gases could also arise from interactions between its interior, surface and atmosphere.Distinguishing life from geologyEarth offers an example of why this distinction is important. Living organisms continually release gases such as oxygen and methane into the atmosphere. These gases react with one another, so their simultaneous presence can suggest that biological processes are replenishing them.An astronomer observing Earth from another star system might therefore consider the combination a possible sign of life. But scientists first need to understand whether non-biological processes could produce similar atmospheric conditions on other worlds.The new model allows researchers to test that possibility. If a planet’s observed atmosphere can be reproduced without including life, the findings may offer a non-biological explanation. If the simulation cannot reproduce the observations, the planet could become a more interesting target for further investigation.The researchers say the work could also inform the design of future space telescopes, including NASA’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which is intended to study potentially habitable planets around other stars.The study does not identify an inhabited exoplanet or detect extraterrestrial life. Instead, it provides a tool for improving how scientists interpret atmospheric observations and distinguish potentially biological signals from the natural evolution of a planet.The study appears in The Planetary Science Journal.

title: US strikes target Iran's Qeshm Island and underground missile base
content: The U.S. military has quietly expanded its campaign against Iran, conducting limited strikes on Qeshm Island as Washington weighs diplomatic options and prepares for a possible return to wider combat.U.S. officials confirmed Monday’s operation, describing it as a defensive response to Iranian surface-to-air missile threats against American assets. The strikes also aimed to limit Tehran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping near the Strait of Hormuz.The operation signals that American forces remain engaged despite President Donald Trump’s public suggestions that the conflict has largely ended. It also raises questions about whether Washington can maintain its military pressure without triggering another major confrontation.Strikes target strategic islandQeshm Island occupies a critical position near the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping routes. Iran operates strategic military infrastructure there, including an underground missile facility and a naval base.The island also hosts a major desalination plant, making it an important part of the region’s infrastructure. Its location gives Iranian forces a strategic position near shipping lanes used by commercial vessels.Explosions reportedly occurred across parts of Qeshm on Monday, according to social media reports. The U.S. has previously targeted the island during earlier phases of the conflict.Washington has also considered seizing the territory, according to reports. However, Monday’s strikes appeared limited and did not indicate preparations for an immediate ground operation.American officials told the Wall Street Journal that Washington had conducted similar attacks secretly in recent weeks. The administration has avoided publicly announcing these operations to prevent signaling a return to large-scale warfare.Pentagon prepares wider optionsThe latest strikes follow weeks of military planning inside the Trump administration. Senior officials have discussed additional airstrikes and presented the president with several options.Those options reportedly include tighter economic sanctions and expanding restrictions on Iranian trade. U.S. Central Command has also prepared for broader military operations.Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, visited the White House last week. He briefed Trump on the conflict and potential military responses.The Pentagon has strengthened its regional posture in recent weeks. American forces have moved additional missile defenses and munitions into the region.Washington has also warned Gulf countries about a possible short, intense military operation after Tuesday’s midterm elections. Such preparations suggest the administration wants to retain the ability to escalate quickly.Trump keeps diplomacy openTrump has recently softened his public position on renewed military action. On Monday, he dismissed suggestions that another round of major strikes would immediately follow the elections.Speaking to reporters, Trump said the United States had already won its confrontation with Iran. He questioned whether the current situation even qualified as a war.The president also suggested that negotiations could produce an agreement. Vice President JD Vance echoed that assessment, saying Washington and Tehran had made progress toward ending hostilities.Iranian officials have maintained that any agreement depends on American concessions. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had clearly communicated its demands.Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has also warned that Iran would retaliate if Washington reignited the conflict. His threats extend beyond the Middle East.The competing signals leave the region facing an uncertain military outlook. Washington continues to strike Iranian targets while keeping diplomatic channels open.Whether those negotiations can prevent another major confrontation remains unclear. The limited operations on Qeshm demonstrate that the United States has not abandoned military pressure.

title: New process targets rare earths in discarded computer hard drives
content: Discarded computer hard drives could become a source of critical raw materials for electric vehicles, wind turbines and other technologies. Researchers in Germany are testing two processes to recover valuable metals from old magnets, including a method that uses ammonium chloride instead of conventional hydrochloric acid.The work is part of the European Union-funded NEO-CYCLE project, in which researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems (IKTS) are working with TU Bergakademie Freiberg to recover neodymium, iron and boron from discarded hard disk drives (HDDs).Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are among the strongest permanent magnets available. They are used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines and electronic products such as speakers, smartphones and hard drives. However, recovering their constituent materials at the required purity for reuse is technically challenging.Neodymium is particularly important because around 90 percent of the material is imported from China, according to Fraunhofer. Much of Europe’s collected magnet waste is also sent to China for processing before the recovered materials are imported again.Recovering metals from old magnetsThe NEO-CYCLE researchers are evaluating two approaches to separate valuable materials from magnets found in discarded computers and laptops.The first is solid-state chlorination, which is being developed by project partner TU Bergakademie Freiberg. Instead of conventional hydrochloric acid, the process uses ammonium chloride added to a mixture containing neodymium, iron and boron recovered from magnet waste.When heated, the mixture is converted into metal chlorides and a high-purity ammonia solution. The approach builds on a patented process already used to recycle fluorescent lamps, which researchers are now testing for magnet recovery.Initial results indicate that the method can separate metal chlorides from magnet material more efficiently, allowing nearly all the metals to be extracted while using comparatively small amounts of chemicals.The second approach uses electrochemical processing. Researchers place powdered magnet waste in an electrochemical cell, where an electrolyte such as diluted sulfuric acid provides the medium for chemical reactions.This process initially extracts boron into a solution, which can then be concentrated for use in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries.Separating valuable materials for reuseAfter the initial processing, researchers at Fraunhofer IKTS use hydrometallurgical techniques to separate the resulting materials. The team applies selective processing to recover neodymium and iron, allowing the metals to be obtained in pure salt forms.The recovered materials can then undergo further processing by project partners for applications across several industries. These include chemicals, pharmaceuticals, hydrogen production, and fertilizers.The researchers are also exploring ways to turn the recovered materials into higher-value products rather than simply extracting them from waste. This could help establish a circular supply chain in which discarded electronic components become feedstock for new industrial applications.The four-year NEO-CYCLE project is funded through the European Union’s Horizon Europe program. Researchers have completed laboratory-scale testing of the recovery approaches, while plans for a pilot plant are underway.The aim is to develop an economically and environmentally viable process that can recover high-quality materials from end-of-life magnets while reducing chemical and water consumption. If successful, the approach could help Europe make better use of its electronic waste and reduce its dependence on imported critical raw materials.

title: US Navy's 1,200-mph Super Hornets to carry four hypersonic missiles
content: The U.S. Navy is preparing to add a new class of high-speed strike weapons to its carrier-based fighter fleet. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle recently examined Blackbeard, a hypersonic missile developed by defense startup Castelion, during a visit to Naval Air Station Patuxent River in Maryland.The October 28 visit provided a closer look at the weapon’s progress toward integration with the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet. The Navy has already conducted an initial flight evaluation, with further testing planned before the missile enters operational service.Caudle inspected the weapon at Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 (VX-23), which handles weapons testing at the installation. The visit also included discussions about the Navy’s broader approach to developing autonomous aircraft and extending the reach of carrier-based operations.Hypersonic weapon nears testingBlackbeard falls into the hypersonic category, which covers weapons capable of exceeding Mach 5. Its flight profile also allows it to change direction during atmospheric flight. This combination could complicate interception attempts by adversary air defense networks.Integrating the weapon onto the Super Hornet has already produced several testing milestones. A Navy presentation in August showed two Blackbeard test articles mounted beneath the fighter’s wings.Engineers took the next step on September 18. A Super Hornet departed Patuxent River carrying two missiles during a developmental flight. The aircraft completed the sortie without releasing either weapon, allowing the Navy to evaluate how the fighter handles their additional weight and external configuration.Coming soon to a theater near you…BLACKBEARD!@USPACOM @CENTCOM @PAEAviation pic.twitter.com/KgBtIqdf8I— NAVAIR (@NAVAIRNews) September 25, 2026Footage released by the Navy on September 25 documented the flight. The service ultimately wants each Super Hornet to accommodate four Blackbeard missiles, potentially giving individual aircraft a substantial strike payload.Navy increases missile ordersCastelion has positioned Blackbeard as a more affordable alternative to existing American hypersonic weapons. The California-based startup was founded by former SpaceX engineers and aims to simplify production to increase manufacturing capacity.The Navy awarded the company a $105 million agreement in April to advance integration with the Super Hornet. The program also includes preparations for live-fire evaluations in the Indo-Pacific.Procurement activity has gathered pace since then. In June, the Navy purchased 50 pre-production missiles for $23.4 million. A September agreement added a production order worth up to $200 million. USNI News reported that the deal covers 444 missiles.@USNavyCNO, meet Blackbeard. pic.twitter.com/xgu5pBVEJJ— Castelion (@Castelion) November 2, 2026The Pentagon has also outlined much larger ambitions for the weapon. A framework agreement calls for at least 500 missiles annually once testing concludes. The Department of War has also indicated plans to seek funding for more than 12,000 units over five years.Multiple launch platforms plannedThe Super Hornet represents just one potential application for Blackbeard. Castelion is pursuing compatibility with several other military platforms.The U.S. Army’s HIMARS rocket artillery system is among the planned launch platforms. The company has also begun adapting the weapon for the Air Force’s F-16 under a research agreement.Naval operations could eventually involve unmanned vessels, too. Castelion intends to demonstrate a launch from Saronic’s Marauder unmanned surface vessel in 2027.The Navy is working toward early operational capability, which would allow a limited missile inventory to reach frontline units. Additional developmental flights at Patuxent River will help prepare the weapon for subsequent live-fire evaluations.An important milestone remains outstanding. The Navy has yet to announce a date for Blackbeard’s first live launch from a Super Hornet. That test will provide a clearer indication of the weapon’s readiness for deployment.

title: New satellite handoff tech cuts network switching to milliseconds
content: Your phone could soon stay connected even when it moves beyond cellular tower coverage, switching seamlessly to satellites instead.AT&T and AST SpaceMobile have demonstrated what they believe is the industry’s first successful handoff between a ground-based cellular network and a direct-to-device satellite network.The milestone could help smartphones switch between conventional cell towers and satellites without dropping calls or losing data connections, bringing seamless satellite connectivity closer to commercial use.The demonstration took place on October 21 at 8:15 a.m. PT near Granite Falls, Washington. It builds on earlier tests in which AST SpaceMobile’s BlueBird satellites supported voice calls, text messages, and video calls using everyday smartphones. The latest test addressed a different challenge: transferring a connection between two networks operating through very different infrastructure.Bridging two network worldsUnder the arrangement, AT&T provides the terrestrial wireless network, while AST SpaceMobile operates the satellite network designed to connect directly with standard smartphones. Ericsson and Nokia supplied the technologies needed to coordinate the transition between them.Ericsson provided AT&T with combined radio and core network technology, alongside intelligent network automation. According to the company, this technology is designed to reduce handoff transition times between ground-based and satellite networks from seconds to milliseconds, helping minimize interruptions as phones move between the two types of coverage.Nokia supplied radio access technology and mobility software for AST SpaceMobile’s satellite network. These technologies support the transfer of connections between terrestrial networks and satellite coverage, helping maintain service continuity as users move between them.The companies are working to make satellite connectivity function as an extension of existing mobile networks rather than a separate service that users must manually activate. This could allow smartphones to move between available ground-based and space-based coverage without requiring users to change devices or network settings.The approach is particularly relevant to areas where conventional cellular infrastructure is difficult to establish or maintain. Remote communities, highways and disaster-hit locations could benefit from satellite coverage that complements existing wireless networks.Moving toward commercial serviceFor AT&T, the satellite network is intended to extend its existing wireless coverage rather than replace terrestrial infrastructure. The company said the integration could help keep customers, first responders, and essential workers connected in locations where traditional mobile coverage is limited.The latest demonstration is an important step, but the technology is not yet ready for widespread commercial use. AT&T said the next phase is expected to include beta services under real-world conditions, allowing the companies to further refine network performance before moving toward commercial deployment.Robert Walters, AT&T’s senior vice president of network, described the successful handoff as a significant milestone, while noting that further testing remains necessary.AST SpaceMobile is developing its BlueBird satellite constellation to deliver 4G and 5G cellular broadband directly to standard, unmodified mobile devices. Its satellites use large communication arrays designed to connect with smartphones without requiring specialized satellite handsets.The companies have not announced a firm commercial launch date for the seamless handoff service. The upcoming beta phase will help determine how reliably the technology performs outside controlled demonstrations and across different coverage conditions.If successful, the development could make satellite connectivity a more seamless part of everyday mobile networks, allowing users to remain connected even when they move beyond the reach of conventional cell towers.

title: US student's jet drone claims world record with 491 mph flight
content: A jet-powered drone built in the dormitory of a U.S. university broke the world record for the fastest jet-powered aircraft, according to a social media post by the Georgia Tech aerospace engineering student Tomas Salvo.​The aircraft, which he named Reaper, hit a speed of 491 miles per hour (790km/hr) and carried a payload of 2.6 pounds (1.2 Kg).​The radio-controlled (RC) drone climbed a maximum height of 6500 feet, covering a total range of 31 miles at the full speed and maintained the flight at that speed for four minutes.Smallest jet-powered drones​He built three such models, and each of them achieved the record speed, Salvo said, claiming them to be “the world’s fastest small jet-powered drones.”​The engineer added the aircraft he built can be launched either from a truck or railway track, reaching peak heights in less than 20 seconds.​”Reaper can be rail- or truck-launched, climb to 2,000 m (6,600 ft) in under 20 seconds, then fly for 50 km (31 mi) at full speed,” he posted on his social media account.​In a video posted online, Salvo, along with two others, was seen demonstrating the launch from an open field, with screeching sounds heard in the background as the aircraft engine ignited before giving it a final thrust for the launch.3D-printed titanium nozzle​Built using 3D-printing, his aircraft has a titanium nozzle on its engine that replaces the stock nozzle. This allows the engine to sit comfortably much further forward and improves the center of gravity without adding extra weight in the frontal region. The exterior is made of custom-molded carbon fiber with a laser-cut internal structure, keeping it lightweight at a total of 11 pounds.​Young engineers claimed record speeds, yet he is still far from reaching Mach 1, which stands at 767.3 mph (1,234.8 km/h).​Earlier in October, a team of graduates from Bath University made a similar attempt to reach 0.8 Mach speeds with their 3D-printed, jet-powered remote-controlled aircraft, Kingchaser. The aircraft, which measured just under a meter, was made out of thermoplastics, Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol-modified (PETG), carbon fiber-reinforced polyphenylene sulfide (PPS-CF), carbon-fiber rods, and aluminum.​It reached a top speed of 205 mph (330 km/hr) when propelled by a miniature jet turbine capable of generating 63 newtons (N) of thrust.​The initial plan involved housing a 150 N jet engine to hit the speed of 614 mph (988km/h). However, the team opted to build a 20 percent larger craft that weighed nearly 20 pounds (9 Kg), heavier than Salvo’s reaper.​The team also used Titanium in their design but limited it to the exhaust sheets to protect the aircraft from the engine’s heat. The main skeleton was composed of an aluminum frame and reinforced with steel to mount the engine.​In the latest demonstration by the U.S. student on October 30, Reaper exceeded the peak speeds reached by Kingchaser by nearly 2.5 times, showcasing a robust engineering design and performance.After his latest tests, Salvos was confident that he has built a reliable and repeatable system. He hopes to push the top speeds past 500 mph (800 km/hr) with small optimization tweaks during his future tests.

title: Hackers turn freezers into 122-degree ovens in six-country attack
content: Cyberattacks against supermarket refrigeration systems have disrupted grocery operations across Europe, with hackers remotely manipulating temperature controls and destroying perishable food. The incidents affected dozens of stores across several countries, exposing the risks associated with connecting industrial equipment to remotely accessible digital systems.Refrigerators and freezers reportedly reached temperatures exceeding 120 degrees Fahrenheit during Monday’s attacks. Affected retailers operate across Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Estonia. The incidents also follow a similar wave of attacks against French supermarkets in October.Investigators have yet to identify those responsible. No hacking group has claimed responsibility for either wave of incidents.Major grocery chains affectedSeveral major European grocery retailers experienced disruptions across their store networks. Belgian and Luxembourg grocery groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents involving their refrigeration infrastructure.Colruyt recorded five affected locations. Belgium also saw disruptions at 15 Carrefour stores, according to Reuters. In Ireland, hackers targeted 13 SuperValu supermarkets.Sweden’s grocery sector experienced similar problems. Seven Coop supermarkets reported refrigeration disruptions. Swedish retailer ICA also suffered an overnight incident affecting a limited number of locations.The attacks extended beyond conventional grocery retailers. Hackers affected at least one IKEA location in Belgium. The Swedish furniture retailer operates food departments across its stores, including restaurants and grocery sections. Refrigeration failures therefore threatened food inventory beyond traditional supermarket operations.An ICA supermarket in Stockholm experienced particularly severe damage. Its freezers reportedly reached 122 degrees Fahrenheit, destroying stored food products. Such temperatures can rapidly compromise frozen inventory and make affected products unsuitable for consumption.Connected refrigeration systemsSome refrigeration units affected during Monday’s incidents used temperature management technology developed by Danish manufacturer Danfoss. The same technology appeared in French supermarkets targeted during October’s cyberattacks.Modern commercial refrigeration systems increasingly depend on electronic controllers. These devices regulate cooling cycles and maintain temperatures across storage areas. Remote management capabilities also allow operators to monitor equipment and adjust settings without physically accessing individual units.However, network connectivity introduces additional cybersecurity risks. Attackers who compromise refrigeration controllers could potentially manipulate operating parameters remotely. Changing temperature settings can compromise entire storage facilities without requiring physical access to supermarket premises.Researchers at cybersecurity firm Claroty previously identified security weaknesses in Danfoss refrigeration controllers. Their August report documented vulnerabilities that could expose connected equipment to cyberattacks. Danfoss subsequently addressed the reported issues through a software update.The connection between the French and European incidents raises questions about whether attackers exploited similar weaknesses. However, investigators have not established whether both campaigns involved the same vulnerabilities or perpetrators.France faced earlier attacksOctober’s incidents affected hundreds of French grocery stores, including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Cooperative U. Attackers similarly manipulated refrigeration equipment, causing widespread food spoilage across affected locations.The financial damage extended across multiple retail groups. Intermarché’s parent company, Les Mousquetaires, estimated losses worth several million euros following the incidents.The repeated attacks demonstrate how compromising industrial control equipment can disrupt essential commercial operations. Refrigeration systems play a critical role in preserving perishable inventory throughout supermarket supply chains.Their increasing dependence on connected controllers creates another potential entry point for cybercriminals. The incidents also illustrate how relatively small changes to industrial equipment settings can produce substantial physical and financial consequences.

title: Solid-state battery survives 400°F heat test, targets 600-mile range
content: Next-generation all-solid-state batteries are gaining attention in the electric vehicle battery market, with several battery makers expanding research in the sector. Sunwoda, a Chinese battery manufacturer, has recently announced advances to its polymer-composite approach used for building solid-state batteries.The company claimed that its latest 20 Ah all-solid-state battery, Xin Bixiao, withstood extreme thermal heat without catching fire or exploding.Built with a nanoscale high-entropy silicon anode, a single cell of these polymer batteries showed strong thermal performance, passing the hot-box test with temperatures raised to 400 degrees Fahrenheit (200 degrees Celsius).High-density, long-rangeThe model has previously achieved an energy density exceeding 400 Wh/kg and a cycle life of more than 1200 cycles at a low external pressure of 1 megapascals (MPa). This it stated is a breakthrough for long-range electric vehicles (EVs), offering a range of over 600 miles (1000 km).With over 1,200 cycles and capacity retention above 80 percent, the company claimed the battery could support vehicle use for over a decade, assuming annual driving of more than 12,000 miles (20,000 km).However, the company noted that the thermal and lifespan performance results were not obtained after integrating the entire battery pack in a vehicle. The testing process started earlier this year in May and is still ongoing.Going forward, the company also plans to build a second-generation sulfide battery by next year at its pre-commercial solid-state battery production line. This manufacturing unit is designed to handle an annual capacity of 0.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh), which is considered small in the battery world, making batteries enough for nearly 2600-2700 electric vehicles per year.Next stop: Aviation batteriesBeyond the planned automotive batteries of 400Wh/kg capacity, the Chinese battery maker is also eyeing developing aviation battery cells of at least 450Wh/kg. For this project, the company is working with the Guangdong Engineering Research Center. Another segment that the company is aiming to make its mark in is the electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft batteries. The company is targeting a continuous discharge power density of at least 1,000 W/kg for these aircraft.However, the company has not yet committed to an official deadline for any of these high-energy-density batteries, nor has it defined the scale of production volumes or commercial orders.Meanwhile, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), another leading Chinese battery manufacturer, is developing its next-generation solid-state batteries using bisulphide chemistry, a different electrolyte technology. The company announced its 20 Ah solid-state prototype two years ago and has reaffirmed its 2027 target for a small-scale batch production trial.Earlier this year, Sunwoda unveiled its latest fast-charging EV battery technology that can add about 62 miles (100 km) of range per minute and charge from 10 percent to 97 percent state of charge (SOC) in 9 minutes at room temperature. The claims were made for its new 15C lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery.The company said the battery can go from 10 percent to 70 percent in about 5 minutes, then reach 97 percent in another four minutes.

title: Revolutionary Technology Could Transform How We Extract Lithium
content:
Technology
An illustration of gathering lithium ions for batteries. Credit: The University of Texas at Austin
A new breakthrough in lithium separation could help overcome major challenges in extracting this essential battery material.
A new technology developed at
The University of Texas at Austin
could make lithium extraction faster and more environmentally friendly by separating the valuable element from other dissolved substances with exceptional precision. The approach uses artificial channels so small they operate at the nanoscale, allowing lithium ions to pass through while blocking many competing ions.
Inspired by the molecular gateways found in living cells, the channels demonstrated two to five times greater lithium selectivity than other recently developed lithium transporters. Researchers report that the structures rank among the most selective lithium channels created to date, offering a potential alternative to conventional extraction methods.
Why Lithium Is So Difficult to Extract
Lithium is essential for batteries used in smartphones, electric vehicles, and electrical grids. It occurs in underground saltwater deposits known as brines, hard rock formations, and used batteries. However, these sources also contain elements such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium, whose ions can be difficult to separate from lithium. Existing extraction techniques often require considerable time and energy and can generate harmful waste.
“Lithium is in our phones, our cars and the power grid, but getting it out of the ground cleanly is still a hard problem,” said Manish Kumar, a professor in the Fariborz Maseeh Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering and the McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering who is one of the leaders of the new research published in the
Journal of the American Chemical Society
. “Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner and easier to run.”
How Artificial Channels Separate Lithium
The researchers designed tiny pores within membranes that mimic the selective transport pathways of biological cells. Their ability to distinguish lithium from other ions depends on two features working together: chemical groups positioned at the channel entrance and the tightly confined space inside. Interactions at the entrance, combined with the channel’s internal structure, favor lithium transport while restricting competing ions.
The study builds on earlier research into separating
rare earth elements
, which are important for technologies including wind turbine magnets and electronic displays. By extending the underlying design principles to lithium, the researchers are developing a broader approach to selectively recovering critical minerals.
“We now have a toolkit rather than a one-off result,” said Harekrushna Behera, a research scientist in Kumar’s lab. “By understanding how ions interact with the chemical groups at the channel entrance, we can work toward designing more selective channels for lithium and potentially other critical minerals.”
Moving Toward Cleaner, Large-Scale Extraction
The next challenge is incorporating these highly selective channels into membranes large enough for practical lithium recovery. The team is exploring a
recently developed material
made from interconnected, cell-like layers that can be constructed using lipids or plastic-like polymers. Such membranes could eventually support continuous lithium separation without harsh chemical solvents.
Although the laboratory results demonstrate strong selectivity, the technology has not yet been validated for industrial extraction. Researchers still need to test its performance using real brines, where numerous dissolved salts coexist, and determine whether the channels can maintain their effectiveness at larger scales.
Beyond recovering lithium from natural deposits, the researchers envision using the same technology to reclaim the element from discarded batteries. Another possible application is improving the separators inside batteries themselves, although further development will be needed to establish whether these uses are practical.
Reference: “Highly Selective Artificial Lithium Channels” by Harekrushna Behera, Tyler J. Duncan, Laxmicharan Samineni, Hyeonji Oh, Chenhao Yao, Raman Dhiman, Siqi Wang, Luke Hatch, Venkat Ganesan and Manish Kumar, 24 October 2026,
Journal of the American Chemical Society
DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c13878

title: Scientists Discover a Mysterious Comet 808 Million Miles From Earth
content:
A composite of eight Euclid VIS exposures of Comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026
A distant comet following a millennia-long orbit could provide valuable insights into how future space missions identify and study these elusive objects.
A space telescope built to study distant galaxies has discovered a previously unknown comet approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (808 million miles) from Earth. The European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope captured the object in images taken between September 16 and 24, 2026, marking its first discovery of a new comet.
Now designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid), the comet follows an orbit that takes thousands of years to complete. Rather than traveling close to the plane where the planets orbit the Sun, it is currently positioned far above that plane, as viewed from the Sun. Its distance from Earth is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point between Jupiter and Saturn.
An Unexpected Discovery in Euclid’s Galaxy Survey
Euclid was designed to map distant galaxies, not track comets and asteroids. Its observing strategy deliberately avoids the dust-rich band of sky along the Solar System’s plane, where scattered sunlight could interfere with sensitive measurements. The telescope also uses a
“step-and-stare”
approach that generally images each region only once, limiting opportunities to track moving objects over time.
Despite these obstacles, University of Helsinki researcher Mikko Pöntinen detected the comet using software he developed to identify moving Solar System objects in Euclid’s images. Working with the Euclid Consortium’s Solar System Objects Science Working Group, he found evidence of the object in five separate image sets.
A composite of eight Euclid VIS exposures of Comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026
“I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position, I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets [4]. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.”
How Astronomers Confirmed the New Comet
The fuzzy cloud surrounding the object was a sign of cometary activity. As ice in a comet warms and releases gas, it can carry dust into space, forming a diffuse envelope known as a coma. This distinguishes active comets from most asteroids, which typically lack such visible clouds.
After finding no matching object in existing comet and asteroid catalogs, Pöntinen reported the observations to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC). The report prompted follow-up observations by ground-based astronomers, and the MPC officially confirmed the discovery on October 8, 2026.
“Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet’s orbit and Euclid’s scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images,” said Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist and a member of the discovery team.
A Potential New Way to Find Distant Comets
Identifying moving objects is necessary for Euclid’s primary science mission because comet trails and other unwanted light can interfere with precise measurements of distant galaxies. The same detection techniques could also help astronomers discover comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun.
The rapid identification and confirmation of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) provides a practical test of how such discoveries could support ESA’s future Comet Interceptor mission. Although this particular comet is not a suitable target, the process demonstrates how Euclid’s observations could help scientists identify and assess other candidates.
“While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are, of course, happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on,” said Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

title: Breakthrough Cancer Treatment Wipes Out Deadly Brain Tumors in Every Mouse Tested
content:
CAR-T cell therapy is a form of cancer immunotherapy that uses genetically modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer. Doctors collect a patient’s T cells and engineer them to produce special receptors that identify proteins on cancer cells. The modified cells are then returned to the body to target the disease. Credit: Shutterstock
A new approach to engineering immune cells has shown remarkable success against a deadly childhood brain cancer in mice.
An experimental immune cell therapy has completely eliminated an aggressive childhood brain cancer in mice, succeeding where conventional treatments have struggled. Developed by scientists at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), the approach uses genetically engineered CAR-T cells that activate their cancer-fighting receptors only after entering the brain.
The treatment, called B-SYNC, cleared tumors in every mouse tested across two models of diffuse midline glioma (DMG). It also provided lasting protection, with treated mice rejecting a second introduction of cancer cells nearly seven weeks later. Researchers are now preparing for human clinical trials that could begin as early as April 2027.
Targeting One of the Deadliest Childhood Brain Cancers
DMG is particularly difficult to treat because it infiltrates healthy brain tissue, often growing within the brainstem. This region regulates essential functions such as breathing, heart rate, and swallowing, making surgical removal extremely dangerous or impossible. Children diagnosed with the disease almost always die within a year.
CAR-T therapy offers a different strategy. It involves modifying immune T cells to recognize specific proteins on cancer cells and attack them. Although this approach has transformed treatment for certain blood cancers, conventional CAR-T therapies have not successfully controlled brain tumors such as DMG.
“It’s been a struggle to make CAR-T cells that overcome DMG without causing unacceptable side effects,” said Hideho Okada, MD, PhD, a UCSF professor of Neurological Surgery and co-corresponding author of the study, published October 28 in
Science Translational Medicine
. “By limiting B-SYNC’s CAR expression to when and where it matters — in the brain — we saw consistent, total shutdown of DMG tumors in the lab.”
Engineering Immune Cells That Activate Inside the Brain
B-SYNC uses a molecular switch that responds to brevican, a protein widely distributed throughout the brain. The researchers equipped T cells with a synthetic sensor called synNotch that detects brevican and triggers the production of cancer-targeting chimeric antigen receptors (CARs).
Once activated, these receptors allow the T cells to attack cells carrying either of two proteins, EphA2 or IL13Rα2, which are found on many brain tumor cells. Because brevican controls when the receptors are produced, the therapy is designed to restrict its tumor-targeting activity to the brain rather than allowing the engineered receptors to remain active throughout the body.
The technology builds on an earlier UCSF treatment called E-SYNC, developed by Okada and Wendell Lim, PhD, a professor of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology. Announced in 2021, E-SYNC used synNotch to recognize EGFRvIII, a mutant protein associated with glioblastoma, before activating receptors targeting EphA2 and IL13Rα2. However, only about 20% of glioblastoma patients have tumors carrying EGFRvIII, and cancer cells can lose this marker as treatment eliminates those that express it.
Replacing EGFRvIII with brevican gave the researchers a more broadly available activation signal within the brain. Since DMG cells also frequently express EphA2 and IL13Rα2, the redesigned system could potentially target this childhood cancer without depending on a mutation present in only a subset of tumors.
Tumors Disappear in Mouse Experiments
To investigate the treatment, UCSF postdoctoral researcher Senthilnath Lakshmanachetty, PhD, administered B-SYNC CAR-T cells intravenously (IV) to mice implanted with human DMG cells. Some of the engineered cells entered the brain, activated their receptors, and attacked the tumors.
Tests showed that B-SYNC cells circulating elsewhere, including in the blood and spleen, did not produce the cancer-targeting receptors. This confirmed that their activation was restricted to the intended tissue, “just as we designed it,” Lakshmanachetty said.
The researchers next delivered the cells directly into the brain’s fluid-filled ventricles through an intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection. This method produced stronger results, completely clearing tumors in every treated mouse across two human DMG models. Conventional CAR-T cells, tested for comparison, again failed to control the cancer.
Engineered T Cells Provide Lasting Protection
The scientists also investigated whether the modified immune cells could remain functional after the original tumors disappeared. Nearly seven weeks after treatment, they introduced another round of DMG cells into the mice. Every animal previously treated with B-SYNC rejected the new cancer cells.
One possible explanation involves T cell exhaustion, a condition in which prolonged stimulation gradually weakens the ability of immune cells to function. By restricting CAR production to the brain, B-SYNC may prevent the cells from becoming exhausted before reaching their targets. The researchers have not yet established whether this mechanism accounts for the treatment’s improved performance.
“We didn’t expect B-SYNC CAR-T cells to necessarily persist,” Lakshmanachetty said. “But they are still patrolling for cancer over 70 days out — and they’re still very functional.”
Preparing to Test the Therapy in Patients
Following these laboratory results, the UCSF team is working with clinical oncologists to bring B-SYNC into human trials at UCSF Health. The first study, potentially beginning in April 2027, will evaluate the therapy in children and young adults with brain tumors. Each patient’s own T cells will be genetically modified to produce the B-SYNC treatment.
The trial, led by Marie Jaeger-Krause, MD, and Sabine Mueller, MD, PhD, will investigate different combinations of intravenous and intracerebroventricular delivery. For direct administration into the brain ventricles, patients will receive an implanted shunt connected to a reservoir beneath the scalp, allowing repeated treatments.
Although the mouse experiments demonstrated complete tumor clearance and durable protection, researchers still need to establish whether B-SYNC is safe and effective in humans.
“Diffuse midline glioma is a heartbreaking diagnosis for patients and their families,” said Mueller, director of the UCSF Pediatric Brain Tumor Center and co-founder of the Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium (PNOC). “This preclinical data is very promising. Mice with DMG are being cured, and we are incredibly excited to bring this therapy to the children and young adults we care for. This is exactly the kind of innovative approach they deserve.”

title: Too Much Exercise Could Change Your Brain Chemistry in Unexpected Ways
content:
While regular exercise supports physical and mental health, excessive training without adequate recovery can have the opposite effect. Overtraining can lead to persistent fatigue, declining performance, muscle pain, sleep disturbances, and hormonal changes. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have uncovered unexpected changes in brain chemistry following prolonged, intense exercise in mice.
Two days after an exercise test, mice subjected to weeks of grueling training still had elevated dopamine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and emotional regulation. The findings suggest that excessive exercise without adequate recovery can produce lasting changes in brain chemistry.
The study, published in the journal
Neuroscience
, was conducted by researchers in Brazil. Because dopamine helps regulate motivation and alertness, the results raise questions about whether similar disruptions could contribute to sleep problems, anxiety, and persistent fatigue in overtrained athletes. However, these possible effects have not been demonstrated in humans.
What Happens to the Brain After Excessive Exercise?
To investigate how different levels of physical exertion affect the brain, the researchers compared mice subjected to two exercise protocols. One group completed a single treadmill session until exhaustion. The other underwent eight weeks of progressively more demanding training designed to simulate the physical strain associated with overtraining syndrome.
During the final week, the heavily trained mice exercised twice daily, with just four hours between sessions. Researchers then examined the animals’ hippocampi, measuring dopamine, serotonin, and proteins involved in neurotransmitter production and regulation.
The mice that completed a single exhausting run showed a rise in dopamine shortly afterward. In contrast, the chronically trained animals had elevated dopamine levels even 48 hours after their performance test, during a period intended for recovery. Levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme essential for dopamine synthesis, also remained elevated.
Researcher Alisson Luiz da Rocha in the laboratory: protocol with animals provides important information on exaggerated physical exercise in humans Credit: Alisson Luiz da Rocha/Universidade de Michigan
Dopamine Changes Without a Similar Rise in Serotonin
Dopamine is involved in several functions, including motivation, reward processing, and wakefulness. Its presence is not inherently harmful, but changes in its regulation could affect brain activity during periods when the body would normally be recovering.
Interestingly, the researchers found no significant changes in serotonin levels. Serotonin has long been investigated as a possible contributor to exercise-related fatigue, but these results suggest that the neurochemical effects of excessive training cannot be explained by serotonin alone.
“Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain,” said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study’s first author. He conducted the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP), with support from FAPESP.
Could These Brain Changes Help Explain Overtraining Symptoms?
Overtraining syndrome occurs when prolonged physical demands exceed the body’s ability to recover, potentially causing declining athletic performance, chronic fatigue, muscle pain, loss of appetite, increased injuries, and changes in immune and metabolic function. Researchers suspect that changes in brain signaling may also contribute to some symptoms.
Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, suggested that similar dopamine disturbances in humans might help explain connections between excessive training and sleep disorders. However, the researchers did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness in the mice, so the findings cannot establish a connection between the observed chemical changes and those symptoms.
The research team is now participating in an international project to identify which biological systems first begin to show abnormal responses when excessive exercise interferes with the body’s usual adaptations to training. Such work could help clarify how beneficial physical activity progresses into a state of insufficient recovery and impaired performance.
Reference: “Excessive training alters hippocampal tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine homeostasis in mice” by Alisson Luiz da Rocha, João Pedro Floriano, Ana Paula Pinto, Dennys Esper Cintra, Eduardo Rochete Ropelle, Ellen Cristini de Freitas, José Rodrigo Pauli and Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, 4 August 2026,
Neuroscience

title: Something Remarkable Is Happening to Dogs Living Near Chernobyl’s Nuclear Plant
content:
Wild dogs living near the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant have survived for generations in one of the world’s most contaminated environments. Scientists have discovered unusual genetic differences in these dogs, raising questions about how natural selection may have shaped their ability to survive under extreme environmental conditions. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists studying wild dogs near the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant have uncovered unusual genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than radiation-induced mutations.
Dogs living near the Chornobyl (previously called Chernobyl) Nuclear Power Plant carry genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than mutations caused by radiation exposure. A new genomic analysis identified more than 100 locations in their DNA showing signs of directional selection, including regions associated with DNA repair, cancer development, and immune function.
The findings suggest that environmental pressures may have favored certain inherited genetic variants, potentially helping some dogs survive in a contaminated environment. However, researchers have not established whether radiation or other environmental hazards directly caused these patterns.
A Surprising Genetic Divide Between Nearby Dog Populations
Earlier research revealed substantial genetic differences between dogs living at the nuclear power plant and those in Chornobyl City, just 10 miles away. City dogs closely resembled populations from Russia, Poland, and surrounding regions, while dogs near the plant had distinctive genetic features, particularly in areas associated with DNA repair.
“This work ties up some of the loose ends from our previous work, where in characterizing the population’s genetic structure we found that while these two dog groups are geographically very close, they have a very high degree of genetic difference, and those differences aren’t due to mutation,” said Megan Dillon, postdoctoral research scholar at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
“With this work, we wanted to explore two additional larger-scale evolutionary drivers – are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?”
Natural Selection or Random Genetic Change?
Natural selection occurs when inherited traits that improve survival or reproduction become more common across generations. Directional selection is a form of this process in which particular traits become increasingly favored, often in response to environmental conditions. Genetic drift, by contrast, involves random changes in the frequency of genetic variants. It can have especially strong effects in small, isolated populations and may reduce genetic diversity over time.
To distinguish between these processes, researchers compared the two Chornobyl dog populations with free-breeding dogs from Eastern Europe and an isolated population from the Galápagos Islands. This allowed them to examine whether geographic isolation alone could explain the unusual genetic patterns near the nuclear plant.
Although the plant dogs had a small effective population size, a measure of how many individuals contribute genetically to future generations, it was not significantly different from that of the city dogs. The plant population also lacked the reduction in genetic diversity expected from substantial genetic drift. Moreover, its genetic makeup differed markedly from other isolated populations, including the Galápagos dogs. Surprisingly, the Chornobyl City dogs were genetically more similar to the Galápagos population than to the dogs living at the nearby nuclear facility.
Genetic Signatures Linked to Cellular Protection
The researchers found evidence consistent with directional selection in genomic regions containing genes involved in DNA replication and repair, cell cycle regulation, cancer-related processes, and immune responses. These biological functions could influence how animals respond to harmful environmental exposures, although the analysis cannot determine whether particular variants actually improve survival.
“While we can’t say for certain whether what we’ve found can be directly confirmed as selection, we do find these genomic signatures suggestive of selection,” Dillon said.
“When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment.”
Did Chornobyl Favor Dogs Already Equipped to Survive?
The genetic differences do not necessarily mean that dogs developed new adaptations after exposure to radioactive contamination. Another possibility is that individuals carrying advantageous genetic variants were more likely to survive earlier environmental pressures, allowing those variants to become more prevalent in subsequent generations.
“When we consider the toxic environment around Chornobyl, I can see why most people would think, ‘Surely there’s got to have been some consequence of living in that environment,’” said Matthew Breen, Oscar J. Fletcher Distinguished Professor of Comparative Oncology Genetics at NC State’s College of Veterinary Medicine and corresponding author of the study.
“But what we’re saying is the consequence may not have gone as far as changing the dogs’ genome in order to adapt, it could be the ones that were able to survive the initial exposures had this level of underlying genetic diversity and variants to offer a higher degree of fitness,” Breen added. “Obviously that’s speculation, and we don’t know exactly what’s happened. But it is fair to say that we used a very robust analysis and found signatures of selection in biologically relevant regions.”
Reference: “Evidence of Selective Response in the Free-Breeding Dog Population in Chornobyl” by Megan N. Dillon, Reade B. Roberts, Jennifer A. Betz, Timothy A. Mousseau, Norman J. Kleiman and Matthew Breen, 26 September 2026,

title: A Hidden Nanoscopic Effect Is Disrupting Some of the World’s Most Sensitive Sensors
content:
State-of-the-art nano-strings have vanishingly small internal friction and record-low thermal noise. They are now so sensitive that they can feel friction from nearby objects — without ever making contact. Credit: Paresa Arabmoheghi 2026 EPFL
Nanomechanical resonators are vital to precision sensing and emerging quantum technologies, but their extraordinary sensitivity comes with an unexpected vulnerability.
A nanomechanical device can lose much of its ability to sustain vibrations without ever touching another object. Researchers at
have discovered that placing insulating materials just a few hundred nanometers from these tiny structures can dramatically increase energy loss, reducing their mechanical quality factor by as much as tenfold.
The findings, published in
Nature Physics
How Vibrations Lose Energy Without Physical Contact
The mechanism begins with static electric charges trapped inside a mechanical resonator. As the structure vibrates, those charges move with it, producing a changing electric field in the surrounding space. When an insulating material such as silicon dioxide or silicon nitride is nearby, the fluctuating field interacts with the material and causes energy to dissipate through its small electrical losses.
This process is related to “noncontact friction,” a phenomenon previously observed in atomic force microscopy. Although the surfaces never touch, mechanical energy is transferred away from the vibrating structure. The resulting damping lowers its quality factor, which measures how efficiently a resonator stores vibrational energy rather than losing it.
Experiments Reveal a Strong Dependence on Distance and Frequency
The researchers developed a theoretical model predicting that lower-frequency vibrations would experience greater energy losses. To test this, they studied silicon nitride strings suspended approximately 500 nanometers (0.00002 inches) above a dielectric layer. By measuring how quickly different vibrational modes decayed, they confirmed that the lowest-frequency modes suffered the strongest additional damping, consistent with the model.
A second experiment examined resonators designed for exceptionally high quality factors. The team positioned vibrating strings between photonic crystal cavities, with separations of only a few hundred nanometers (roughly 0.00001 inches). As the gaps narrowed, the quality factor declined sharply, sometimes falling by a factor of ten. The researchers also demonstrated that their modeling approach could reproduce the effects of trapped charges in these more complicated device geometries.
Implications for Quantum Technology and Precision Sensors
Nanomechanical resonators are microscopic vibrating components fabricated on chips, operating at frequencies from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz. Their sensitivity makes them useful for detecting extremely small changes in mass, force, temperature, and pressure. They also serve as components in radiofrequency filters and chip-based clocks. Advanced versions can even be used to prepare quantum states of comparatively large mechanical objects and investigate fundamental physics.
Many of these applications require resonators to operate extremely close to other structures, particularly when measuring motion or coupling mechanical vibrations to light and electrical systems. The EPFL results show that trapped charges and dielectric losses must be considered when designing such closely integrated devices, even when no physical contact occurs.
The same interaction could also have practical uses. By measuring how mechanical vibrations lose energy near insulating surfaces, researchers may be able to characterize electrical losses in thin films or develop controlled interactions between mechanical resonators and other electrical systems. Understanding these effects could help engineers preserve mechanical coherence while integrating increasingly sensitive resonators into complex quantum and sensing devices.
Reference: “Non-contact friction in ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators near dielectric materials” by Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Guillermo Arregui, Mohammad J. Bereyhi, Yi Xia, Nils J. Engelsen and Tobias J. Kippenberg, 7 July 2026,
Nature Physics
DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03350-z
Funding: Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF)

title: Researchers Discover a New Way To Control Magnetism Without Changing a Material’s Chemistry
content:
Before and after neutron diffraction patterns show how mechanical strain changes magnetic domain populations in altermagnetic materials, demonstrating a potential way to control magnetism for future spintronic technologies. Credit: Phoenix Pleasant/ORNL, U.S. Dept. of Energy
Neutron experiments have uncovered an unexpected connection between magnetic structure and electrical behavior.
A gentle squeeze can change the magnetic structure of certain crystals and alter their electrical behavior. Scientists at the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) demonstrated this effect in altermagnets, an emerging class of magnetic materials being investigated for advanced electronics.
Using neutron beams to examine the materials at the atomic scale, the researchers found that mechanical strain could shift their magnetic organization and influence an electrical response associated with electron transport. The findings, published in back-to-back papers in
Physical Review X
Advanced Materials
, point to a possible method for controlling magnetic properties without altering a material’s chemical composition.
How a Small Squeeze Changes Magnetic Behavior
The researchers placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between two titanium plates and applied mechanical pressure. They then used neutron diffraction at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source to investigate how the strain affected magnetic domains, regions within a material that have different orientations of magnetic order.
The measurements showed that squeezing the crystals changed the relative populations of these domains. The researchers also detected changes in the anomalous Hall effect, an electrical response that produces a voltage perpendicular to the direction of an applied current. Together, the results connect changes in magnetic domain organization with changes in electrical transport behavior.
“By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies,” said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.
A New Approach to Controlling Spintronic Materials
Altermagnets are attracting research interest because their unusual magnetic properties could support spintronics, a technology that uses electron spin alongside electrical charge to store and process information. Conventional electronics relies on electron charge, while spintronics could provide additional ways to control information in electronic devices.
Developing practical spintronic technologies requires materials whose magnetic and electronic properties can be reliably manipulated. Altermagnets are among the candidates being explored for potential applications ranging from wireless communications to quantum computing. The ORNL experiments suggest that mechanical strain could offer another way to adjust these properties, although translating the findings into working devices will require further research.
“What’s exciting is that one creative experimental idea — a small mechanical squeeze between two plates — can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism,” said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author of both studies.

title: Hubble Uncovers a Mysterious 93-Billion-Mile Structure Hiding in a Nearby Star System
content:
In this artist’s illustration of the Beta Pictoris debris disk – seen edge-on as it appears from Earth – the swirling gas and dust are depicted in orange. A secondary disk, discovered previously, appears as a whitish feature below the plane of the main disk. On the right, the “Cat’s Tail” feature is visible, reaching far into space. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Ralf Crawford (STScI)
New observations of a young star system reveal an unexpected cosmic structure
Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between planetary bodies. Known as the “Cat’s Tail,” the feature stretches across as much as 1,000 astronomical units (about 93 billion miles) in the young Beta Pictoris star system.
Located 63 light-years from Earth in the constellation Pictor (which is Latin for “painter”), Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rocky debris. The Cat’s Tail was discovered in infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, but had remained hidden from telescopes observing shorter wavelengths. Now, new Hubble Space Telescope images, combined with observations spanning more than 14 years, are helping astronomers investigate its composition, geometry, and possible origins.
Why This Enormous Dust Structure Was Nearly Invisible
“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while,” said Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the University of Arizona who led the research.
The explanation may lie in the dust itself. “We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar explained. “It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”
The observations also suggest that the structure contains microscopic dust grains with an exceptionally porous, fluffy composition. Although the particles are only about a micron across, their internal structure is difficult to explain through conventional models of planetary collisions. “How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.
This study’s observations, made with the Hubble Space Telescope, revealed the “Cat’s Tail” structure for the first time in the visible light spectrum (white arrow). Unlike the original discovery observations made with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detected the dust grain’s heat emissions using infrared radiation, the tail appears shorter in the new images, because the further the trail of dust grains extends from the star, the less light they reflect. Credit: Avsar et al.
Could a Violent Collision Have Created the Cat’s Tail?
Beta Pictoris is roughly 20 million years old, making it a valuable laboratory for studying the turbulent environments in which planets develop. Its debris disk contains material left behind from planet formation, including particles produced when larger objects collide.
“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” said Avsar, who works with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory. Such an impact could have scattered enormous quantities of dust, although the exact process that produced the observed particles remains uncertain.
One possibility is that the impact generated enough heat to transform solid carbon into vapor, which later cooled and formed new particles. “It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” said Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at Steward Observatory.
Hubble Reveals an Unexpected Shape
The new observations have also changed astronomers’ understanding of the Cat’s Tail’s position in space. Earlier interpretations suggested that the feature extended far behind Beta Pictoris from Earth’s perspective, creating the appearance of a long structure stretching away from the star.
The findings, published in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters
, suggest that much of the structure’s apparent length lies across our field of view rather than extending deep into space. Its precise three-dimensional arrangement remains dependent on the models used to interpret the observations.
A Giant Planet May Be Distorting the Surrounding Dust
Using Hubble in a new observing configuration, the team also identified a previously unseen warp in the dust halo surrounding Beta Pictoris. The distortion may result from the gravitational influence of Beta Pictoris b, one of three known planets in the system and a gas giant approximately 10 times Jupiter’s mass.
“This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said. “It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.”
Similar gravitational interactions likely occurred during the early history of our solar system. When the Kuiper Belt was about 20 million years old, it may have contained hundreds of Pluto-sized objects packed into a much denser region than exists today. Over time, the gravitational influence of the giant planets altered the orbits of many of these bodies, scattering some into different regions or ejecting them from the solar system entirely.
The Beta Pictoris observations provide a way to investigate comparable processes in a much younger planetary system, where collisions and gravitational disturbances are still shaping the distribution of material around its star.
Reference: “Deep HST/STIS Coronagraphic Imaging of the β Pictoris Debris Disk: On the Scattered Light Component of the Cat’s Tail” by Arin M.
