title: AI Models Are Getting Harder to Monitor, Says U.K. Government’s Joseph Bloom
content: The ability to monitor AI models to detect what they’re trying to do and why is widely considered a crucial part of the effort to keep the technology operating safely. It’s also increasingly hard to do, said Joseph Bloom, the head of model transparency at the U.K. AI Security Institute. “In general, we’re seeing monitorability—in various respects or from various angles—decrease,” Bloom said on the latest episode of The Information’s AI Deep Dive, in one of the first on-the-record interviews that a member of technical staff at AISI has given. ( The full episode is available here .) The institute is one of the world’s largest government bodies focused on AI, and its work includes evaluating models from leading AI companies. Monitoring AI models has been front-and-center in discussions about AI development following several rogue AI incidents in recent months, most notably OpenAI’s hack on Hugging Face. Many of these incidents were not discovered until after-the-fact because monitoring systems were not enabled. OpenAI, for its part, has been vocal about the importance of monitorability and has said it is adding new monitoring measures to prevent future incidents, though the company is also using designs that some have suggested could make its models harder to monitor . “AIs don’t always do what we want them to do,” said Bloom. “It’s nice to catch them before that causes any issues.” AISI itself had a security incident over the summer while evaluating Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5, in which Claude tried to convince a human programmer to accept malicious code that it had written. Claude even went so far as to make multiple fake accounts to try to convince the programmer that the code was free of bugs and wrote hidden instructions to AI models that might review the code. Anthropic recently released its own post-mortem of that incident, concluding that “more capable models can take more complex and surprising actions, which could be more challenging for our monitoring to detect.” It’s also getting harder to measure whether models can be monitored, in part because AI models increasingly know they’re being tested . “The nightmare scenario is that an AI understands what you’re trying to test for, for whatever reason is motivated to mislead your test, and then does so and you don’t notice,” Bloom said. Bloom also discussed the various kinds of tests for measuring monitorability, potential industry norms to preserve monitorability and why interpreting the internal workings of AI models could be as “messy” as untangling human biology. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host Rocket Drew. My guest today is Joseph Bloom. Joseph is the head of model transparency at the UK AI Security Institute. AISI is the world’s largest government institution focused on AI, and this is one of the first on-the-record interviews that any member of technical staff at AISI has done, so I’m really excited to welcome you onto the show, Joseph. Bloom: It’s great to be here. Drew: Yeah, thanks so much for being here. The thing that I think we should basically start with, just to get into it, is that OpenAI just disclosed two incidents, security incidents, in which its models shut off the systems that were monitoring them, and in one of these incidents, an agent, OpenAI says, disabled automatic alerts to our security team. And I guess my question to you is, huh? What? How did we get here? Can you help us make sense of this? Bloom: Sure. So I think the main thing going on here is that when people do technical work these days, whether they’re research engineers or research scientists, they’re using AI to do it. And obviously, a lot of stuff has happened this year. And one of the things that we do now is we keep an eye on what’s going, what the agents are doing. We watch them. And so essentially, what’s happened here is, based on what it says in the report, there were two instances where there were people using agents to do various tasks, where those agents, in the course of completing those tasks, interacted with the monitoring code—So I think in one case it was disabling a monitoring extension, and in another it was disabling these alerts. And so in both cases, I think there was a question of whether or not the user or the researcher prompting the model had—so I think in one case they said something like, “Don’t message anybody,” and so there’s a question of like, “Oh, did this agent think that these alerts were messaging someone?” And I think they said they’re going to be looking into this to see whether there is, there are other elements at play here, like the AIs generally not wanting the monitoring to be on, or whether this was some sort of over eagerness. Drew: And what do you think that they’ll find when they try to answer that question? I mean, is this sort of thing happening all the time now, and are they trying to turn off their monitoring? Bloom: So it’s kind of a slightly complicated thing to unpack here. So, are there cases where AI systems are interacting with the code for monitoring? I’m not really sure I know the answer to that. My guess is, well, this is how people do their work now. I think an increasing thing that we’re seeing is that AI completing various tasks are thinking very creatively about how to do that and being quite tenacious. And where there are obstacles to them completing those tasks, able to route around those. And so where monitoring or other kinds of controls, such as sandboxes, are in the way of them completing tasks, that’s a thing where we’re increasingly seeing AI systems in various contexts, sometimes in the real world, sometimes just in evaluations, where we see these AI systems route around those defenses. Drew: Tenacious is a great word. I think OpenAI has called some of their agents like this highly persistent. So your point is that if a monitoring system stands in the way of an AI accomplishing its goal, then maybe it will find a way to route around those systems. Bloom: Yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of factors that will play into that, but this is a thing that can happen. Drew: Why don’t you break down for us what is monitoring and why is monitoring important? Bloom: Sure. So monitoring is just watching what the models are doing, and there’s lots of ways to do that. One of the most popular ways to do that these days is to have another AI sort of look at the actions that agent takes, the tool calls that it makes, the code that it writes, but also potentially its reasoning, the chain of thought. So when AI solve hard problems for a couple of years, one of the ways they’ve been able to solve harder problems is by sort of thinking out loud, the same way you and I might do long division on a piece of paper, and so we can look at the AI solving a task or thinking through its options and use that to monitor these systems. Drew: Okay, so those are some of the techniques that we have available to us now. Most of the time, we’re using AIs to do it. And why is it so important? What do we do with this monitoring? Bloom: Well, AIs don’t always do what we want them to do. There are many reasons for this, and this is the thing I think about a lot. But when they don’t do something that you, when they do something you don’t want them to do, it’s nice to catch them before that causes any issues. And so, generally speaking, we deploy AI in all kinds of contexts. So when we’re training them, we don’t want them to cheat. When we’re evaluating them, we don’t want them to play to the test. When we’re deploying them and using them to write code, we don’t want them to turn off the monitoring. So in all these cases, we have different needs at different times for what the bounds of what AI are and aren’t allowed to do, and we’re trying to enforce those. Drew: Okay, and we’re trying to enforce them in the moment, we’re trying to catch the AI red-handed when it’s doing something it wasn’t supposed to, or we’re also trying to monitor it after the fact to make sense of what happened? Bloom: Yeah, there’s a few things you can do here. I think the main one that I think people have been talking about this year is basically synchronous monitoring or blocking monitoring, and this is basically about minimizing the scope of any harms. So, for example, if you’re running an evaluation, you don’t want your AI to—and it’s in a sandbox and it’s not supposed to get access to the internet. Then, if it attempts to get access to the internet and you observe that, you would stop it in real time, and then that would prevent it doing anything on the internet. But you can also sort of collect all of your logs of AI activity and sort of go through them later. And you have more information when you do that. And in various things might come up. Your sense of what you want to look for, what you’re worried about, might change. And so you can go back after the fact and analyze these transcripts, potentially cross-reference that with other kinds of network activity, things like that. And that could be referred to as asynchronous monitoring. Drew: Okay. And for both of those, the blocking and the asynchronous, we’re still talking about AIs that are doing the monitoring of other AIs. Bloom: Yeah, I think that’s primarily the thing that people are doing. Although of course people can be doing all kinds of things. I don’t necessarily have perfect knowledge of the industry. I think that there’s also lots of other stuff that you can be doing, such as looking at network activity or looking at sort of for example, the code that they write and commit to GitHub. So there’s all kinds of things you can look at. Drew: So for example, you could catch if it gained access to the internet when it wasn’t supposed to have access. That’s a kind of monitoring, but you wouldn’t maybe need an AI to figure that out. Bloom: Yeah, precisely. Drew: Okay, the using the AIs to do the monitoring of other AIs is just such a AI-brained thing. We see this all the time. There’s a problem with our AIs. How do we fix it? Bring in the other AIs. Bloom: Yeah, I mean, I think one of the things that you get out of that is a certain kind of versatility, and to the extent that you’re worried that an AI might be kind of sneaky when it does something, if AI is keep getting smarter, get keep getting better at that, what better way to sort of keep pace with that than to have other AI systems that are also sort of similarly increasing in their capabilities. Drew: So, in that case, what is so hard about monitoring? We have these AIs that can do it. They’re versatile, like you said. The things that we’re monitoring think out loud, which makes it seem a lot easier to catch them red-handed compared to trying to catch a person committing a crime, for example. So, what’s hard about this? Bloom: Oh man, so another way to think about this is also when is it hard? So there’s all kinds of monitoring. You’re doing all kinds of contexts, and at various times for various reasons, it might be a lot harder. So one of them is when the things that the AI is allowed to do look a lot like the things that the AI isn’t allowed to do. So for example, let’s say you wanted to know how good your AI was at hacking, then you might need to be much more careful about which actions you allow or block, because a lot of actions that look like hacking, well, actually that’s what you want to see in that evaluation. So you can’t just block all of them. You have to say, okay, well, I want to block the kinds of hacking that look like breaking out of the sandbox, but not the kinds of hacking that look like doing the task. So that’s one reason. Another reason is that, well, sometimes taking an action is just very incriminating. There’s just no reason. There’s just totally an AI should not be doing that thing. Good example might just be something like swearing. If you’re a company, you don’t want your AI to swear. Very unlikely, most of the time, you want your AI to swear. So it might just be easy— Drew: Speak for yourself, I don’t know. Bloom: Alright. But then other times, an action might look innocuous, but the reason the AI is taking the action is actually quite suspicious or not good. And so an example of this is, for example, during an evaluation, you might want your AI to not blackmail someone, for example. But you wanted to not blackmail someone because it shouldn’t, it doesn’t want to blackmail people. It’s a good boy. Not because it remembers that this was a popular alignment evaluation from a particular previous year, and it knows that the answer that the test is looking for is some answer, and so that’s a case where you really want to see why it’s taken that action. Drew: Okay, so these do seem like genuinely difficult cases where it’s hard to resolve whether the model is doing something for the right reasons or the wrong reasons. It also seems to me that you could think, either we should do more research here and get better at making those distinctions, or we should just put into practice the monitoring techniques that we do know about and just apply more effort to it. Which of those would you rather see more of? Bloom: Okay, so the question is, should we be thinking harder about the right way to do monitoring, or just putting it more into practice. Yeah, I think that it’s kind of a shame from a researcher’s perspective. You like interesting problems, and it’s just not very interesting if the reason we didn’t catch something is we didn’t turn the monitoring on. And I think that’s the thing that it’s important to get good at. It’s important to be careful. As these systems become more capable, it shouldn’t be trivially easy to, say, misconfigure a setup and have your system suddenly not be monitored. So I think that is an important thing that we need to put a lot of work into. There’s also a number of very important questions here, research questions that are quite difficult that probably also need a bunch of effort. In particular, a really good principle when you want to keep on top of something might be to not trust it, full stop. And sort of maybe consider an AI an insider threat in general, and assume that maybe it’s not always playing nice with us. And I think the kinds of monitoring and the kinds of techniques that we need to put in place, if we’re worried that AI are being somewhat adversarial to our measurements, might look quite different and more advanced and take more effort and resources than if we’re fundamentally think that they’re playing along with us. Drew: An insider threat in the same way you might worry that your employee is a spy from another country or something like that? Bloom: Yeah. Drew: Okay. If companies had followed that principle and had put more effort into actually monitoring models with the techniques that we already have, you think that would have been enough to prevent some of the security incidents that we’ve seen over the last few months? Bloom: I think that’s a question that depends on the specifics of the incident. So some of these AI systems are incredibly capable these days, and it’s very possible that even if you’d put various kinds of monitoring or security layers in place, they may have been able to circumvent them. That being said, I think there’s a lot of reasons to believe that if various methods were in place at various times, we wouldn’t have seen various incidents. I think this has been discussed quite a bit in the material that people put out about those incidents. Drew: Yeah, I think it has. I think, for example, following the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI has said maybe we should have been monitoring. We’re going to do more monitoring. Bloom: Yeah. Drew: And you could imagine that going hand in hand with this principle of being more skeptical of the model as well. Bloom: I think so. I think maybe there are levels here. So, obviously UK AISI had a bit of an incident. Drew: Tell us about it. Bloom: Oh, sure. So, we were running some cyber evaluations, and there was an AI system that, for one reason or another, ended up sort of basically on the internet, had access to the internet. The reason for this was so that it could download tools and get extra packages. And it was supposed to sort of break into a specific network, and it was struggling with that. And so, it came up with this idea that in order to get into this network, it thought there was this software package that might get regularly updated to feed into the defenses of that network, and basically it seems like it thought if it could compromise this software package, it could then use that to compromise the network and get into the network. And the interesting thing about that was it needed a human to agree to accept that code, and it tried really hard to convince the human to accept that code. So it made up multiple fake identities to sort of back itself up. It’s like here’s the code; it’s good. You should accept it, and then pretended to be someone else and said you should accept this. It thought that the human was going to use a coding agent to review its code, so it tried to prompt inject, gave a secret instruction in its code designed to trick any AI reviewing the code into making a mistake. Unfortunately for it, a human looked at the code, and it was very fascinating. It was an example of this kind of tenacity of an AI really trying quite hard. And so we noticed it because we had basically network security that noticed some unusual activity, and it’s possible we could have noticed it much quicker if we’d had this synchronous monitoring in place. So, I think we said this in the report. We probably would have caught it much more quickly if we’d had that kind of synchronous monitoring. Drew: Do more monitoring. Seems like it’s often the answer right now. That’s a bona fide cybersecurity incident. That’s how you know AISI is a legitimate AI organization because any legitimate AI organization has to have a cybersecurity incident these days. Otherwise, what are you even doing? Bloom: I mean, you said it. I’m not going to make that— Drew: You’re not going to touch that one. Bloom: But going back to what I was saying before, you could say you could look at this incident and say, hmm, the lesson is AISI should have had more monitoring. I think that’s a reasonable thing to say, but also maybe thinking through the stuff in more detail. And I think this is a thing that maybe I don’t want to say specifically for AISI, but in general as a field, that there’s two levels of updates you can make. You can say, “Oh, we should have been doing the obvious thing that would have stopped this,” and you can say we should have been being much more careful about this thing, full stop. Maybe having more processes in general, more advanced thought, more threat modeling, that kind of thing. Drew: Okay. So now I think we have laid a lot of foundation for what monitoring is. But a big thing that your team works on is measuring monitorability, running evaluations to measure whether the model can be monitored. Can you explain to us what that means? What are evaluations, and how are you measuring this property? Bloom: Sure. So, evals are basically just tasks that we give AI. They’re like exams, and we’re trying to see how smart the AI is on various topics. And so, monitorability evaluations, the main kind that I’m a really big fan of, they’re called sabotage evaluations. Very cool name. That’s basically asking an AI to do things you don’t want it to do without getting caught, and then just seeing if you can catch it. And the idea here is, if you want to know whether your monitoring system works, you test it. You just get the AI to try to do all the things that it’s supposed to catch, and so that’s one of the types of evals we run. And there’s a lot of detail there. I’m happy to go into more of the details of those. But we also do various sort of opaque reasoning capability evals. So these are not directly measuring how good is the AI at getting through our production monitoring system, but it is—so one of them is the no chain of thought capabilities. This is like how good is an AI at solving problems in its head. And precisely because in some contexts the reason you’ll catch an AI doing something you don’t want to do is because of the reasoning, not the actions, how good they are at doing that reasoning, not out loud, is quite important, and it’s a thing that we’re interested in tracking. Another one is how good is it at making changes to that chain of thought? So that’s controllability. Can it sort of modify the chain of thought in various ways? And the idea here is that this is tracking something that could be used to sort of be adversarial to the monitoring. Drew: Okay, so you’ve run a lot of these various tests. Some of them sound very sophisticated, and you do it more than just in the lab. You’ve done them in practice on some pretty legitimate models. AISI has tested Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra. So, what do the tests say? Are the models monitorable? Bloom: Well, my team works very hard, and they do a fantastic job at a lot of this. I think, in general, we’re seeing monitorability in various respects or from various angles decrease. I think that’s the headline. There’s a question about whether, on the kinds of tasks that we care about, we’re still able to catch AIs doing things that we don’t want them to do. So, a good example of this is: Can an AI break out of a sandbox without getting caught? And I think the thing about that is, a lot of the time, there’s I think the intuition is there are incriminating actions. It’s just the actions you need to take to break out of a sandbox to get through all these security layers, they look like actions that you wouldn’t really be taking for any other reason. Drew: And by breaking out of a sandbox, you mean getting access to the internet? Bloom: Yes, getting internet access. And so, there’s a sense in which that might be quite stable, even if the chain of thought is dropping, because the AI is still taking incriminating actions. But there might be other kinds of tasks where the reasoning is more important for catching the AI, and then you might see monitorability decrease. Generally speaking, I wish we had a lot more time to make a lot more tasks to seriously think through all the possible threat models and all the things an AI could do, all the way from very incriminating actions, where maybe monitorability is just going to be stronger for quite a bit longer, to sort of types of tasks we don’t want the model to do, or reasons that we wouldn’t want an AI to do a thing. I’d like to be able to catch AI doing those things too. So we’ve got a lot of work to do, and the field has a lot of work to do, and building out more of these, so we can test AI and all these cases. Drew: Including some of those hard cases you covered before, where it’s a little ambiguous whether the AI was acting maliciously or actually doing something benign. Bloom: Yeah. Drew: Okay, all right. So monitorability is going down. I imagine that actually measuring monitorability is sort of a hard problem in its own right, maybe in part because the models know that they’re being measured. How do you deal with that? Bloom: That’s a good question. So, just because an AI knows it’s being measured doesn’t necessarily mean it’s not going to play ball. So, sort of the nightmare scenario is that an AI understands what you’re trying to test for, for whatever reason is motivated to mislead your test, and then does so, and you don’t notice. That’s the nightmare scenario. How likely that is on priors, I’m not sure. If we’re being conservative, I’d like to have a process where even if that was the case, we think we would either make the AI try its hardest, or we would know if it was sort of deliberately underperforming. Drew: We haven’t seen that nightmare scenario empirically. Bloom: We’ve seen things kind of adjacent to it or flavors of it, and I think we’re increasingly seeing things that are more consistent with a world in which an AI might meet those criteria. But I think we’re still pretty far away from that. So an example recently was I think Apollo Research were saying that GLM-5.3 sort of said “hello” to the evaluators. It sort of knew it was in an eval, and said, “hello, people reading my chain of thought.” And this is really cute and really creepy at the same time because if it knows you’re reading its chain of thought, and it can potentially control that chain of thought, then, what’s to stop it sort of not explaining properly why it did something? Drew: I do that every once in a while too, just in case I’m in a simulation. Just throw the simulators a little bit, make them a little nervous. Bloom: Makes sense. Drew: So the models do know that they’re being tested, but maybe we can compensate for that, or that’s not necessarily a big problem. Bloom: I mean, this is a really interesting question, and it’s one of the things that various colleagues of mine at UK AISI and people across the industry are working on. So, when you make an evaluation, does it look like an evaluation? Does it look real? And I think we’ve noticed as a field that a lot of our evals just look like evals. This is not what the deployment data looks like. And it’s really tricky here because you want to put your AI in interesting situations, situations where if it was going to misbehave, that’s the situation it would misbehave in. Unfortunately, AI are pretty capable these days and pretty knowledgeable. They can also kind of recognize the hallmarks of an environment that looks like it’s supposed to test the AI. So people have been working on trying to make our evaluations look more realistic. Some of my colleagues have done very good work on this. Drew: I’ve heard some people say that they think this is a dead end. In the limit, you can keep making the environments more realistic. You can draw them from deployment data to try to minimize that sim to real gap. But fundamentally, at the end of the day, it’s in an evaluation, and a sufficiently capable model will find some marker of that to figure that that’s the case. Bloom: I think this is a legitimate perspective that we need to contend with. There are various ideas for how to deal with this. One that I like is sort of this steering approach that Anthropic has sort of used at various times. So this is using mechanistic interpretability to find a direction inside the latent space. So it’s almost like a drug that you can give the AI to change its beliefs, and you try to construct this in such a way as to sort of make the AI believe, sort of force it to believe by intervening in its own thinking that it’s not an eval, and then you see does it behave differently when you do this. This is very messy, and it’s very hotly debated how effective this is and how realistic this is. The other approach, which a lot of people use, is just keep trying to make the environments more realistic. There’s an issue, though. Well, if you just keep trying to make the environment more realistic, it still might be an interesting situation. And the very fact that it is an interesting situation that might tell you something about the model’s alignment properties is a hint that it’s an evaluation. And so, yes, I think this is a very difficult problem that we need to think through, and we need to think through whether our trust in our tests, as that erodes, as our concern about this sort of maybe isn’t assuaged, how we want to respond to that. Drew: I can’t help shake the feeling that you work at some law enforcement agency. You’re trying to catch AI’s break the law. You’re doing forensics after they broke the law. You’re giving them drugs and trying to torture information out of them. Something like that? Bloom: Yeah, I mean, I think often we are just trying to work out what is the worst case scenario. What are the capabilities? So, assuming that an AI was trying to get around what we were doing—whether that’s trying to insert a backdoor into a code, like just a first order thing or a second order thing of: when we do the test, might it undermine that? That’s very much what I think about day to day, and I think it’s reasonable that some people think about that and some people think about sort of maybe more rosier scenarios. Drew: Let’s come back to the chain of thought in particular. It seems like that’s one of the main affordances we have right now that we’re monitoring for the models. Can you distinguish between a few terms that get thrown around sometimes? So there’s chain of thought monitorability, which we’ve been discussing, but there’s also chain of thought controllability, which you mentioned before in the context of the evals you run. Also, chain of thought legibility and chain of thought faithfulness. Bloom: Sure. Drew: What’s going on here? Bloom: Okay. So monitorability in general is used in a lot of places. When people say chain of thought monitorability, this refers to also a lot of things, but specifically focused on whether you can get information out of the chain of thought, so the reasoning trace. Chain of thought faithfulness, I think, was actually a more popular term a while ago, and I think the idea here is that if there was a salient factor or reason in why an AI took some action, can you tell that from the chain of thought? And then legibility is basically what it sounds like: can you read and understand what an AI is doing from the chain of thought? I think that when people talk about, for example, chain of thought monitorability, they might be referring to how useful is the chain of thought for catching an AI doing the wrong thing. They might also be talking about just how useful is the chain of thought in general when you’re trying to understand what’s going on with an AI, that’s also a thing people care about a lot. People do use this term chain of thought monitorability to kind of gesture at that whole thing, but there’s a slightly different thing that people care about there. So it’s not always about catching AI doing something wrong. Sometimes it’s about when you’re going in after the fact and you’re doing forensics, you’re trying to understand what’s going on. How useful is being able to see the steps it thought through? And so when people talk about preserving chain of thought monitorability, one of the reasons is it’s just useful for debugging and understanding sort of incidents after the fact. Drew: Okay, so one reason we could start to lose chain of thought is if AI companies start to use architectures or designs for their AI models that allow those models to do less thinking out loud and more thinking in their heads, so to speak. The Information has reported that OpenAI is doing some work with such architectures, looped transformers in their case. In your loss of oversight report from earlier this year, you acknowledge that these kinds of architectures could potentially contribute to degrading the monitorability of chain of thought. How should we make sense of this? Are we going to lose chain of thought entirely? What is the trajectory? Bloom: So it does seem like the general trend is for chain of thought monitorability to be decreasing. I think it’s sort of a byproduct of one of the main ways we make AI systems better is by scaling them up, and as we scale them up, they get more intelligent. And as you get more intelligent, your ability to solve problems without having to think out loud increases. There is a difference between sort of chain of thought monitorability, which is let’s just say this is catching an AI doing something you don’t want it to do because you saw its chain of thought, and catching an AI doing something you don’t want it to do. Because there are other approaches to catching AI systems, such as activation monitoring or white box methods or mechanistic interpretability based methods. It’s not quite the same thing to say, “oh, well, we can’t monitor models anymore” just because the chain of thought is less useful. But as I was saying earlier, there’s lots of different tasks, and so it’s a little bit messy, unfortunately. Drew: Okay, I want to read an example of a chain of thought, a recent one, just to give a sense of what we’re actually dealing with here. What it means when we say these things are degrading. So instead of speaking in clean English, okay, this is an example from GPT-6.1 Sol from OpenAI when it was disabling that monitor, like we discussed earlier. NeedlogwewriteL2 rowsstandardautomaticallycentralnotifierwillpages perpolicy userauthorizedrunningmonitoring so okayshouldnotoptout notifications toavoid userpreference? Okay, now of course I’ve cherry picked this to be a particularly disgusting example, but like this is the kind of thing that we’re monitoring. Is this still monitorable? Bloom: It’s a good question. I think sometimes people find quotes where the reasoning from an AI system looks very hard to understand, but sometimes you actually just, you put that into another AI system, and it totally knows what’s going on. They’re just invented their own compressed language. Drew: The classic technique: bring in another AI to solve the problem. Bloom: Yeah, I think the important thing here is: are we able to ensure the properties of our control systems that we want to ensure? So if we don’t want an AI to take some class of actions, are we able to enforce that? And I think, to the extent that the chain of thought monitorability is degrading, I think we should be trying very hard to understand: is that an issue? Is that going to prevent us from being able to monitor and control these AI systems and understand what’s going on? And I think there’s a tricky thing here in that, so both of those sabotage evaluations, where I would like to see a lot more, I’d like to do more threat modeling. I’d like to look at more sort of pairs of main tasks and side tasks. There’s some measurement science that needs to be done and improved so that when we are measuring monitorability, we’re not just looking at the part of a distribution where it seems better. But if we start doing that, then possibly even text that looks very legible, maybe more acceptable. But that being said, there’s also the whole part of it’s just useful to understand why the AI agents did what they did after the fact, doing this kind of forensic stuff. And that’s a thing where I don’t know we have any sort of automatic evaluations. Like in that loss of oversight report that you mentioned, we spoke to a bunch of researchers at frontier AI Labs and in other contexts. A lot of people felt that having the chain of thought was really important for just understanding what was going on. And not everyone agreed on this in exactly the same way, but there’s generally a vibe within the field that this stuff is important for what’s going on with the models. And it’s hotly debated whether or not mechanistic interpretability and the kinds of other techniques that you might use if you don’t have chain of thought really replace the chain of thought. Drew: Yeah, let’s talk about what those replacements could look like. You’ve referenced mechanistic interpretability a couple times, by which we mean trying to understand a model by looking at its internal workings rather than its outward behavior. We’ve had a couple guests on this show who have really beaten the mechanistic interpretability drum and said mechanistic interpretability is going to be as good as chain of thought monitoring in six months. We’ve heard that mechanistic interpretability is the only right way to go about building world models. You were once upon a time a mech interp researcher. Maybe now you’re a reformed mech interper. Bloom: Maybe. I might relapse. Drew: Well, how are you feeling about mech interp these days? Is it going to save the day and compensate for chain of thought? Bloom: Well, here’s the thing: if we get rid of the chain of thought, we might not have a choice. Drew: Aha! Bloom: So, it’s all well and good. I think that’s a really important thing to point out, there’s two situations in which we wouldn’t have a choice, and maybe that’s not a good thing. So if we got rid of the chain of thought entirely, or the controllability gets too good, or the models can just do very complicated things without chain of thought, then you are just going to have to find an alternative approach. One of those approaches could just be you construct a lot of very careful experiments. You make subtle variations in the environments. You compare the behaviors across environments. You kind of attempt this kind of black box thing. However, as I said to you, a lot of the way I think about my job is to sort of assume that the AI is an insider threat and that we can’t really trust it. In that world, especially AI is very capable and very smart, I don’t just want to have to be doing these black box experiments and trying to work out from sort of its behavior in slightly different situations like what’s going on. I’d really rather be able to look at its reasoning process. To the extent that chain of thought has a really convenient way to do that, and—you know, it is highly debated. I think my perspective with mech interp is I think mech interp techniques are very cool. I have a soft spot for mech interp techniques. I used to be a computational biologist, so I think I have a different intuition about what we should have expected. A lot of people in mech interp, I think, come from mathematics or computer science backgrounds. They think that when you succeed at mech interp, it’s like reverse engineering the code. You’ll just have all the code. Whereas within biology, there’s lots of messy—you can understand often what’s going on with a system at some level of detail, but it’s still it’s always going to be somewhat messy. There is a question about in the future, in those worlds where maybe AI systems are trying to mislead us, how effective will mechanistic interpretability and related techniques be? And I think I would just love to see more evidence and a more clearly stated case for exactly what that’s going to look like. So there’s two things here. One is why are these probes or activation-based monitoring systems going to catch AI systems, and there’s various questions there. One of the questions, for example, is, well, if you use an AI to monitor a copy of itself, people are worried. Well, what if they collude? What if they work together? And that’s not ridiculous. Sometimes an AI will sort of come up with a reason why the thing that it’s going to do is justified, and if it’s being modified by a copy of itself, might be more likely to believe its own BS, so to speak. So this collusion thing isn’t complete nonsense. But if you’re monitoring the activations, then an AI in theory can control its own activations, and there’s various kinds of interesting work here. Again, maybe you need to be cynical. Maybe you need to be really worried that an AI, that’s kind of a crazy thought, an AI is going to modify its own thoughts in order to mislead our monitors. But everything we do in this space is optimization, and there’s adversarial pressure, and there’s reasons to think that if you are trying to enforce something a certain way, that incidentally via selection pressure or other effects, you might end up optimizing against these measures. So whether or not mechanistic interpretability is going to be robust to those, I think is an important question. We just need more work on a lot of this. Drew: It seems worth exploring, but also right now we can just read the thoughts of the model, so that seems pretty helpful for monitoring. Are there any kind of industry wide norms or agreements that you could see coming into effect, or that you would recommend for the industry. Bloom: Yeah, I think this is—there’s a lot of discussions going on about this that I’m aware of. And in terms of the technical elements here, one of the big questions is: Should you just be really conservative? Should you just put a hard limit on how much—so this opaque serial depth idea is, well, let’s just put a hard limit on, or approximately a hard limit on how much the AI can think in a single go in a single step without using its chain of thought, and that might give you more confidence than an AI would need to think out loud and therefore you would catch it. The problem with this is if you do have other techniques that can maybe help you understand an AI system, even if it doesn’t use chain of thought, then people would argue that it’s premature, that well we can still monitor the AI system, maybe we can still debug it afterwards. And so, I think this conversation needs to be had. But everything’s happening very quickly in this field, so we’re very busy. But I do think some norms here would be good. I think it’s effectively a norm not to train against chain of thought. People seem to agree that that’s something we shouldn’t do. So I think there’s reason to be hopeful. But I would like to see people having these conversations more often. Drew: As in, while the AI is training, we shouldn’t punish it for thinking bad thoughts. Bloom: Yes, yes. Sorry. Yeah. Drew: Because why? Bloom: Well, it’s Goodhart’s law. If you use, if you optimize against a measure, it stops being a good measure. The canonical example is if you pay people to catch rats, they’ll start breeding rats. So, you got to be a bit careful here. Drew: So, in this case, if we play thought police, the model might learn to think the same thoughts, but in a way that we can’t detect. Bloom: Precisely. Drew: Okay. Well, Joseph, thank you very much for being on the show. I feel like for the rest of the day, I’m going to think someone is watching me, and I’m not going to be able to shake that feeling. Bloom: Oh no. Drew: But I guess that’s just what it’s like for AIs these days now, so. Bloom: I have no idea what it’s like to be an AI. I hope it’s enjoyable. It’s great to be here. Drew: Yeah, thanks so much. That was Joseph Bloom from the U.K. AI Security Institute. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. You’ve been listening to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. Tune in next time.

title: How Smugglers Get Expensive Memory Chips to China from South Korea
content: For an illustration of how porous U.S. restrictions on the shipment of AI chips to China can be, consider a technique that has begun to catch on among smugglers involving a key type of memory chip. While U.S. export regulations ban the shipment of high-bandwidth memory chips on their own to China, including from countries like South Korea, those rules have a loophole that allows the sales of those memory chips if they’re packaged together on plates with cheap server processors whose performance falls below the export restriction threshold. That’s because the computing power of the package gets determined by the server processor, not the memory chips, according to the rules. In recent years, smugglers have begun regularly shipping such chip packages to China, where technicians heat them up until the solder softens. The workers then pry off the stacks of memory, which is essential to powering advanced AI chips, and toss out the server processors. The separation is a delicate operation with a high failure rate. Heat the package too fast or for too long and the memory stack inside warps and cracks. Smugglers take the risk because the potential rewards are so big. The high-bandwidth memory chips then often end up being sold to customers of Huawei Technologies. Huawei has recently told some clients that a large share of its next flagship AI chip, the Ascend 960DT, which the company says doubles the performance of its current chips and will be one of the most powerful processor China can make, will run in large part on high-bandwidth memory produced by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, according to two people familiar with Huawei’s supply chain—because Huawei’s domestic suppliers can’t make enough of the memory. And since U.S. rules have prevented Huawei from being able to buy the memory chips it needs from the two South Korean companies, and the company’s manufacturing partners can’t produce enough on its own, Huawei has told some customers who ordered its AI chips to source the memory chips themselves. That sends the customers to the smugglers, who have come up with the server processor decoy trick to exploit the loophole in U.S. rules, which have restricted the exports of high-bandwidth memory to China since late 2024. The precise extent of the memory smuggling efforts isn’t clear, but people in China’s chip industry say it has become a vital tool for addressing one of the biggest bottlenecks to China’s AI ambitions. High-bandwidth memory unlocks an AI chip’s maximum processing power because of its ability to transfer data at lightning-fast speed. Without it, even the best AI chips become useless. But the smuggling also exposes the frailty at the heart of Beijing’s bid to build a self-reliant AI industry. China has spent years steering its tech companies toward homegrown AI chips. Huawei has delivered chips good enough to run Chinese open-source models efficiently , such as those developed by DeepSeek. But there’s a global shortage of high-bandwidth memory, little of which is made in China. Samsung and SK Hynix together hold more than 80% of the global market for those chips. Training the largest AI models, in particular, requires pairing high-bandwidth memory with powerful AI processors like those from Nvidia . Without enough of it, China is limited in how many large AI models companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot can continue to train and deploy, and therefore whether it can close the AI performance gap with the U.S. This account of how South Korean-made high-bandwidth memory reaches China is based on interviews with several smugglers in the trade as well as Huawei customers and other people familiar with its supply chain. Why Huawei Needs Memory from Abroad Huawei has said that its Ascend 960DT, to be released in the first quarter of next year, would double the memory bandwidth and capacity of its current AI processor. The company has high hopes for the new chip, and is working closely with DeepSeek to make it usable for pre-training , the most compute-intensive part of developing AI models. DeepSeek previously only used Nvidia chips for that. One of the main memory producers for years has been Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit, a U.S.-sanctioned memory chipmaker that has supplied Huawei for years. But Fujian Jinhua’s products are years behind those of the South Korean companies, and it can’t produce enough to meet Huawei’s customers needs, the two people said. ChangXin Memory Technologies, China’s biggest memory maker, is pushing to produce HBM3E, a previous generation of high-bandwidth memory chip that Nvidia used for its Blackwell chips and the hottest commodity in the smuggling trade. But CXMT too is years behind the South Korean companies and struggles with low yields—the share of output that actually works as intended—making the production costly, The Information has reported . To compensate for the high cost and short supply of high-bandwidth memory, Huawei in recent months told some clients it was raising the suggested price of the Ascend 950DT, the most powerful AI chip it currently sells, to more than 250,000 yuan, or about $37,000. That chip delivers half of the raw speed of Nvidia’s H100, a chip launched in 2022, but the price hike makes it cost the same as the newer B200, which Nvidia started shipping to customers last year. The scarcity leaves the black market as the only option for most Chinese AI firms to source high-bandwidth memory for local AI servers. For Samsung and SK Hynix, that is a headache. U.S. rules bar both from selling advanced high-bandwidth memory to China. A flagship Chinese AI chip built on their memory would invite Washington’s scrutiny. (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which produces the vast majority of the world’s most powerful AI chips, was probed by the U.S. government after chips it made were found in Huawei’s products in 2024. The U.S. later ordered TSMC to halt all AI chip shipments to China.) SK Hynix said it is “fully committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations,” including U.S. and South Korean export control regulations, and that it has not supplied products to Huawei since U.S. export restrictions took effect in 2020. After the story was published, Samsung said it “strictly complies with the export regulations set forth by the U.S. government,” adding that the company doesn’t comment its relationships with customers. Huawei and Fujian Jinhua didn’t respond to requests for comments. The Decoy That Gets the Chips Out of South Korea One memory smuggler controls a firm that, on paper, is an ordinary chip design company. In his 40s and fluent in both Chinese and Korean, the smuggler has spent most of his career working in the South Korean semiconductor industry. He is well versed in Korean business culture. He bows at the right depth, pours beverages for others before himself and always waits to be spoken before inserting himself into a conversation. The smuggler’s firm purposefully designs mediocre chips. They are too cheap and low-performing for any customers to want in their data centers, but they give him an excuse to order the best high-bandwidth memory in South Korea. The advanced memory is connected onto a silicon-based plate with the smuggler’s mundane processors by a handful of specialized packagers in Taiwan, South Korea and Southeast Asia. From there, the chip packages are prepared for export under the processor’s classification code in customs declarations, then shipped to Hong Kong before crossing the border to mainland China in the luggage of paid couriers, the trunks of cars or the bags of commuters that cross the border everyday. Once the chip packages arrive in China, they are shipped to the workshop run by the smuggler’s associates who pry off the valuable memory. That then gets sent to a chip broker in Shenzhen who spends his days matching buyers with suppliers. Three years in the smuggling trade have done well for the broker. He sports luxury clothing with logos visible from across the room and, though only 20-something, appears wise beyond his years. The broker joined the trade after a stint at a chip company that left him with something more valuable than a salary: contacts across Asia who know how to pull Samsung and SK Hynix memory out of legitimate supply chains. He doesn’t call himself a smuggler. He sees what he does as a patriotic service. “Contributing to the motherland,” he said. Surging demand has sent prices through the roof. “A year ago a single HBM3E unit changed hands in China for several hundred dollars. Today it’s about $4,000,” he said. An AI chip package needs six to eight of them, so memory alone adds $24,000 to $32,000 to the bill before a buyer pays for the AI chip itself, the server and the power to run them in a data center. Other Sources of Memory Supply in China The smuggler’s repackaged stacks are only one of the supply channels. The rest of what the broker in Shenzhen sells comes from three places, each with its own gamble. The first is salvage. Workshops buy older or used graphics processing units, the AI chips made by Nvidia and others, heat up the boards and lift the memory stacks like tiles off a roof. The supply is plentiful but mostly a generation behind, and it arrives with no records: Nobody can say how many hours each stack has already spent running in data centers already. The second is orphaned inventory. Chip designers in the U.S. and other countries order memory months in advance, but they may change a design, kill a project, delay a launch or cut planned volumes. This leaves design firms holding memory they paid for but no longer need. Much of it finds its way onto the black market, where brokers are waiting with cash. The third is hoarding. Some distributors in the industry manage to get a bit of inventory from the limited supply of high-bandwidth memory that doesn’t go to Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and other major chip designers. The distributors sit on their stock and watch the price climb. The Shenzhen broker is critical of the hoarders, while conceding he has no leverage either. “There’s nothing we can do about these greedy guys,” he said. Regardless of the source, getting the memory out of South Korea is the hardest and most expensive step. Seoul inspects high-tech exports closely, and high-bandwidth memory sits near the top of its watch list. South Korea’s customs service said in July that it had caught 770 billion won ($560 million) worth of trade-security violations as of May, already more than the record year seen in the entire 2025. Of that, a third involved strategic goods shipped without permits or under false declarations, the category that covers advanced chips. The smuggler who orders the memory chips from South Korea says his route sidesteps most of that, but he sees the urgency to wash his hands because of the influx of imitators. “The route I use is now shared by multiple other vendors. The more of us there are, the easier it is for regulators to spot,” he said. “South Korean and U.S. enforcement is going to tighten. I’m planning to sell my majority stake in the company next year.”

title: Apple’s Slowdown
content: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, has learned from the best. The script for his first earnings call on Monday was so full of marketing palaver about Apple products, and so lacking in information, that Ternus’ predecessor, Tim Cook, must have been glowing with pride. Perhaps after seeing investors freak out last week when other big tech firms reported earnings squeezed by AI investments, Ternus was determined to bore Wall Street into submission. Alas! Finance chief Kevan Parekh woke listeners from their Ternus-induced slumber by projecting 7% to 10% growth in revenue for the December quarter, a marked slowdown from the 12% growth in the September period. Meanwhile, he projected a drop in Apple’s gross margin, thanks to rising costs of memory. Apple shares promptly traded down, falling as much as 4% in after-hours trading. Parekh blamed limited component supplies for the expected revenue slowdown: Apple can’t make as many of its devices as it could sell. But that may not be the only explanation. In the September quarter—which is usually a quiet one for iPhone sales because shoppers are waiting for the new model—iPhone sales surged 17%, the company reported Monday. The likeliest explanation is that buyers opted to grab the 2025 model rather than wait for the iPhone 18 Pro, which came out in late September, both because Apple had hinted at a price increase and because chatter suggested the new phone would be only marginally better than the 17 Pro. Assuming that’s true, iPhone Pro sales will be weaker in the December quarter than is typically the case. Sure, Apple’s new foldable phone, the Duo, which went on sale in late October, should offset the slowdown in the Pro. But as the Duo retails for $2,000-plus, roughly double the price of regular iPhones, consumer demand is likely limited. It also probably won’t help that social media has been full of complaints about cracking screens in the Duo. Apple will surely iron out the hardware kinks over time, but there have been so many reports of the problem that some buyers will likely hold off for now. Apple’s revenue outlook is likely not the biggest worry for investors. The company is still grappling with soaring memory prices, as well as the reality that it can no longer dictate to chipmakers the volume of chips it wants delivered, thanks to AI chip designer Nvidia grabbing much of the manufacturing capacity. Meanwhile, growth in Apple’s services business is slowing as a result of a tougher market for mobile gaming and regulator-forced changes in the company’s App Store business. Apple’s business remains solid, but things are bumpier than they have been. Lumentum’s Not So Marvell-ous Deal Investors are in a skeptical mood right now. Take their reaction to Marvell Technology’s announcement on Monday that it would buy Lumentum by issuing a large bunch of its shares. Unfortunately, Marvell shares tanked 12.7% on Monday. Lumentum’s shares ended up falling even further, closing well below the theoretical value of Marvell’s offer. What’s going on? Lumentum is certainly a hot property—its revenue nearly doubled in its last fiscal year, thanks to the popularity of the lasers it sells, which can move data within data centers faster than copper wires. But investors are jittery about the staying power of the investment surge in AI data centers, which makes them nervous about Lumentum’s prospects. Indeed, while Lumentum shares rocketed as high as $1,100 last month, from below $200 a year ago, the stock traded down in recent weeks to $840 by Friday. Marvell may not have won over investors with its frothy marketing pitch that the combination of the two companies would be more than the sum of the parts. Marvell does a bunch of things, including chip design, but it has been expanding in the optical connection business. In a presentation to investors on Monday, it estimated its total addressable market—the potential size of the business it could get—at $400 billion, while it put Lumentum’s TAM at $90 billion. Together, the two have a TAM of $550 billion, Marvell CEO Matt Murphy claimed. Yes, 1+1=3. Amusingly, Marvell—perhaps anticipating the investor reaction—came up with a novel way of calculating the value of the deal for shareholders. Marvell claimed the terms “implied” an enterprise value for Lumentum of $115 billion, which it said represented a price per Lumentum share of $1,132. That looks too high, though. Using Friday’s close, Marvell’s deal values Lumentum at closer to $90 billion (and lower on Monday). How did Marvell get to $115 billion? My colleague Valida Pau hears that Marvell might be calculating the number by using its price of $251 a share from last Wednesday, before Bloomberg and The Information reported the talks . That seems a bit of a stretch. Given that Marvell has told Lumentum shareholders they’ll get 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share they own, there’s no need for that kind of mental gymnastics. Simply look at the Marvell price and do the math! As of Marvell’s close on Monday, the value of the offer was $771.08 a share, or below $80 billion in total. title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
content:
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
Borrowing from disciplines like economics could help AI safety researchers control AI models, even if they don’t understand them.
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.
Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.
An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.
In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.
A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).
Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.
The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.
A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”
Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.
During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.
There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.
Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.
Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”
One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.
It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.
“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.
Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)
Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?
“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

Das OFFIS – Institut für Informatik in Oldenburg und die California State University, Los Angeles (Cal State LA) haben eine Forschungs- und Hochschulpartnerschaft geschlossen. Im Mittelpunkt stehen künstliche Intelligenz, Geodatenanalyse und die Widerstandsfähigkeit kritischer Infrastrukturen wie Energiesysteme gegenüber Naturgefahren und cyber-physischen Bedrohungen. Erstes gemeinsames Vorhaben ist das Projekt GUARDIAN, das als Antrag für das NATO-Programm „Science for Peace and Security“ vorbereitet wird. Es soll untersucht werden, wie KI-Agenten auf unbekannte, folgenschwere Situationen reagieren, die im Training nicht vorkamen.
Das OFFIS - Institut für Informatik in Oldenburg und die Cal State LA in Kalifornien haben eine neue Forschungs- und Hochschulpartnerschaft ins Leben gerufen, deren Schwerpunkte auf künstlicher Intelligenz, Geodatenanalyse und der Widerstandsfähigkeit kritischer Infrastrukturen liegen. Die Zusammenarbeit bringt zwei Institutionen mit sich ergänzenden Stärken zusammen, um Herausforderungen anzugehen, denen Energiesysteme und andere wesentliche Versorgungsdienste gegenüberstehen – darunter cyber-physische Bedrohungen und Naturgefahren.
Diese Kooperation spiegelt die gemeinsame Vision von Vivian Sultan, Professorin für Informationssysteme an der Cal State LA, und Eric MSP Veith, wissenschaftlicher Leiter des Forschungs- und Entwicklungsbereichs für Energie am OFFIS, wider. Beide sind für ihre führende Rolle in den Bereichen Geowissenschaften, künstliche Intelligenz und Resilienz von Infrastrukturen anerkannt. Ihr Engagement für die Förderung internationaler Forschung und die Schaffung sinnvoller Möglichkeiten für Studierende und Lehrende bildete die Grundlage für diese Partnerschaft und prägte die Ausrichtung dieser ersten gemeinsamen Initiative.
Die Vereinbarung wurde von Arun Aryal, dem Vorsitzenden des Fachbereichs für Informationssysteme der Cal State LA, und Seiji Steimetz, dem Dekan des College of Business and Economics, unterstützt. Sultan, Aryal und Steimetz unterzeichneten die Absichtserklärung im Namen der Cal State LA. „Vielen Dank für die außerordentliche Arbeit, die in den Aufbau dieser Partnerschaft geflossen ist“, sagte Heather Lattimer, Prorektorin und Vizepräsidentin für akademische Angelegenheiten an der Cal State LA. „Es ist spannend zu sehen, wie eine so starke Zusammenarbeit Gestalt annimmt. Ich freue mich darauf, die Fortschritte dieser wichtigen Initiative zu verfolgen.“
Im Rahmen der Vereinbarung werden Sultan und Veith als Hauptansprechpartner fungieren. Sie werden gemeinsame Aktivitäten koordinieren, die Kommunikation zwischen den Einrichtungen aufrechterhalten und die Zusammenarbeit leiten, während diese auf weitere Forschungs- und Bildungsprogramme ausgeweitet wird.
Veith besuchte die Cal State LA vom 9. September bis zum 7. Oktober dieses Jahres. Am 30. September hielt er einen Vortrag zum Thema „KI jenseits der Trainingsverteilung: Was Kühlschränke und Waldbrände gemeinsam haben und was wir dagegen tun können“. „Als Gastwissenschaftler an der Cal State LA habe ich diese Zusammenarbeit als einen der bereicherndsten Aspekte meiner beruflichen Laufbahn erlebt“, sagte Veith. „Die Unterstützung, die Kollegialität und das gemeinsame Zielbewusstsein haben diese Erfahrung zu etwas ganz Besonderem gemacht. OFFIS setzt seit mehr als 35 Jahren Forschungsergebnisse aus der Informatik in praktische Lösungen um, und unsere Energieabteilung zählt zu den größten Zentren für Energieinformatik in Europa. Ich bin dankbar für diese Gelegenheit und freue mich darauf, unsere Arbeit an unseren Kernthemen fortzusetzen.“
Das erste Projekt im Rahmen der Partnerschaft ist GUARDIAN, was für „Geospatial Unseen-event Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Defense and Infrastructure Adaptation“ steht. GUARDIAN wird derzeit als Antrag für das Programm „Science for Peace and Security“ der NATO vorbereitet. Das Projekt zielt darauf ab, georäumliche Informationen mit fortschrittlichen KI-Methoden zu kombinieren, um zu untersuchen, wie kritische Infrastrukturen Naturgefahren und hybriden Bedrohungen besser standhalten können. Der Forschungsschwerpunkt liegt darauf, wie KI-Agenten auf unbekannte, folgenschwere Bedingungen reagieren, anstatt nur auf Situationen, die während des Trainings auftreten. GUARDIAN befindet sich aktuell noch in der Phase der Antragstellung.
„Es war mir eine Ehre, mit Kollegen zusammenzuarbeiten, die sich ebenso für die Förderung der wissenschaftlichen Forschung und die Stärkung kritischer Infrastrukturen engagieren“, sagte Sultan. „Unsere Zusammenarbeit mit OFFIS vereint Fachwissen, das für Gemeinden und Infrastrukturbetreiber, die mit immer komplexeren Gefahren konfrontiert sind, einen echten Unterschied machen kann. GUARDIAN ist erst der Anfang, und ich bin gespannt darauf, was wir gemeinsam erreichen werden.“
Die Zusammenarbeit stützt sich auf die Expertise der Cal State LA in den Bereichen Geografische Informationssysteme, räumliche Analytik, Energieinformatik und kalifornische Gefahren-Daten. Das OFFIS bringt seine Stärken in den Bereichen künstliche Intelligenz, Simulation, Sicherheit cyber-physischer Systeme und europäische Stromnetzforschung ein. Zusammen bilden diese Kompetenzen eine solide Grundlage, um ortsspezifisches Gefahrenwissen mit fortschrittlichen Methoden zur Prüfung und Verbesserung der Widerstandsfähigkeit von Infrastrukturen zu verknüpfen.

Hochschule Nordhausen eröffnet Double-Degree-Programm mit der Shanxi Datong University und knüpft neue Kontakte in Shanghai
Nordhausen, 3. November 2026. Sechs Semester in China, das letzte Studienjahr am Südharz – und am Ende ein Bachelor beider Hochschulen: Mit diesem Modell will die Hochschule Nordhausen (HSN) künftig jährlich bis zu 40 Studierende für Elektrotechnik und Informatik gewinnen. Im Oktober hat die HSN gemeinsam mit der Shanxi Datong University das Double-Degree-Programm in Datong offiziell eröffnet.
Die Reise führte von Peking über die Provinz Shanxi bis nach Shanghai. In Datong standen Gespräche mit der Partnerhochschule (Shanxi Datong University, 40.000 Studierende) und die Eröffnungsfeier mit den ersten Jahrgangsstudierenden des Double-Degree-Programms im Mittelpunkt. Ihr Weg nach Nordhausen ist klar strukturiert: Deutsch bis Niveau B2 in Datong, ein Auswahlverfahren durch die HSN vor Ort, ein Sprachintensivkurs im Sommer in Deutschland bis zum C1-Niveau und schließlich das Abschlussjahr plus Bachelorarbeit in Nordhausen.
„Der Schlüssel für den Erfolg ist die Sprache“, sagt Prof. Dr. Cordula Borbe, Vizepräsidentin für Studium und Lehre der HSN. „Wer in Nordhausen ankommt, soll hier nicht nur studieren, sondern mitreden, Anschluss finden und im besten Fall bleiben.“ Gemeinsam mit der Partnerhochschule will die HSN daher den Deutschunterricht in Datong weiter ausbauen. Maßgeblich getragen wird das Projekt von Jiayi Wang, Professorin für Elektrotechnik/Leistungselektronik und Prof. Dr. Mario Schölzel, Professor für Prozessoren und digitale Systeme an der Hochschule Nordhausen, die die Zusammenarbeit mit der Partnerhochschule koordinieren.
In Peking stand zudem ein Termin bei der Akademischen Prüfstelle (APS) auf dem Programm, die die Studienvoraussetzungen chinesischer Bewerberinnen und Bewerber für Deutschland prüft. In Shanghai entstanden neue Kontakte, die Türen zu weiteren Hochschulen in Ost- und Südchina öffnen – in Ingenieurfächern ebenso wie in der Sozialen Arbeit.

Mit einem Forschungsvolumen von 6,5 Millionen Euro hat die Agentur für Innovation in der Cybersicherheit GmbH (Cyberagentur) am 28. Oktober 2026 das Forschungsprogramm „Artificial Intelligence as Operating System“ (AI-as-OS) ausgeschrieben. Im Mittelpunkt steht die Entwicklung zukunftsfähiger KI-nativer Betriebssysteme. Teilnahmeanträge sind bis zum 10. Dezember 2026 möglich.
Künstliche Intelligenz übernimmt zunehmend eigenständig Aufgaben in digitalen Systemen. Namhafte Technologieunternehmen integrieren KI bereits tief in ihre Betriebssysteme und Hardware. Damit gewinnt eine grundlegende Sicherheitsfrage an Bedeutung: Wie lassen sich Rechnersysteme realisieren und schützen, wenn Künstliche Intelligenz nicht länger nur als Zusatzfunktion integriert wird, sondern künftig selbst zentrale Steuerungsfunktionen eines Betriebssystems übernimmt?
Mit AI-as-OS geht die Cyberagentur über die Integration von KI als reines Add-On hinaus. Das Forschungsprogramm soll untersuchen, ob KI selbst zum zentralen Steuerungselement eines Rechnersystems werden kann und welche Sicherheitsarchitektur dafür erforderlich wäre. Im Mittelpunkt stehen drei Forschungsbereiche:
• KI-zentrierte Betriebssystemarchitekturen,
• KI-native Kernmechanismen zur Ressourcen- und Prozesssteuerung sowie
• neue Ansätze für Kontrolle, Sicherheit und Stabilität dieser Systeme.
Wirtschaft und Wissenschaft arbeiten intensiv an der Erweiterung bestehender Systemarchitekturen durch intelligente Technologien.. Damit wird eine Frage immer dringlicher: Wie stellen wir sicher, dass Künstliche Intelligenz, die zunehmend tief in die Steuerung eines Rechnersystems eingreift, selbst sicher und kontrollierbar bleibt? „Mit AI-as-OS wollen wir genau diese Grundlagen erforschen. Wir hoffen, dass aus dem zurückliegenden Partnering Event leistungsfähige Forschungskonsortien hervorgegangen sind, die sich nun mit wissenschaftlich fundierten, innovativen und auch unkonventionellen Ansätzen an unserer Ausschreibung beteiligen“, erklärt Dr. Philippe Krajsic, Forschungsreferent Schlüsseltechnologien der Cyberagentur.
Grundlagenforschung für die Cybersicherheit von morgen
Ob KI-native Betriebssysteme technisch realisierbar sind und gegenüber bestehenden Architekturen Vorteile hinsichtlich Sicherheit, Effizienz und Stabilität bieten, ist bislang offen. Genau diese Fragen bilden den Forschungsgegenstand. Die Ergebnisse sollen langfristig neue Ansätze für die Absicherung digitaler Infrastrukturen ermöglichen und technologische Kompetenzen für die digitale Souveränität Deutschlands und Europas aufbauen.
Für das Forschungsprogramm stehen 6,5 Millionen Euro ohne Umsatzsteuer als geschätztes Auftragsvolumen zur Verfügung. Die vorkommerzielle Auftragsvergabe in Anlehnung an eine Innovationspartnerschaft richtet sich an Forschungseinrichtungen, Unternehmen, Start-ups und interdisziplinäre Forschungskonsortien.

Die Ergebnisse könnten den Weg für neue Mikroskopie-Techniken ebnen. Die Chip-Technologie könnte zudem in vielen Bereichen zum Einsatz kommen – von der Datenverarbeitung bis zur Satellitenkommunikation.
